Work each exercise on paper (or in the lesson notebook), type your answer into the box to check it, and open the solution to compare your working. Answers can be decimals (round to 3 places), fractions like 2/3 or percentages like 75%. Every answer has been checked with Python. For hands-on coding practice, the lesson notebook ends with two coding challenges: fill in one missing line and an automatic check tells you whether it's right.

Exercise 1By hand

Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability their sum is 7?

Check your answer:

Show solution
36 equally likely outcomes; 6 give 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). Probability $6/36 = 1/6$.
Exercise 2By hand

For the data $2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9$, compute the mean, the variance (divide by $n$) and the standard deviation.

Check your answers:

Show solution
Mean $= 40/8 = 5$. Squared deviations: $9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16$ → sum 32. Variance $= 32/8 = 4$. Standard deviation $= 2$.
Exercise 3By hand

20% of emails are spam. The word "winner" appears in 50% of spam and 5% of normal emails. An email contains "winner". What is $P(\text{spam} \mid \text{winner})$?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$P(\text{winner}) = 0.5\times0.2 + 0.05\times0.8 = 0.10 + 0.04 = 0.14$.
$P(\text{spam} \mid \text{winner}) = 0.10/0.14 \approx 0.714$ — about 71%.
Exercise 4By hand

Test scores are normal with $\mu = 70$, $\sigma = 10$. What is the z-score of 85? Between which two scores do about 95% of students fall?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$z = (85 - 70)/10 = 1.5$. About 95% lie within $2\sigma$: between $70 - 20 = 50$ and $70 + 20 = 90$.
Exercise 5Intermediate

Calls to a help desk follow a Poisson distribution with an average of 2 per hour. What is the probability of exactly 4 calls in an hour? (Use $P(k) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$.)

Check your answer:

Show solution
$P(4) = e^{-2}\,2^4/4! = 0.1353 \times 16/24 = 0.0902$.
Exercise 6Intermediate

With a Beta(2, 2) prior, you observe 3 successes and 7 failures. Give the posterior's parameters, its mean, and the MAP estimate.

Check your answers — for several numbers, separate them with commas:

Show solution
Posterior Beta($2+3$, $2+7$) = Beta(5, 9). Mean $= 5/14 \approx 0.357$. MAP $= (5-1)/(5+9-2) = 4/12 \approx 0.333$. (The MLE would be $3/10 = 0.3$; the prior pulls both towards 0.5.)
Exercise 7Intermediate

A model is right on 850 of 1,000 test examples. Using the CLT, give its accuracy's standard error and an approximate 95% confidence interval.

Check your answers — for several numbers, separate them with commas:

Show solution
$\hat{p} = 0.85$, $\text{SE} = \sqrt{0.85 \times 0.15/1000} = 0.0113$. Interval: $0.85 \pm 1.96 \times 0.0113 = 0.85 \pm 0.0221$, so about $[0.828,\ 0.872]$.
Exercise 8Intermediate

An A/B test has 200 conversions out of 4,000 for A and 250 out of 4,000 for B. Compute the pooled rate and the z-statistic.

Check your answers:

Show solution
$\hat{p}_A = 0.05$, $\hat{p}_B = 0.0625$, pooled $\hat{p} = 450/8000 = 0.05625$. SE $= \sqrt{0.05625 \times 0.94375 \times (2/4000)} = 0.005152$. $z = 0.0125/0.005152 \approx 2.43$, so $p \approx 0.015$.
Exercise 9Code · intermediate

Change the bootstrap code to estimate a 95% interval for the mean of the 60 prices instead of the median, keeping the same random seed. Compare it with $\bar{x} \pm 1.96\,s/\sqrt{n}$.

Check your answer — for several numbers, separate them with commas:

Show solution
Replace np.median with np.mean in the resampling loop. The bootstrap gives about $[68.6,\ 88.3]$ and the formula about $[68.2,\ 88.4]$: very similar, because the CLT already applies at $n = 60$. The bootstrap's advantage shows for statistics like the median, where no simple formula exists.
Practice with new numbers

Part 2 · Learning from labelled data · ~45 min

Lesson 5: Data, Features & Generalization

Datasets, train/validation/test splits, overfitting vs underfitting, and cross-validation.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Explain generalization and why training error can mislead
  • Recognise underfitting and overfitting from training and test errors
  • Split data correctly into training, validation and test sets
  • Run and interpret k-fold cross-validation, and avoid data leakage
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 1: What Is Machine Learning? — A model maps features $x$ to a prediction $\hat{y}$. Training adjusts its parameters to make a loss (such as MSE) small, and the real goal is doing well on new data.
  • Lesson 4: Probability & Statistics — Probabilities run from 0 to 1. Bayes' theorem turns $P(B\mid A)$ into $P(A\mid B)$. Mean and standard deviation summarise data; the z-score $(x-\mu)/\sigma$ standardises it.

Where this fits: Before building models, you need a fair way to test them. Everything you learn here is reused in every later lesson whenever we evaluate a model.

1.The real goal: doing well on data you've never seen

In Lesson 1 we said learning means "find the parameters that make the loss small". That's true — but there's a catch. A model's job is not to describe the data it was trained on; we already know the answers for that data. Its job is to make good predictions on new data: next month's houses, tomorrow's emails, a patient who walks in next week.

This ability is called generalization, and it is the single most important idea in machine learning. This lesson explains how data is organised, why a model can fool you by memorising, and the techniques everyone uses to measure generalization honestly.

Analogy: the exam

A teacher gives students 50 practice questions. Student A memorises the 50 answers. Student B learns the methods behind them. On the practice questions both score 100%. On the real exam — new questions — Student A fails and Student B passes. A model that memorises its training data is Student A. We want Student B, and we need a fair exam to tell them apart.

2.What a dataset looks like

A typical supervised dataset is a table: one row per example, one column per feature, plus a label column. From Lesson 2, the features form a matrix $X$ of shape $n \times d$ ($n$ examples, $d$ features) and the labels form a vector $\mathbf{y}$ of length $n$.

Kinds of features

  • Numerical — measured quantities: size in m², age, temperature. Can be continuous (any value) or discrete (counts like number of bedrooms).
  • Categorical — one of a fixed set of categories: colour (red/green/blue), city, product type. Computers need these converted to numbers (Lesson 20 shows how).
  • Ordinal — categories with a natural order: small < medium < large; ratings 1–5 stars.
  • Binary — yes/no, true/false, encoded as 1/0.
  • Text, images, audio — unstructured data that must be turned into numbers first (e.g. word counts, pixel values).

Good data matters more than clever algorithms

A model can only learn patterns that are actually in the data. Common problems:

  • Missing values — blanks in the table.
  • Errors and outliers — a house listed at 5 m², a typo adding three zeros to a price.
  • Too few examples — the model can't tell real patterns from coincidences.
  • Unrepresentative data — training only on city flats, then predicting rural farmhouses.
  • Wrong labels — mislabelled examples teach the wrong lesson.
The i.i.d. assumption

Most ML assumes examples are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.): each one is drawn from the same underlying source, without depending on the others. In plain words: the future data will look like the past data. When that stops being true — fashions change, a new competitor arrives — models quietly get worse. This is called distribution shift or drift.

3.Underfitting, good fit and overfitting

Imagine data that follows a gentle curve, plus some random noise. We can fit models of different complexity (flexibility):

  • Underfitting — the model is too simple to capture the pattern, e.g. a straight line through a curve. It's wrong on the training data and on new data. High error everywhere.
  • Good fit — the model captures the real pattern and ignores the noise. Low error on training data, and similarly low on new data.
  • Overfitting — the model is so flexible that it bends to pass through every training point, noise included. Training error is tiny, but on new data it makes wild mistakes.
Definitions

Training error: the loss measured on the data the model was trained on.
Test (generalization) error: the loss on new data the model has never seen.
Overfitting: training error ≪ test error. Underfitting: both are high.

Training error almost always keeps falling as complexity grows — a more flexible model can always fit the training points better. Test error, however, falls at first and then rises again once the model starts fitting noise. The sweet spot is the bottom of the test-error curve.

4.Try it: watch overfitting happen

The blue dots are training data and the orange dots are test data, both drawn from the same hidden curve plus noise. The green line is a polynomial of the chosen degree fitted to the training dots only. Increase the degree and watch: training error keeps shrinking, but past a point the curve starts wiggling to chase individual points, and the test error grows.

A polynomial of degree $k$ is $\hat{y} = w_0 + w_1x + w_2x^2 + \dots + w_kx^k$. With 12 training points, a degree-11 polynomial has 12 parameters and can pass through every point exactly — a perfect training score and a terrible model.

5.The train / validation / test split

The fix is simple and non-negotiable: evaluate on data the model did not train on. Before doing anything else, split your data:

SetUsed forTypical share
Training setFitting the model's parameters.~70%
Validation setComparing models and choosing settings (like the polynomial degree).~15%
Test setOne final, honest estimate of performance on new data.~15%

Google's Machine Learning Crash Course uses exactly this 70 / 15 / 15 illustration. The exact percentages vary; with very large datasets the validation and test sets can be a smaller share.

Why a separate validation set?

If you try 20 different models and pick whichever scores best on the test set, you have used the test set to make decisions — you've tuned to it. Its score is now optimistic. The test set must stay locked away until the very end. Choices are made on the validation set; the test set gives the final verdict. Validation and test sets also "wear out": the more you reuse them, the less trustworthy they become.

Rules for a good split:

  • Shuffle randomly before splitting (unless the data is a time series — then train on the past and test on the future).
  • Make sure the test set is representative — the same mix of cases as real-world data.
  • No duplicates between training and test sets, or you're testing on memorised examples.
  • For classification, use a stratified split so each set has the same proportion of each class.

6.k-fold cross-validation

Picture itJudging a restaurant by one meal is risky: maybe the chef was off that night. Eat there five times and you know it far better. Cross-validation tests a model five times on five different slices of data for the same reason.

With a small dataset, a single validation split is unreliable: the score depends heavily on which examples happened to land in it. k-fold cross-validation uses the data more efficiently:

  1. Split the training data into $k$ equal parts called folds (commonly $k = 5$ or $10$).
  2. Train on $k-1$ folds and evaluate on the remaining fold.
  3. Repeat $k$ times, so each fold is the validation fold exactly once.
  4. Report the mean (and standard deviation) of the $k$ scores.
$$\text{CV score} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k} \text{score}_j$$
Worked example — 5-fold CV

A model's accuracy on the 5 validation folds: $0.82,\ 0.85,\ 0.80,\ 0.84,\ 0.84$.

Mean: $(0.82 + 0.85 + 0.80 + 0.84 + 0.84)/5 = 4.15/5 = 0.83$.

Deviations from the mean: $-0.01,\ 0.02,\ -0.03,\ 0.01,\ 0.01$. Squared: $0.0001,\ 0.0004,\ 0.0009,\ 0.0001,\ 0.0001$. Variance $= 0.0016/5 = 0.00032$, standard deviation $= \sqrt{0.00032} \approx 0.018$.

We report 0.83 ± 0.02. The ± tells you how much the score depends on the particular split — if two models differ by less than this, the difference may just be luck.

Make sense of it

The situation: You're choosing between models for a client and want a score you can trust, not one that depends on a lucky split.

What the result tells you: 0.83 is the model's average accuracy across five different validation folds. The ± 0.02 says the score moves by about two points depending on which data it's tested on.

What if…?

  • One bad fold. If the third fold scored 0.70 instead of 0.80, the mean drops to 0.81 and the standard deviation more than triples to 0.056. A big spread is a warning that the model is unstable or one fold is unusual.
  • A rival model scores 0.84, 0.86, 0.82, 0.85, 0.83: mean 0.84 ± 0.014. It's ahead by 0.01, less than the spread of either model — not convincing evidence that it's better.

Why it matters in ML: Every score you compute is an estimate from a sample. Reporting the spread stops you from "improving" a model by chasing noise, and a high spread across folds is a clue to overfitting or data problems.

Every example is used for validation exactly once and for training $k-1$ times. The cost: you train $k$ models instead of one. You still keep a separate test set for the very end.

Read the formulaCross-validation score
$$\text{CV score} = \htmlClass{fd-1}{\frac{1}{k}}\htmlClass{fd-2}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}}\htmlClass{fd-3}{\text{score}_j}$$
  • 1/k — average over the k folds
  • Σ — add up over every fold
  • scoreⱼ — the score when fold j is the validation set

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

7.Data leakage: the silent killer

Data leakage happens when information from outside the training data sneaks into training, making evaluation look better than reality. Classic examples:

  • Preprocessing before splitting. Computing the mean and standard deviation for standardisation (Lesson 4) on all data, including the test set. The model has indirectly "seen" the test data.
  • Features that contain the answer. Predicting whether a customer will cancel, using a column "cancellation fee charged".
  • Time travel. Using future information to predict the past, e.g. randomly splitting stock prices so the model trains on Wednesday to predict Tuesday.
  • Duplicates across train and test.
The golden rule

Split first. Then learn everything — scaling statistics, feature choices, model parameters — from the training data only, and merely apply it to validation and test data. scikit-learn's documentation states it directly: never call fit on the test data.

8.Putting it together

  1. Split off a test set and don't look at it.
  2. On the training set, use cross-validation (or a validation set) to compare models and settings.
  3. Pick the best, then retrain it on the full training set.
  4. Evaluate once on the test set and report that number.

9.In Python

This experiment reproduces the demo: fit polynomials of increasing degree and compare training and test error.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 30)
y = np.sin(x) + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 30)          # hidden curve + noise
X = x.reshape(-1, 1)                             # sklearn wants a 2D matrix

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=1)

for degree in [1, 3, 9, 12]:
    model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), LinearRegression())
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    train_mse = mean_squared_error(y_train, model.predict(X_train))
    test_mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
    print(f"degree {degree:2d}: train MSE {train_mse:.3f}   test MSE {test_mse:.3f}")

Output:

degree  1: train MSE 0.217   test MSE 0.188
degree  3: train MSE 0.041   test MSE 0.092
degree  9: train MSE 0.010   test MSE 0.250
degree 12: train MSE 0.006   test MSE 0.492

Degree 1 underfits: a straight line can't follow a sine wave, so both errors are high. Degree 3 fits well: both errors are low. As the degree rises to 9 and 12, training error keeps falling — but test error climbs to more than five times its best value. That's overfitting.

And 5-fold cross-validation in two lines:

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(3), LinearRegression())
scores = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
print(-scores.mean(), scores.std())     # mean MSE across the 5 folds, and its spread

(scikit-learn reports errors as negative numbers so that "higher is better" for every score; we flip the sign back.)

10.Running example: Chennai Homes

With only 12 houses, a single split leaves just 3 for testing — far too few to trust. Cross-validation uses every house for testing once: predicting price from size alone, the error per fold ranges from 8.9 to 20 lakh. That spread is a warning that such a small dataset gives noisy estimates.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
X, y = df[["size_m2"]], df["price_lakh"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
print(len(X_train), "train /", len(X_test), "test houses")
scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=4, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
print("MAE per fold:", (-scores).round(1), " mean:", round(-scores.mean(), 1))

Output:

9 train / 3 test houses
MAE per fold: [14.4  8.9 14.5 20. ]  mean: 14.4
Where this is used
  • Every serious ML project
  • Model competitions keep a hidden test set for exactly this reason

Choose it when: Always.

Think twice when: Never skip it: a model evaluated on its own training data tells you almost nothing.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythA high training score proves the model is good.

RealityOnly performance on data the model hasn't seen is evidence of generalization.

MythCross-validation replaces the test set.

RealityCross-validation is for choosing models and settings. You still need an untouched test set for the final, honest number.

Responsible AI · Bias starts in the data

A model can only be as fair as its data. Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019) found that a widely used US healthcare algorithm under-referred Black patients because it predicted future healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — and less had historically been spent on Black patients with the same needs. Ask who is missing from the data, how labels were produced, and whether people consented to their data being used. "Datasheets for Datasets" (Gebru et al.) is a useful checklist.

11.Questions beginners often ask

How big should the test set be?

Big enough that its score is stable — often 10–30% of the data. With millions of examples, 1% may be plenty.

Can I ever look at the test set?

Only at the very end, once. If you change the model after seeing the test score, that score is no longer an honest estimate.

What k should I use for cross-validation?

5 or 10 are common defaults. Larger k uses more data for training each time but costs more runs.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Tuning on the test set — then its score is no longer an honest estimate.
  • Preprocessing (scaling, imputing, selecting features) before splitting the data.
  • Splitting time-ordered data randomly, so the model trains on the future.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Validation set vs test set — Validate many times; test once.
  • Overfitting vs data leakage — Overfitting shows up in validation; leakage hides from it.
  • Cross-validation vs a train/test split — One opinion vs five.
  • Training error vs generalisation error — Grading yourself vs being graded.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Why do you need both a validation set and a test set?

The trap: "The test set is enough."

Every time you use a set to choose something (model, hyperparameters, threshold), its score becomes optimistically biased. The validation set absorbs that tuning; the untouched test set gives the final honest estimate. Use it once.

You select the 20 best features using all the data, then run 5-fold cross-validation. What's wrong?

The trap: Thinking cross-validation protects you automatically.

Leakage: feature selection has already seen the validation folds' labels, so the CV score is optimistic — sometimes wildly (it can find "predictive" features in pure noise). Every learned step, including selection, scaling and imputation, must happen inside each fold — use a Pipeline.

Your training error is higher than your validation error. Is something broken?

The trap: Assuming training error is always lower.

Not necessarily. Regularisation that's only active in training (dropout, data augmentation) makes training look worse; a small or easy validation set can score well by luck. It can also signal leakage or duplicates between the sets, so check.

Will collecting more data fix underfitting?

The trap: "More data always helps."

Mostly no. More data reduces variance (overfitting). An underfitting model is too simple; it needs more features, a more flexible model or less regularisation.

All 12 hidden questions for this lesson →

12.Key takeaways

  • The goal is generalization: good performance on new, unseen data.
  • Underfitting = too simple (both errors high). Overfitting = memorising noise (training error low, test error high).
  • Always split: train to fit, validation to choose, test once at the end.
  • k-fold cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate: report mean ± standard deviation.
  • Avoid data leakage: split first, fit everything on training data only.

13.Check your understanding

1. Training error 0.01, test error 2.5. What's happening?

A huge gap between low training error and high test error means the model memorised the training data: overfitting.

2. Training error 3.1, test error 3.3, and a simple model. What's the likely problem?

Both errors are high and similar: the model is too simple to capture the pattern — underfitting. Try a more flexible model or better features.

3. Which set should you use to choose between 10 candidate models?

Choices are made on validation data. The test set is reserved for one final, unbiased evaluation; the training score is too optimistic.

4. In 5-fold cross-validation, how many models are trained?

One per fold: each of the 5 folds takes a turn as the validation set.

5. You standardise all your data using its overall mean, then split into train and test. What's wrong?

The mean was computed partly from test data. Split first, compute statistics on the training set only, then apply them to the test set.

14.Going deeper: validation that you can trust

In plain wordsWhen the usual validation habits quietly break: tuning makes your best score look better than it really is (nested cross-validation fixes it), time series and repeated customers need special splits, learning curves tell you whether more data would help, and adversarial validation detects when new data no longer looks like your training data.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

The lesson above gives you the core habits: split your data, cross-validate, avoid leakage. This section covers the situations where those habits quietly break: when tuning itself inflates your score, when your rows aren't independent (time series, repeated customers), when you need to know whether more data would help, and when tomorrow's data no longer looks like yesterday's. Each one is a common cause of models that look great in testing and disappoint in production.

You'll need: k-fold cross-validation and data leakage from this lesson.

Tuning inflates scores: nested cross-validation

When you try many settings and keep the one with the best cross-validated score, that best score is optimistic. Some settings win partly by luck on these particular folds, the same way the best of 20 coin-flippers looks skilled. Lesson 4's "Going deeper" called this multiple testing. The honest fix is nested cross-validation:

  • An inner loop chooses the settings, using only the training part of each outer fold.
  • An outer loop scores the whole procedure ("tune, then fit") on data the tuning never saw.

Below, a support-vector classifier (Lesson 15) is tuned over 25 combinations of settings on a small, noisy dataset:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, cross_val_score, KFold
from sklearn.svm import SVC

# A small, noisy problem where tuning can easily "overfit the validation folds"
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=120, n_features=40, n_informative=4, flip_y=0.2, random_state=0)
grid = {"C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100], "gamma": [0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1]}
inner, outer = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1), KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=2)

search = GridSearchCV(SVC(), grid, cv=inner).fit(X, y)
print("best score inside the search (optimistic):", round(search.best_score_, 3))
nested = cross_val_score(GridSearchCV(SVC(), grid, cv=inner), X, y, cv=outer)
print("nested cross-validation (honest):        ", round(nested.mean(), 3))

Output:

best score inside the search (optimistic): 0.633
nested cross-validation (honest):         0.608

The search reports 0.633, but the nested estimate is 0.608. The gap grows with the number of settings you try and shrinks with more data. Nested CV is the right way to report a tuned model's performance. To build the final model, you still run the ordinary search on all the data. Nested CV tells you how well that recipe is likely to do.

When rows aren't independent: time and groups

Ordinary k-fold assumes each row is an independent draw. Two very common cases break that:

  • Time series. Neighbouring days look alike. A shuffled split puts Tuesday in training and Wednesday in validation, so the model just "remembers" the nearby level, which it won't be able to do for next month.
  • Groups. Several rows per customer, patient or house. If one customer's rows land on both sides of the split, the model learns that person rather than the pattern.

Here's a daily sales series that drifts slowly over time, scored both ways with a random forest (Lesson 14):

from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor

# Daily sales that drift slowly over time: neighbouring days look alike
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = np.arange(600)
trend = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 1, 600))                  # a slow random walk
Xt = np.column_stack([t, np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 7)])      # day number and weekday pattern
yt = trend + 3 * Xt[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 1, 600)

model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=0)
shuffled = cross_val_score(model, Xt, yt, cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0), scoring="r2")
forward = cross_val_score(model, Xt, yt, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5), scoring="r2")
print("shuffled k-fold R²:   ", round(shuffled.mean(), 3))
print("time-ordered split R²:", round(forward.mean(), 3))

Output:

shuffled k-fold R²:    0.957
time-ordered split R²: -0.609

Shuffled k-fold says $R^2 = 0.957$: superb. A time-ordered split (TimeSeriesSplit, which always trains on the past and validates on the future) says $-0.609$: worse than predicting the average. The random forest can't extrapolate a drifting trend at all, and the shuffled split hid that completely. For grouped data, the same idea is GroupKFold: all of one group's rows go to the same side of the split. For time series with groups, combine them. A useful rule: split the way the model will be used.

Learning curves: would more data help?

Collecting data is expensive, so it's worth checking first whether it would help. A learning curve trains on growing subsets of the data and plots training and validation scores against training-set size:

from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

Xb, yb = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
sizes, tr, va = learning_curve(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)), Xb, yb,
                               train_sizes=[0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0], cv=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
for s, a, b in zip(sizes, tr.mean(axis=1), va.mean(axis=1)):
    print(f"{s:4d} training examples: train accuracy {a:.3f}   validation accuracy {b:.3f}")

Output:

  22 training examples: train accuracy 1.000   validation accuracy 0.916
  45 training examples: train accuracy 0.991   validation accuracy 0.968
 113 training examples: train accuracy 0.995   validation accuracy 0.968
 227 training examples: train accuracy 0.989   validation accuracy 0.970
 455 training examples: train accuracy 0.989   validation accuracy 0.981

How to read it:

  • Big gap, validation still rising (high variance): more data is likely to help. Here, validation accuracy climbs from 0.916 with 22 examples to 0.981 with 455, and the gap to training (0.989) is now small.
  • Both curves low and close together (high bias): more data won't help much. You need a more flexible model or better features.
  • Both flat and close, both high: you're near the limit for this model and these features.

This is the bias–variance trade-off (Lesson 10) made visible. It answers a question that cross-validation alone can't.

When the world changes: distribution shift

All validation assumes future data comes from the same distribution as your training data. In practice it often drifts:

  • Covariate shift: the inputs change, but the relationship stays (a new city with bigger homes).
  • Label shift: the class balance changes (fraud rises during a holiday season).
  • Concept drift: the relationship itself changes (after a rule change, the same features mean something else).

A neat trick to detect the first kind is adversarial validation. Label training rows 0 and new rows 1, and train a classifier to tell them apart. If it can't (AUC near 0.5), the two look alike. If it can, the shift is real, and its feature importances show where it is.

from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

# Adversarial validation: can a model tell training rows from "production" rows?
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
train_rows = rng.normal(0, 1, size=(500, 3))
prod_same = rng.normal(0, 1, size=(500, 3))
prod_shift = rng.normal(0, 1, size=(500, 3)); prod_shift[:, 0] += 0.8   # one feature has drifted

cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
for name, prod in [("no shift", prod_same), ("feature 0 drifted", prod_shift)]:
    Xa = np.vstack([train_rows, prod]); ya = np.r_[np.zeros(500), np.ones(500)]
    clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=10, random_state=0)
    p = cross_val_predict(clf, Xa, ya, cv=cv, method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
    imp = clf.fit(Xa, ya).feature_importances_
    print(f"{name:18}: AUC {roc_auc_score(ya, p):.3f}   feature importances {imp.round(2)}")

Output:

no shift          : AUC 0.540   feature importances [0.34 0.34 0.32]
feature 0 drifted : AUC 0.695   feature importances [0.59 0.21 0.2 ]

With no shift, the AUC is 0.540, close to chance, and the importances are evenly spread. When feature 0 drifts by 0.8 standard deviations, the AUC jumps to 0.695 and feature 0's importance rises to 0.59, pointing straight at the culprit. In production, teams monitor this kind of drift continuously and retrain when it appears (Lesson 20).

A validation checklist

SituationUse
Reporting a tuned model's scoreNested CV, or a test set used once at the very end
Data ordered in timeTime-ordered splits (TimeSeriesSplit); never shuffle
Several rows per person, item or placeGroupKFold
Rare classesStratified splits (StratifiedKFold)
Deciding whether to collect more dataA learning curve
New data might differ from training dataAdversarial validation and drift monitoring
Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

What's nested cross-validation, and when do you need it?

The trap: Thinking the best grid-search score is an unbiased estimate.

Two loops: an inner CV chooses hyperparameters using only the training part of each outer fold, and the outer CV scores the whole "tune then fit" procedure on data the tuning never saw. You need it when you want an honest performance estimate for a tuned model and don't have a separate test set. The best inner score is biased upwards, more so with many settings and little data.

Your model scores R² = 0.95 in cross-validation but fails badly in production a month later. List likely causes.

The trap: Blaming bad luck.

Leakage (a feature that won't exist at prediction time, or preprocessing fitted on all data). A split that doesn't match use, such as shuffled folds on time-ordered data or the same customer on both sides. Distribution shift, where production inputs differ from training (check with adversarial validation). Overfitting to the validation set through many tuning rounds. Fix: time-based or group splits, pipelines, a final untouched test set and drift monitoring.

How do you decide whether collecting more data is worth it?

The trap: "More data always helps."

Plot a learning curve: train and validation scores against training-set size. If the validation score is still rising and there's a big gap to training (high variance), more data should help. If both are low and close together (high bias), more data won't, and you need better features or a more flexible model. You can extrapolate the curve's trend to estimate the gain.

What's the difference between covariate shift, label shift and concept drift?

The trap: Using "data drift" for all three.

Covariate shift: the distribution of inputs $P(x)$ changes but $P(y\mid x)$ stays the same. Label shift: the class balance $P(y)$ changes but $P(x\mid y)$ stays. Concept drift: the relationship $P(y\mid x)$ itself changes. Covariate shift can be detected without labels (adversarial validation, statistical tests on features); concept drift needs fresh labels to detect, and usually retraining to fix.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. You try 200 hyperparameter settings and report the best cross-validated score. That score is probably…

Picking the best of many includes some luck. Nested cross-validation (or an untouched test set) gives an honest estimate.

2. Which split suits forecasting next month's sales?

Split the way the model will be used: it will always predict the future from the past.

3. A learning curve shows training accuracy 0.99 and validation accuracy 0.80, with validation still rising as data grows. What's likely to help?

A large gap that is still closing is high variance: more data or a simpler (more regularized) model helps.

4. In adversarial validation, a classifier separates training rows from new rows with AUC 0.95. What does that mean?

If train and new rows were alike, telling them apart would be impossible (AUC ≈ 0.5).

5. Your dataset has 10 rows per patient. Which cross-validation should you use?

Keep each patient's rows together, so the model is scored on patients it has never seen.
