Lasso: $2 - 0.5 = 1.5$; $0.4 < 0.5$ so $0$; $-1 + 0.5 = -0.5$. Ridge: $2/1.5 = 1.333$, $0.4/1.5 = 0.267$, $-1/1.5 = -0.667$.
Exercise 6Intermediate

In a simulation, the average prediction at a test point is 4.2, the true value is 5.0, and predictions across training sets have standard deviation 0.6. The noise variance is 0.25. Compute bias², variance and the expected squared error at that point.

Check your answers:

Show solution
Bias² $= (4.2 - 5.0)^2 = 0.64$. Variance $= 0.6^2 = 0.36$. Expected error $= 0.64 + 0.36 + 0.25 = 1.25$.
Exercise 7Intermediate

Elastic net with $\lambda = 2$ and l1_ratio $\rho = 0.25$: what are the effective L1 and L2 penalty strengths, using $\lambda\rho\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1 + \lambda\frac{1-\rho}{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2^2$?

Check your answers:

Show solution
L1: $2 \times 0.25 = 0.5$. L2: $2 \times 0.75/2 = 0.75$.
Exercise 8Code · intermediate

In the correlated-features code, change Lasso(alpha=1.0) to ElasticNet(alpha=1.0, l1_ratio=0.5) inside the bootstrap loop. How often is each pattern chosen now?

Check your answer:

Show solution
Elastic net keeps both features in essentially all 200 bootstrap samples, with similar weights each time. The L2 part removes the arbitrary choice between near-duplicates.
Practice with new numbers

Part 3 · Classic algorithms · ~40 min

Lesson 11: k-Nearest Neighbours

Classify by asking the neighbours: distances, choosing k, scaling and the curse of dimensionality.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Classify and regress with the k-nearest neighbours algorithm by hand
  • Compute Euclidean and Manhattan distances
  • Explain how k controls the bias–variance trade-off
  • Explain why feature scaling and the curse of dimensionality matter
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 2: Vectors & Matrices — A vector is a list of numbers; a dataset $X$ is a matrix with one row per example. The dot product $\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} = \sum w_ix_i$ is how linear models predict, and $\|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\|$ is the distance between two examples.
  • Lesson 4: Probability & Statistics — Probabilities run from 0 to 1. Bayes' theorem turns $P(B\mid A)$ into $P(A\mid B)$. Mean and standard deviation summarise data; the z-score $(x-\mu)/\sigma$ standardises it.
  • Lesson 5: Data, Features & Generalization — Always judge a model on data it hasn't seen: split into train / validation / test, or use k-fold cross-validation. Overfitting = low training error but high test error. Never let test data leak into training.

Where this fits: Starts Part 3, the classic algorithm toolbox. kNN is the simplest one — no training at all — and highlights why scaling matters.

1.The simplest idea in machine learning

Picture itNew to a city and wondering whether a restaurant is any good? Ask the three people who live closest to it. That's k-nearest neighbours: no formula, just "you're probably like the examples you're near".

"Tell me who your neighbours are, and I'll tell you who you are." That proverb is the k-nearest neighbours algorithm (kNN). To classify a new example, find the $k$ training examples most similar to it and let them vote.

kNN has no equations to fit and no weights to learn — and yet it can draw curved, complex decision boundaries that linear models can't. It's a great way to understand the idea of similarity, which runs through all of ML, and it teaches two crucial lessons: the importance of feature scaling and the curse of dimensionality.

Analogy: estimating a house price

An estate agent valuing a house doesn't solve equations. They look at the 3–5 most similar houses that sold recently nearby (similar size, area, condition) and take something like their average price. That's kNN regression.

2.The algorithm

Training: just store all the training examples. That's it. (kNN is called a lazy learner, because all the work happens at prediction time.)

Predicting for a new point $\mathbf{q}$:

  1. Compute the distance from $\mathbf{q}$ to every training example.
  2. Pick the $k$ examples with the smallest distances — the nearest neighbours.
  3. Classification: predict the most common class among those $k$ (majority vote). Regression: predict the average of their $y$ values.

kNN is non-parametric: it doesn't summarise the data in a fixed set of weights. The training data itself is the model.

3.Measuring distance

"Nearest" needs a distance. The most common is the Euclidean distance (straight-line distance, from Pythagoras — Lesson 2):

$$d(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{d}(a_j - b_j)^2}$$

Alternatives:

  • Manhattan distance $\sum_j |a_j - b_j|$ — like walking along city blocks; less dominated by one big difference.
  • Minkowski distance $\big(\sum_j |a_j - b_j|^p\big)^{1/p}$ — the general family: $p = 1$ is Manhattan, $p = 2$ is Euclidean. scikit-learn's default is Minkowski with $p = 2$.
  • Cosine distance — based on the angle between vectors (Lesson 2), popular for text.
Worked example — classify a point by hand

Training points: two red, three blue.

PointCoordinatesClassDistance to $\mathbf{q} = (2, 2)$
A(1, 1)red$\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = 1.414$
B(2, 1)red$\sqrt{0^2 + 1^2} = 1.000$
C(4, 3)blue$\sqrt{2^2 + 1^2} = 2.236$
D(5, 4)blue$\sqrt{3^2 + 2^2} = 3.606$
E(3, 3.5)blue$\sqrt{1^2 + 1.5^2} = 1.803$

Sorted by distance: B (1.000), A (1.414), E (1.803), C (2.236), D (3.606).

  • $k = 1$: nearest is B → red.
  • $k = 3$: B, A, E → 2 red, 1 blue → red.
  • $k = 5$: all five → 2 red, 3 blue → blue.

The answer depends on $k$. With $k = 5$ we're just counting every point, so the larger class wins regardless of where $\mathbf{q}$ is.

Make sense of it

The situation: A new customer, $\mathbf{q} = (2, 2)$, arrives. The two red points are customers who left; the three blue ones stayed. Will this one leave?

What the result tells you: kNN copies its nearest neighbours. With $k = 1$ or $3$ the closest customers are mostly red, so it predicts red. With $k = 5$ it asks everyone, and the majority (blue) wins wherever $\mathbf{q}$ is.

What if…?

  • Move the customer to (3.5, 3): the three nearest are all blue, so every $k$ from 1 to 5 says blue.
  • Move to (3, 2): the nearest red and the nearest blue are both exactly 1.414 away — a tie that the order of the data has to break.
  • Weight votes by 1/distance with $k = 5$: red scores $1/1 + 1/1.414 = 1.71$, blue scores 1.28, so close neighbours win and the answer is red again.

Why it matters in ML: $k$ controls how local the model is: small $k$ follows every quirk of the data (overfitting); large $k$ smooths everything towards the majority (underfitting). Pick it by cross-validation.

Read the formulaEuclidean distance
$$d(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \Big(\htmlClass{fd-2}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}}\htmlClass{fd-3}{(a_j - b_j)^2}\Big)^{\htmlClass{fd-1}{1/2}}$$
  • power ½ — the square root brings the units back (Pythagoras)
  • Σ — add up over every feature
  • (aⱼ − bⱼ)² — the squared difference on feature j — big-scale features dominate unless you scale them

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

4.Choosing $k$: bias vs variance again

  • Small $k$ (e.g. 1): the boundary follows every single training point, including noisy or mislabelled ones. Jagged boundary, little islands of the wrong class. High variance → overfitting. Note that with $k = 1$, training accuracy is always 100% — each point is its own nearest neighbour — which tells you nothing.
  • Large $k$: votes average over a big neighbourhood, so the boundary is smooth. Too large and it blurs real structure, eventually just predicting the majority class everywhere. High bias → underfitting.

Choose $k$ by cross-validation (Lesson 5). For two classes, odd values avoid tied votes.

Distance-weighted voting

Instead of one vote each, neighbours can vote with weight $1/d$, so closer ones count more. In scikit-learn: weights="distance". This makes the choice of $k$ less sensitive.

5.Try it: kNN decision regions

Three classes of points. The background colour shows what kNN would predict at every location. Change $k$ and watch the boundaries go from jagged (small $k$) to smooth (large $k$). Click anywhere to place a query point and see its $k$ nearest neighbours and their vote.

6.Feature scaling is essential

Distances add up differences across all features. If features are on different scales, the large-scale feature completely dominates.

Worked example — age vs income

Person P is 30 years old earning 50,000. Q is 60 earning 51,000. R is 31 earning 70,000.

$d(P, Q) = \sqrt{30^2 + 1000^2} \approx 1000.4$
$d(P, R) = \sqrt{1^2 + 20000^2} \approx 20000.0$

So Q is "much closer" to P than R is — even though Q is twice P's age — because the income differences (thousands) swamp the age differences (tens). Age is effectively ignored.

After standardising each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (Lesson 4), a 30-year age gap and a 20,000 income gap are each measured relative to how much that feature normally varies, so both count.

Make sense of it

The situation: A dating app matches people by age and income. P is 30 earning 50,000; Q is 60 earning 51,000; R is 31 earning 70,000. Who is P's closest match?

What the result tells you: On raw numbers Q looks 20 times closer than R, purely because income is measured in thousands and age in tens. The 30-year age gap barely registers.

What if…?

  • Standardise both features (using these three people): P–Q becomes 2.16 and P–R 2.17. Now the age gap and the income gap count about equally — a very different picture.
  • Income in thousands (50, 51, 70): P–Q $= \sqrt{30^2 + 1^2} \approx 30.0$ and P–R $= \sqrt{1 + 20^2} \approx 20.0$, so R becomes the closer one. The "nearest" person depends entirely on the units.

Why it matters in ML: Every distance-based method (kNN, k-means, SVMs with RBF kernels) is sensitive to scale. Standardising is not optional for them.

The code below shows the real effect on a dataset: accuracy jumps from 67% to 93% just by scaling.

7.kNN for regression

For a numeric target, predict the average of the neighbours' values:

$$\hat{y}(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \in N_k(\mathbf{q})} y_i$$

where $N_k(\mathbf{q})$ is the set of the $k$ nearest neighbours. With distance weighting, it's a weighted average. Example: the three nearest houses sold for 300k, 320k and 340k, so predict 320k.

8.The curse of dimensionality

In plain wordsWith many features, data points spread out so much that even the "nearest" neighbours are far away. That's the curse of dimensionality — kNN works best with fewer, relevant features.

kNN relies on nearby points being similar. In high dimensions, "nearby" stops meaning much — this is the curse of dimensionality.

Worked example — how big is a "neighbourhood"?

Suppose data is spread evenly inside a unit cube, and we want a small cube-shaped neighbourhood that contains 10% of the data. Its volume must be 0.1, so each side has length $0.1^{1/d}$:

Dimensions $d$12310100
Side length needed0.100.320.460.790.98

In 10 dimensions, to capture just 10% of the data, the "neighbourhood" must span 79% of each feature's range. In 100 dimensions, 98%. The "nearest" neighbours aren't near at all — they're scattered almost across the whole space.

Make sense of it

The situation: You want the 10% of houses most like yours. With one feature (size) that's a narrow band. Add more features and see what happens to "nearby".

What the result tells you: In 10 dimensions, a box holding 10% of the data must stretch 79% of the way along every feature. Your "neighbours" differ from you on almost everything.

What if…?

  • Ask for only 1% of the data as neighbours: the side length is still 0.63 in 10 dimensions and 0.955 in 100.
  • To keep a side of 0.1 (truly local) in 10 dimensions, the box holds only $0.1^{10}$ — one ten-billionth of the data. You'd need billions of examples to find a single neighbour.

Why it matters in ML: This is the curse of dimensionality: with many features, data becomes sparse and distances lose their meaning. Remove irrelevant features or reduce dimensions (Lesson 17) before using kNN.

Consequences: in many dimensions, all points end up roughly the same distance from each other, so nearest neighbours become nearly meaningless, and you'd need exponentially more data to fill the space. Remedies: remove irrelevant features, or reduce dimensions first with PCA (Lesson 17).

9.Strengths and weaknesses

StrengthsWeaknesses
Simple to understand and explainSlow predictions: compares to every training point
No training timeMust store the whole training set
Flexible, curved decision boundariesNeeds feature scaling
Works for classification and regressionStruggles in high dimensions and with irrelevant features

To speed up the search, libraries use tree-shaped indexes such as KD-trees and ball trees, which skip whole regions of space that can't contain a nearest neighbour. They work well in low dimensions; scikit-learn chooses automatically (algorithm="auto").

10.In Python

The wine dataset: 178 wines, 13 chemical measurements with very different scales (one ranges up to 1,680, others are below 1), and 3 grape varieties.

from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)

raw = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5).fit(X_train, y_train)
print("without scaling:", round(raw.score(X_test, y_test), 3))

scaled = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)).fit(X_train, y_train)
print("with scaling:   ", round(scaled.score(X_test, y_test), 3))

for k in [1, 5, 15, 51, 81, 101]:
    s = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)),
                        X_train, y_train, cv=5)
    print(f"k={k:3d}  CV accuracy {s.mean():.3f} ± {s.std():.3f}")

Output:

without scaling: 0.667
with scaling:    0.933
k=  1  CV accuracy 0.918 ± 0.054
k=  5  CV accuracy 0.940 ± 0.038
k= 15  CV accuracy 0.932 ± 0.037
k= 51  CV accuracy 0.962 ± 0.023
k= 81  CV accuracy 0.593 ± 0.065
k=101  CV accuracy 0.399 ± 0.019

Two lessons in one output. Scaling lifts accuracy from 67% to 93%. And $k$ matters: small $k$ is noisier (look at the larger ± for $k = 1$), moderate values work well, and once $k$ approaches the size of the training folds (about 106 examples), the vote is dominated by whole classes and accuracy collapses — extreme underfitting.

11.Running example: Chennai Homes

A new 100 m², 5-year-old house 6 km from the centre: after scaling, its 3 nearest neighbours are houses 5, 4 and 2 (88, 55 and 82 lakh), so kNN predicts their average, 75 lakh.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
cols = ["size_m2", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
knn = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=3)).fit(df[cols], df["price_lakh"])
new = pd.DataFrame({"size_m2": [100], "dist_km": [6], "age_yrs": [5]})
dist, idx = knn[-1].kneighbors(knn[0].transform(new))
print("nearest houses:", (df["id"].iloc[idx[0]]).tolist(), "prices:", df["price_lakh"].iloc[idx[0]].tolist())
print("predicted price:", round(knn.predict(new)[0], 1), "lakh")

Output:

nearest houses: [5, 4, 2] prices: [88, 55, 82]
predicted price: 75.0 lakh
Where this is used
  • Simple recommenders ("customers similar to you bought…")
  • Filling in missing values from similar rows (KNNImputer)
  • A quick baseline for small datasets

Choose it when: Small to medium data, few features, and a meaningful notion of similarity.

Think twice when: Very large datasets (slow predictions) or many features (curse of dimensionality).

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythkNN learns a model from the data.

RealityIt just stores the data and compares at prediction time.

MythLarger k is always safer.

RealityToo large k blurs real boundaries and, in the extreme, predicts the majority class everywhere.

Responsible AI · A model that stores its data

kNN keeps every training example and uses it at prediction time, so deploying it means deploying the raw data — with all its privacy obligations, including deleting a person's record if they ask. Distances also treat every feature as meaningful: if a sensitive attribute (or a proxy) is among the features, "similar people" will be judged alike for the wrong reasons.

12.Questions beginners often ask

How do I choose k?

Try a range (e.g. 1–50) with cross-validation and pick the best. Odd numbers avoid ties for two classes.

Why is kNN slow to predict?

It compares each new point with every training example. Tree indexes (KD-tree, ball tree) speed this up in low dimensions.

Does kNN learn anything?

Not in the usual sense — it stores the data. All the work happens at prediction time, which is why it's called a lazy learner.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Running kNN on unscaled features.
  • Judging $k = 1$ by its training accuracy (always 100%).
  • Keeping many irrelevant features, which dilute the meaning of distance.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • kNN vs k-means — kNN looks at neighbours; k-means moves centres.
  • Lazy vs eager learning — Pay now or pay later.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

What does a kNN model learn during training?

The trap: Describing weights or a boundary.

Nothing beyond storing the training data (and perhaps building a search index). It's a "lazy" learner: all the work happens at prediction time, which is why predictions get slow on large datasets and why deploying it means deploying the data.

With $k = 1$, what's the training accuracy, and what does it tell you?

The trap: Reporting it as evidence the model is good.

Essentially 100%: each training point's nearest neighbour is itself (unless identical points have different labels). It tells you nothing about generalisation — always evaluate kNN on held-out data.

Why is an odd $k$ often recommended for two-class kNN?

The trap: Not noticing ties.

With an even $k$ the vote can tie (2 vs 2). An odd $k$ avoids ties for two classes; with more classes ties can still happen, so implementations break them by distance or order.

Your kNN accuracy jumps after you standardise the features. Why?

The trap: "Scaling just helps."

Distances are dominated by features with large numeric ranges. In Lesson 11, income in units of thousands drowned out age entirely. Standardising lets every feature contribute in proportion to how much it normally varies.

All 10 hidden questions for this lesson →

13.Key takeaways

  • kNN predicts from the $k$ most similar training examples: majority vote (classification) or average (regression).
  • It needs a distance — usually Euclidean $\sqrt{\sum(a_j - b_j)^2}$.
  • Small $k$ → jagged boundary, overfitting; large $k$ → smooth boundary, underfitting. Choose $k$ by cross-validation.
  • Always scale features — otherwise large-scale features dominate the distance.
  • The curse of dimensionality: in many dimensions, neighbourhoods stop being local.

14.Check your understanding

1. What is the Euclidean distance between $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 6)$?

$\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$. (7 is the Manhattan distance.)

2. With $k = 1$, what is kNN's accuracy on its own training data (no duplicate points)?

Each training point's nearest neighbour is itself, so it's always "correct" — which says nothing about generalization.

3. Your kNN boundary is jagged with many small islands. What should you change?

Jagged boundaries mean high variance. Averaging over more neighbours smooths the boundary.

4. The 3 nearest neighbours of a house sold for 200k, 260k and 230k. What does kNN regression ($k = 3$, unweighted) predict?

The average: $(200 + 260 + 230)/3 = 230$k.

5. Why does kNN struggle with hundreds of features?

The curse of dimensionality: neighbourhoods must stretch across most of the space, so neighbours aren't really similar.

15.Going deeper: distances, dimensions and fast neighbour search

In plain wordsWhy kNN struggles with many features (all distances become nearly equal), which distance and weighting to choose, how k-d trees and approximate search find neighbours among millions of points quickly (the same technology behind vector databases and LLM retrieval), and how good kNN can get with lots of data.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

kNN is simple to describe but has three practical questions that the lesson above only touches on: why it breaks down with many features (the curse of dimensionality, measured), which distance and weighting to use, and how to find neighbours quickly in millions of points. The last one matters far beyond kNN: modern search engines, recommendation systems and the "retrieval" step of LLM applications all rely on fast neighbour search over embeddings.

You'll need: this lesson, and norms from Lesson 2's "Going deeper".

The curse of dimensionality, measured

kNN assumes that "nearest" means "similar". In high dimensions that assumption weakens, because distances concentrate: all points end up almost the same distance away. Here are 1,000 random points in a unit cube and one query point:

import numpy as np

# Distance concentration: in high dimensions the nearest and farthest points are almost equally far
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for d in [2, 10, 100, 1000]:
    pts = rng.uniform(size=(1000, d)); q = rng.uniform(size=d)
    dist = np.linalg.norm(pts - q, axis=1)
    print(f"{d:4d} dimensions: nearest {dist.min():6.2f}   farthest {dist.max():6.2f}   ratio {dist.max() / dist.min():5.2f}")

Output:

   2 dimensions: nearest   0.01   farthest   1.33   ratio 135.62
  10 dimensions: nearest   0.47   farthest   2.11   ratio  4.48
 100 dimensions: nearest   3.35   farthest   4.65   ratio  1.39
1000 dimensions: nearest  12.17   farthest  13.55   ratio  1.11

In 2 dimensions the farthest point is 136 times farther than the nearest. In 1,000 dimensions the ratio is only 1.11: the "nearest" neighbour is barely nearer than the farthest, so it carries little information. The intuition: each dimension adds a little independent random difference, and sums of many random differences are all close to their average (the central limit theorem again, Lesson 4's "Going deeper").

Real data is rescued by the fact that it rarely fills all its dimensions. Images, text embeddings and sensor readings usually lie near a much lower-dimensional surface (the manifold hypothesis), so their intrinsic dimension is small. That's why reducing dimensions first (PCA, Lesson 17) or using learned embeddings often makes kNN work well again.

Choosing the distance and the weighting

Three common distances:

  • Euclidean (L2): the default for measurements on comparable, standardised scales.
  • Manhattan (L1): less dominated by a single large difference; sometimes better with many features or outliers.
  • Cosine distance, $1 - \cos\theta$: compares directions and ignores length. The standard for text and embeddings, where a document twice as long shouldn't count as "farther".

Distance weighting lets closer neighbours count more (weight $1/d$) instead of every one of the $k$ getting an equal vote. It makes the result less sensitive to the exact choice of $k$. On the standardised breast-cancer data with $k = 15$:

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
for metric in ["euclidean", "manhattan", "cosine"]:
    for weights in ["uniform", "distance"]:
        m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15, metric=metric, weights=weights))
        print(f"{metric:9} {weights:8}: accuracy {cross_val_score(m, X, y, cv=10).mean():.3f}")

Output:

euclidean uniform : accuracy 0.961
euclidean distance: accuracy 0.963
manhattan uniform : accuracy 0.954
manhattan distance: accuracy 0.956
cosine    uniform : accuracy 0.963
cosine    distance: accuracy 0.963

All six combinations land between 0.954 and 0.963. On this dataset the choice hardly matters, which is common once features are standardised; the gaps are within cross-validation noise (Lesson 9's "Going deeper"). The things that matter most for kNN are, in order: scaling the features, choosing $k$ by cross-validation, and using meaningful features. The metric is worth tuning mainly for text, images or mixed data types.

Finding neighbours fast

Brute-force kNN compares a query with all $n$ stored points: $O(nd)$ work per query, too slow for millions of points answered in milliseconds. Two families of solutions:

  • Space-partitioning trees (k-d trees and ball trees) split space into nested boxes or balls. A search walks down to the query's box and skips whole regions that can't contain anything closer than the best point found so far. This is exact and very fast in low dimensions (roughly $O(\log n)$ per query), but the benefit fades above about 20 dimensions, again because of distance concentration.
  • Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) methods trade a little accuracy for huge speed-ups in high dimensions. Graph-based methods such as HNSW hop through a "small world" graph linking each point to its near neighbours. Others use clustering or quantization (as in the FAISS library). They typically find over 95% of the true neighbours, thousands of times faster. Vector databases are built on them.
import time
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

data = rng.normal(size=(200000, 3)); queries = rng.normal(size=(2000, 3))
found, times = {}, {}
for algo in ["brute", "kd_tree"]:
    nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=5, algorithm=algo).fit(data)
    t = time.perf_counter(); found[algo] = nn.kneighbors(queries)[1]; times[algo] = time.perf_counter() - t
print("same neighbours found by both:", np.array_equal(np.sort(found["brute"]), np.sort(found["kd_tree"])))
print("k-d tree faster:", times["kd_tree"] < times["brute"])   # exact timings vary from computer to computer

Output:

same neighbours found by both: True
k-d tree faster: True

On 200,000 points in 3 dimensions, the k-d tree finds exactly the same neighbours as brute force, much faster. (Exact timings depend on your computer, so the code only prints whether it was faster; try printing times to see them.) Scikit-learn's default, algorithm="auto", picks brute force, a k-d tree or a ball tree based on the data's size and dimension.

How good can kNN get?

A classic result (Cover and Hart, 1967): as the amount of data grows, the error of 1-nearest-neighbour is at most twice the Bayes error, the error of the best possible classifier for that problem. With $k$ growing slowly as $n$ grows (so $k \to \infty$ but $k/n \to 0$), kNN's error approaches the Bayes error itself. kNN is therefore consistent: with enough data it can learn any decision boundary. The catch, as above, is how much data "enough" is when there are many dimensions.

Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

How would you serve nearest-neighbour search over 100 million embeddings with low latency?

The trap: Proposing brute force or a k-d tree.

Use an approximate nearest-neighbour index: graph-based (HNSW) or inverted-file with product quantization (IVF-PQ, as in FAISS), often in a vector database. Normalise the embeddings if using cosine similarity. Tune the index (graph degree, number of probed clusters) for the recall/latency trade-off, measure recall against brute force on a sample, and shard across machines when the index doesn't fit in memory.

Why do distances concentrate in high dimensions, and why does kNN still work on images and text?

The trap: Saying kNN never works in high dimensions.

Each dimension adds an independent random difference, so squared distances are sums of many terms, whose relative spread shrinks like $1/\sqrt{d}$. Nearest and farthest become similar. Real data, though, lies near a much lower-dimensional manifold, so its intrinsic dimension is small. Good representations (PCA, learned embeddings) expose that structure, and kNN works in that space.

When would you choose cosine distance over Euclidean?

The trap: "Cosine is always better for text." without saying why.

When the length of a vector reflects something irrelevant, such as document length or overall activity, and only the pattern matters. TF-IDF vectors, word and sentence embeddings, and user-preference vectors are typical. On unit-length vectors, cosine and Euclidean rank neighbours identically, because $\lVert\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\rVert^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta$.

What's the theoretical guarantee for 1-nearest-neighbour as data grows?

The trap: Claiming it reaches perfect accuracy.

Cover and Hart (1967): as $n \to \infty$, the 1-NN error is at most twice the Bayes error (the best achievable). With $k \to \infty$ and $k/n \to 0$, kNN's error approaches the Bayes error itself. The data needed to get close grows exponentially with dimension, which is the practical catch.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. In 1,000 dimensions, the farthest of 1,000 random points is only about 1.1 times farther than the nearest. What does that mean for kNN?

When all distances are similar, the nearest neighbours are hardly more similar than random points.

2. Which distance ignores vector length and compares only direction?

Cosine distance is $1 - \cos\theta$, which is why it's standard for text and embeddings.

3. What does weights="distance" do in kNN?

Each neighbour's vote is weighted by $1/d$.

4. When do k-d trees stop helping much?

In high dimensions, distance concentration means the search can rarely skip regions.

5. Approximate nearest-neighbour methods such as HNSW trade…

They usually find most true neighbours, far faster, which is what vector databases need.

Work each exercise on paper (or in the lesson notebook), type your answer into the box to check it, and open the solution to compare your working. Answers can be decimals (round to 3 places), fractions like 2/3 or percentages like 75%. Every answer has been checked with Python. For hands-on coding practice, the lesson notebook ends with two coding challenges: fill in one missing line and an automatic check tells you whether it's right.

Exercise 1By hand

Training points: A $(0,0)$ red, B $(1,1)$ red, C $(4,4)$ blue, D $(5,4)$ blue, E $(1,4)$ blue. Classify $\mathbf{q} = (2, 1)$ with $k = 1, 3, 5$.

Show solution
Distances: B $= 1$, A $= \sqrt5 \approx 2.236$, E $= \sqrt{10} \approx 3.162$, C $= \sqrt{13} \approx 3.606$, D $= \sqrt{18} \approx 4.243$.
$k = 1$: B → red. $k = 3$: B, A, E → 2 red, 1 blue → red. $k = 5$: 2 red, 3 blue → blue.
Exercise 2By hand

Compute the Euclidean and Manhattan distances between $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 6)$.

Check your answers:

Show solution
Euclidean: $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$. Manhattan: $3 + 4 = 7$.
Exercise 3Concepts

A dataset has "age" (20–70) and "salary" (20,000–200,000). Without scaling, which feature will dominate kNN distances? What should you do?

Show solution
Salary — its differences are thousands of times larger. Standardise both features (fitted on training data) before kNN.
Exercise 4By hand

In 5 dimensions, what side length must a cube-shaped neighbourhood have to contain 10% of uniformly spread data?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$0.1^{1/5} \approx 0.63$ — 63% of each feature's range. Hardly "local" any more.
Exercise 5Intermediate

Show that for unit-length vectors, $\lVert\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\rVert^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta$. If the cosine similarity is 0.8, what is the Euclidean distance?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$\lVert\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert^2 + \lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert^2 - 2\,\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = 1 + 1 - 2\cos\theta$. With $\cos\theta = 0.8$: $\sqrt{2 - 1.6} = \sqrt{0.4} \approx 0.632$.
Exercise 6Intermediate

A query has 3 neighbours at distances 1, 2 and 4, with classes A, B and B. Which class wins with uniform votes, and which with distance weights $1/d$?

Show solution
Uniform: B wins 2 to 1. Distance-weighted: A gets $1/1 = 1$; B gets $1/2 + 1/4 = 0.75$, so A wins.
Exercise 7Intermediate

Brute-force kNN on $n = 10^6$ points with $d = 100$ features: roughly how many multiply-adds does one query need?

Check your answer:

Show solution
About $n \times d = 10^6 \times 100 = 10^8$ multiply-adds per query. At $10^9$ per second that's about 0.1 seconds per query: too slow for live serving, which is why indexes exist.
Exercise 8Code · intermediate

Change the concentration code to use 1,000 points from a normal distribution (rng.normal) instead of the cube. Does the farthest/nearest ratio still shrink towards 1 as dimension grows?

Show solution
Yes. The ratio falls in the same way (large in 2 dimensions, close to 1 in 1,000), because concentration comes from adding many independent differences, not from the cube's shape.

Part 3 · Classic algorithms · ~40 min

Lesson 12: Naive Bayes

Bayes' theorem as a classifier — the classic spam filter, built step by step.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Turn Bayes' theorem into a classifier
  • Explain the naive independence assumption and its limits
  • Build a spam filter by hand with Laplace smoothing
  • Choose between Multinomial, Bernoulli and Gaussian Naive Bayes
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 4: Probability & Statistics — Probabilities run from 0 to 1. Bayes' theorem turns $P(B\mid A)$ into $P(A\mid B)$. Mean and standard deviation summarise data; the z-score $(x-\mu)/\sigma$ standardises it.
  • Lesson 9: Evaluating Models — Accuracy can mislead. Precision $= TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $= TP/(TP+FN)$, and F1 balances them. Moving the threshold trades one for the other; ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds.

Where this fits: A second classic algorithm, built directly on Bayes' theorem. Fast and a great baseline, especially for text.

1.A classifier built from Bayes' theorem

In Lesson 4 you used Bayes' theorem to update a belief given evidence: a positive test changed the probability of disease. Naive Bayes turns that idea into a classifier. The "evidence" is the example's features; the "hypothesis" is the class.

It's one of the oldest and simplest ML methods — the classic spam filters of the early 2000s were Naive Bayes — and it's still useful today: it trains almost instantly, needs little data, and works surprisingly well on text. In this lesson you'll build a spam filter completely by hand.

2.Bayes' theorem for classification

We want the probability of each class $y$ given the features $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_d)$:

$$P(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{P(y)\;P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)}{P(\mathbf{x})}$$
  • $P(y)$ — the prior: how common the class is overall (e.g. 40% of emails are spam).
  • $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$ — the likelihood: how probable these features are for this class.
  • $P(\mathbf{x})$ — the evidence: the same for every class, so for comparing classes we can ignore it.

So the prediction is the class with the largest $P(y)\,P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$. We can always divide by the sum over classes at the end to get proper probabilities.

3.The "naive" assumption

The hard part is $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$: the probability of a whole combination of features. An email has thousands of possible words, and we'll never see most combinations even once, so we can't count them.

Naive Bayes makes a bold simplification: assume the features are independent of each other, given the class. Then the joint probability is just a product (the multiplication rule from Lesson 4):

$$P(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d \mid y) = P(x_1 \mid y)\,P(x_2 \mid y)\cdots P(x_d \mid y) = \prod_{j=1}^{d} P(x_j \mid y)$$

which gives the Naive Bayes classifier:

$$\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y}\; P(y)\prod_{j=1}^{d} P(x_j \mid y)$$

($\arg\max_y$ means "the value of $y$ that makes this largest"; $\prod$ means "multiply together", like $\sum$ means "add up".)

Why "naive"?

The assumption is usually false. In real emails, "free" and "money" tend to appear together — they're not independent. Naive Bayes ignores that. Yet it often classifies well anyway, because it only needs to get the ranking of classes right, not the exact probabilities. Its probability estimates, however, tend to be over-confident (too close to 0 or 1).

Step-by-step derivationFrom Bayes' theorem to the Naive Bayes rule
  1. $$P(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{P(y)\,P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)}{P(\mathbf{x})}$$

    Bayes' theorem for a class $y$ and features $\mathbf{x}$.

  2. $$\hat{y} = \arg\max_y\ P(y)\,P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)$$

    $P(\mathbf{x})$ is the same for every class, so it can't change which class wins.

  3. $$P(\mathbf{x} \mid y) = \prod_{j} P(x_j \mid y)$$

    The naive assumption: features independent given the class.

  4. $$\hat{y} = \arg\max_y\ P(y)\prod_{j} P(x_j \mid y)$$

    Substitute.

  5. $$\hat{y} = \arg\max_y\ \Big[\ln P(y) + \sum_j \ln P(x_j \mid y)\Big]$$

    Take logs: the logarithm only ever increases, so the winner is the same — and sums don't underflow.

Read the formulaThe Naive Bayes rule
$$\hat{y} = \htmlClass{fd-1}{\arg\max_y}\ \htmlClass{fd-2}{P(y)}\htmlClass{fd-3}{\prod_{j=1}^{d} P(x_j \mid y)}$$
  • argmax — pick the class with the highest score
  • P(y) — prior — how common the class is
  • Π P(xⱼ | y) — multiply the evidence from each feature (the naive independence assumption)

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

4.Worked example: a spam filter by hand

Our tiny training set: 10 emails, 4 spam and 6 not spam ("ham").

Spam (4)Ham (6)
win money nowmeeting at noon
free money offerlunch with the team now
win a free prize nowproject meeting notes
claim your free prizesee you at lunch
your project report is ready
notes from the team meeting

Task: is the new email "free money now" spam?

Step 1 — priors

$P(\text{spam}) = 4/10 = 0.4$, $\quad P(\text{ham}) = 6/10 = 0.6$.

Step 2 — word probabilities (likelihoods)

We treat each email as a "bag of words" and count how often each word appears in each class. The spam emails contain 15 words in total; the ham emails contain 25. There are 24 different words in the vocabulary overall.

The probability of a word given a class is its count divided by the total word count of that class. But there's a trap: "free" never appears in ham, so $P(\text{free} \mid \text{ham}) = 0/25 = 0$ — and since we multiply, a single zero would make the whole ham probability zero, no matter what the other words say. One unseen word shouldn't be able to veto everything.

Laplace (add-one) smoothing

Pretend every vocabulary word was seen once more than it really was:

$$P(w \mid y) = \frac{\text{count}(w, y) + 1}{\text{total words in } y + |V|}$$

where $|V|$ is the vocabulary size (24). This guarantees no probability is ever zero. (In scikit-learn this "+1" is the parameter alpha=1.0.)

WordCount in spamP(w | spam)Count in hamP(w | ham)
free3$\frac{3+1}{15+24} = \frac{4}{39} = 0.1026$0$\frac{0+1}{25+24} = \frac{1}{49} = 0.0204$
money2$\frac{3}{39} = 0.0769$0$\frac{1}{49} = 0.0204$
now2$\frac{3}{39} = 0.0769$1$\frac{2}{49} = 0.0408$

Step 3 — multiply

$$\text{spam score} = 0.4 \times 0.1026 \times 0.0769 \times 0.0769 \approx 0.000243$$ $$\text{ham score} = 0.6 \times 0.0204 \times 0.0204 \times 0.0408 \approx 0.0000102$$

Step 4 — normalise into probabilities

$$P(\text{spam} \mid \text{"free money now"}) = \frac{0.000243}{0.000243 + 0.0000102} \approx 0.96$$

96% spam. Notice how each word contributed: "free" is about 5× more likely in spam than ham, "money" about 3.8×, and "now" about 1.9× — together they overwhelm the prior, which favoured ham.

5.Working with logs

In plain wordsMultiplying many small probabilities gives numbers too small for a computer to store, so in practice we add their logarithms instead. The winning class stays the same.

A real email has hundreds of words. Multiplying hundreds of numbers like 0.001 gives results so small that computers round them to exactly 0 (underflow). The fix: take logarithms. Since $\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b$, products become sums:

$$\ln\!\Big(P(y)\prod_j P(x_j \mid y)\Big) = \ln P(y) + \sum_j \ln P(x_j \mid y)$$

The logarithm keeps the ordering (bigger stays bigger), so we can compare the log-scores directly. Every Naive Bayes implementation works this way.

Worked example — the same email in log space

Spam: $\ln 0.4 + \ln 0.1026 + \ln 0.0769 + \ln 0.0769 \approx -0.916 - 2.277 - 2.565 - 2.565 = -8.32$.

Ham: $\ln 0.6 + \ln 0.0204 + \ln 0.0204 + \ln 0.0408 \approx -0.511 - 3.892 - 3.892 - 3.199 = -11.49$.

Spam's log-score is higher (less negative) → predict spam. The difference, $-8.32 - (-11.49) = 3.17$, means spam is $e^{3.17} \approx 24$ times more likely, i.e. $24/25 = 0.96$. Same answer.

Make sense of it

The situation: A real spam filter multiplies hundreds of small probabilities. Computers can't store numbers that tiny, so they add logarithms instead.

What the result tells you: The log scores −8.32 (spam) and −11.49 (ham) differ by 3.17, so spam is $e^{3.17} \approx 24$ times more likely: a 96% chance.

What if…?

  • The email also says "meeting" (3 times in ham, never in spam): the chance of spam falls to 88%. One ham-like word pulls it back.
  • "free" appears twice: its evidence counts twice, and the chance rises to 99.2%.
  • Spam is rarer (prior 0.1 instead of 0.4): the same words now give 80%. The prior matters.
  • No smoothing: "free" has probability 0 in ham, the ham score is 0, and the email is 100% spam whatever else it says.

Why it matters in ML: Each word adds its own log-evidence for or against a class, so the model is easy to explain: you can list the words that pushed the decision. The "naive" independence assumption makes repeated or correlated words over-count.

Advanced · optionalNormalising log-scores safely: the log-sum-exp trick

To turn class log-scores $a_k$ into probabilities you need $P(k) = e^{a_k}/\sum_j e^{a_j}$, but $e^{a_k}$ underflows to 0 when $a_k$ is around −800. Subtract the largest score $m = \max_j a_j$ first:

$$\log\sum_j e^{a_j} = m + \log\sum_j e^{a_j - m}, \qquad P(k) = e^{\,a_k - m}\Big/\sum_j e^{a_j - m}.$$

Every exponent is now ≤ 0 and the largest is exactly $e^0 = 1$, so nothing overflows and the sum is at least 1. Example: scores $-1000$ and $-1001$ would both underflow, but after subtracting $m = -1000$ they become $0$ and $-1$, giving probabilities $1/(1+e^{-1}) \approx 0.731$ and $0.269$. The same trick sits inside every softmax in Lessons 18–19.

6.Try it: your own spam filter

This filter is trained on exactly the 10 emails above. Type any message and see the score each word contributes. Green bars push towards spam, purple bars towards ham; the bar length is $\ln\frac{P(w \mid \text{spam})}{P(w \mid \text{ham})}$. Words never seen in training are ignored. Try "win a free lunch", "team meeting now", or "claim your prize".

7.Variants for different kinds of features

In plain wordsDifferent kinds of features need different versions: word counts (Multinomial), yes/no features (Bernoulli) or measurements like height (Gaussian, which assumes a bell curve for each class).

The formula $P(y)\prod_j P(x_j \mid y)$ is always the same; what changes is how $P(x_j \mid y)$ is modelled.

VariantFeatures$P(x_j \mid y)$ comes fromTypical use
Multinomial NBCountsSmoothed relative frequencies (as above)Text classification
Bernoulli NBBinary (present / absent)Fraction of examples where the feature is 1Short texts, yes/no features
Gaussian NBContinuous numbersA normal distribution per class and featureMeasurements
Complement NBCountsStatistics from all other classesImbalanced text data
Categorical NBCategoriesSmoothed frequency of each categoryCategorical data

Gaussian Naive Bayes

For continuous features, assume each feature follows a normal distribution (Lesson 4) within each class, with its own mean $\mu_{y}$ and standard deviation $\sigma_{y}$ estimated from the training data:

$$P(x_j \mid y) = \frac{1}{\sigma_{y}\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x_j - \mu_{y})^2}{2\sigma_{y}^2}\right)$$
Worked example — apple or orange?

From training data: apples weigh on average $\mu = 150$ g ($\sigma = 20$); oranges $\mu = 200$ g ($\sigma = 25$). Equal priors (0.5 each). A fruit weighs 170 g.

Apple: $z = (170 - 150)/20 = 1$. Density $= \frac{1}{20\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-1^2/2} \approx 0.01995 \times 0.607 \approx 0.0121$.

Orange: $z = (170 - 200)/25 = -1.2$. Density $= \frac{1}{25\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-1.44/2} \approx 0.01596 \times 0.487 \approx 0.0078$.

$P(\text{apple} \mid 170\text{ g}) = \frac{0.5 \times 0.0121}{0.5 \times 0.0121 + 0.5 \times 0.0078} \approx 0.61$.

A 61% chance it's an apple — 170 g is closer to the apple average, measured in standard deviations. With more features (colour, diameter…) we'd multiply in more densities.

Make sense of it

The situation: A fruit-sorting machine on a conveyor belt weighs each fruit and must decide: apple or orange?

What the result tells you: 170 g is 1 standard deviation above the apple average but 1.2 below the orange average, so it's a bit more apple-like: 61%.

What if…?

  • 160 g: 80% apple. 175 g: 49% — almost a coin toss. 185 g: 25%. 200 g: 5%.
  • 80% of the fruit are apples (prior 0.8): a 170 g fruit becomes 86% apple, and even 185 g is 56% apple. A strong prior shifts the boundary.

Why it matters in ML: Gaussian Naive Bayes turns each feature into a likelihood using its mean and standard deviation, then multiplies. It trains instantly and gives probabilities — a good first baseline.

8.Strengths and weaknesses

StrengthsWeaknesses
Extremely fast to train: just countingThe independence assumption is usually false
Works with little data and many features (like text)Probabilities are often over-confident
Handles many classes naturallyCan't learn interactions between features
Easy to explain: each feature adds evidenceGaussian NB assumes bell-shaped features

Naive Bayes is an excellent baseline: quick to try, hard to break. If a more complex model can't beat it, the complexity isn't earning its keep.

9.In Python

The spam filter from this lesson, with scikit-learn. CountVectorizer turns each text into word counts:

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB

spam = ["win money now", "free money offer", "win a free prize now", "claim your free prize"]
ham = ["meeting at noon", "lunch with the team now", "project meeting notes",
       "see you at lunch", "your project report is ready", "notes from the team meeting"]

vec = CountVectorizer(token_pattern=r"(?u)\b\w+\b")   # keep 1-letter words like "a"
X = vec.fit_transform(spam + ham)
y = [1] * 4 + [0] * 6                                   # 1 = spam, 0 = ham

nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(X, y)                 # alpha=1 is Laplace smoothing
tests = ["free money now", "meeting notes for the team", "win lunch now"]
print(nb.predict_proba(vec.transform(tests)).round(3))  # columns: [P(ham), P(spam)]

Output:

[[0.04  0.96 ]
 [0.985 0.015]
 [0.335 0.665]]

The first row matches our hand calculation exactly: 96% spam. "win lunch now" is mixed — "win" points to spam, "lunch" to ham — giving 67% spam.

Gaussian NB on the wine dataset from Lesson 11:

from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB

X, y = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)
print(round(GaussianNB().fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_test, y_test), 3))   # 0.956

95.6% accuracy with no scaling and no tuning, trained in milliseconds — better than kNN's 93.3% on the same split.

10.Running example: Chennai Homes

Naive Bayes on the listing text alone: words like "new" and "metro" push towards selling fast, "old" and "renovation" away. "New flat near metro" scores 0.96; "old villa needs renovation" just 0.02; "quiet flat with garden" is mixed (0.59).

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
vec = CountVectorizer()
Xw = vec.fit_transform(df["description"])
nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(Xw, df["sold_fast"])
for text in ["new flat near metro", "old villa needs renovation", "quiet flat with garden"]:
    print(f"{text:28s} P(sells fast) = {nb.predict_proba(vec.transform([text]))[0, 1]:.2f}")

Output:

new flat near metro          P(sells fast) = 0.96
old villa needs renovation   P(sells fast) = 0.02
quiet flat with garden       P(sells fast) = 0.59

⇄ Compare side by side: Naive Bayes vs logistic regression

Where this is used
  • Spam and sentiment classification
  • Document categorisation
  • A very fast baseline for text

Choose it when: Text or many features, little data, and when speed matters.

Think twice when: Features strongly interact, or you need well-calibrated probabilities.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythNaive Bayes needs the features to really be independent.

RealityIt often works well even when they aren't — it only needs the right class to score highest.

MythNaive Bayes probabilities are reliable confidence levels.

RealityThey tend to be pushed towards 0 and 1. Use them for ranking, not as exact confidence.

Responsible AI · Language models of who is "normal"

Text classifiers learn which words go with which label. Sap et al. (2019) found that tweets written in African-American English were far more likely to be labelled offensive by widely used toxicity datasets and the models trained on them. A spam or moderation filter can silence some groups more than others; test it on varied dialects and writing styles before trusting it.

11.Questions beginners often ask

If the independence assumption is wrong, why does it work?

Because classification only needs the correct class to score highest. Errors in the exact probabilities often don't change which class wins.

Which variant should I use?

Multinomial for word counts, Bernoulli for present/absent features, Gaussian for continuous measurements.

Is Naive Bayes still used today?

Yes — as a fast baseline, for text classification with little data, and wherever training must be nearly instant.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Forgetting smoothing, so one unseen word sets a class's probability to zero.
  • Multiplying many raw probabilities instead of adding log-probabilities (underflow).
  • Trusting Naive Bayes probabilities as well-calibrated confidence levels.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Generative vs discriminative models — Describe each class vs draw the line between them.
  • Prior vs likelihood vs posterior — Before, evidence, after.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Why is Naive Bayes called "naive", and why does it still work?

The trap: Thinking the assumption must hold for it to work.

It assumes features are independent given the class, which is rarely true (words like "free" and "prize" go together). It still classifies well because it only needs the right class to score highest, not accurate probabilities — the ranking often survives the wrong assumption.

Can you trust Naive Bayes probabilities?

The trap: Reporting them as calibrated.

Usually not. Counting correlated evidence several times pushes probabilities towards 0 or 1 — in Lesson 12, repeating "free" lifted the spam probability from 96% to 99.2%. Use it for ranking or decisions, and calibrate if you need probabilities.

A word never appeared in any ham email during training. What happens without smoothing?

The trap: Thinking one word can't matter much.

Its estimated probability in ham is 0, so the whole ham score is 0 and the email is classified as spam with certainty, whatever its other words say. Laplace (add-one) smoothing prevents this.

Why do implementations add log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?

The trap: "It's just a convention."

Multiplying hundreds of small numbers underflows to 0 in floating point. Logs turn the product into a sum of moderate numbers, and the class ranking is unchanged because log is increasing.

All 9 hidden questions for this lesson →

12.Key takeaways

  • Naive Bayes picks the class maximising $P(y)\prod_j P(x_j \mid y)$ — Bayes' theorem plus an independence assumption.
  • The "naive" independence assumption is usually wrong, but the classifier often works well anyway.
  • Laplace smoothing (+1 counts) prevents a single unseen word from zeroing out a class.
  • Implementations add log-probabilities instead of multiplying, to avoid underflow.
  • Multinomial NB for word counts, Bernoulli for yes/no features, Gaussian for continuous measurements.

13.Check your understanding

1. What does the "naive" assumption say?

Conditional independence lets us multiply individual feature probabilities instead of modelling every combination.

2. Why is Laplace smoothing needed?

Without smoothing, one zero factor in the product wipes out all the other evidence.

3. A class has 20 words in total, the vocabulary has 30 words, and "deal" appears 4 times in the class. With add-one smoothing, $P(\text{deal} \mid \text{class})$ is…

$(4 + 1)/(20 + 30) = 5/50 = 0.1$.

4. Why do implementations add log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?

Products of hundreds of small probabilities become too small to store. Logs turn them into sums of manageable numbers, without changing the ranking.

5. Which variant suits features like height and weight?

Continuous measurements are modelled with a normal (Gaussian) distribution per class.

14.Going deeper: smoothing, text pipelines and generative models

In plain wordsWhy naive Bayes adds a small count to every word (it's a Bayesian prior), how to read which words push towards each class, how real text classifiers are built (word pairs, TF-IDF, complement naive Bayes), and the difference between generative models (how each class creates data) and discriminative ones (the boundary only).

Intermediate · skip on a first read

Naive Bayes is still a strong, fast baseline for text. This section explains where its smoothing rule really comes from, how to read what it has learned, how a real text pipeline is built (TF-IDF and word pairs), and the big idea it represents: generative models, which learn how each class produces data, compared with discriminative models such as logistic regression, which learn the boundary directly.

You'll need: this lesson, and Bayesian estimation with priors from Lesson 4's "Going deeper".

Where smoothing comes from

Without smoothing, a word never seen in one class gets probability 0 for that class, and a single such word wipes out all the other evidence. In this tiny spam example, both new messages contain words that appeared in only one class:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB

texts = ["win cash prize now", "cheap meds win big", "claim your free prize", "free cash offer now",
         "meeting moved to monday", "lunch on monday?", "project report attached", "see you at the meeting"]
labels = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0])                # 1 = spam
vec = CountVectorizer().fit(texts)
Xc = vec.transform(texts)
for alpha in [1e-10, 1.0]:
    nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=alpha).fit(Xc, labels)
    p = nb.predict_proba(vec.transform(["free lunch on monday", "win a free meeting"]))[:, 1]
    print(f"alpha {alpha:g}: P(spam) for the two new messages {p.round(3)}")

Output:

alpha 1e-10: P(spam) for the two new messages [0. 1.]
alpha 1: P(spam) for the two new messages [0.184 0.735]

With essentially no smoothing ($\alpha = 10^{-10}$) the answers are absurdly certain, exactly 0 and 1, decided by one unseen word each. With $\alpha = 1$ (Laplace smoothing) they become sensible: 0.184 and 0.735. The smoothing formula,

$$P(\text{word } j \mid c) = \frac{\text{count}_{j,c} + \alpha}{\text{total}_c + \alpha V}$$

where $V$ is the vocabulary size, is not an arbitrary fix. It is the Bayesian posterior mean when the word probabilities get a symmetric Dirichlet prior, which is the many-category version of the Beta prior in Lesson 4's "Going deeper". Adding $\alpha$ to every count is like having seen every word $\alpha$ extra times before training. $\alpha$ is a regularization strength: tune it by cross-validation (values between 0.01 and 1 are common for text).

Reading what the model learned

Naive Bayes is easy to interpret. For each word, the log-ratio $\log P(\text{word}\mid\text{spam}) - \log P(\text{word}\mid\text{ham})$ is exactly how much that word adds to the spam score each time it appears:

# Which words push towards spam? The log-ratio log P(word | spam) − log P(word | ham)
nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(Xc, labels)
ratio = nb.feature_log_prob_[1] - nb.feature_log_prob_[0]
words = vec.get_feature_names_out()
order = np.argsort(ratio)
print("most spam-like:", [(str(words[i]), float(round(ratio[i], 2))) for i in order[::-1][:4]])
print("most ham-like: ", [(str(words[i]), float(round(ratio[i], 2))) for i in order[:4]])

Output:

most spam-like: [('win', 1.07), ('cash', 1.07), ('now', 1.07), ('prize', 1.07)]
most ham-like:  [('monday', -1.12), ('meeting', -1.12), ('at', -0.72), ('attached', -0.72)]

"win", "cash", "now" and "prize" each add 1.07 to the log-odds of spam; "monday" and "meeting" subtract 1.12. Notice the classifier is linear in the word counts: the log-odds is a weighted sum of counts plus a constant (the log prior ratio). Multinomial naive Bayes is a linear classifier, just like logistic regression, but with its weights set by counting rather than by optimisation.

A realistic text pipeline

Real text classifiers usually add three things:

  • Word pairs (bigrams), so "not good" isn't treated as "not" plus "good".
  • TF-IDF weighting: term frequency × inverse document frequency. Words that appear in almost every document ("the", "to") are down-weighted, and distinctive words count more.
  • Complement naive Bayes: estimates each class's word statistics from all the other classes. It's more stable when classes are imbalanced, and often beats standard multinomial NB on text.
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.naive_bayes import ComplementNB

# A text pipeline: words and word pairs, TF-IDF weighting, then naive Bayes
pipe = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)), ComplementNB(alpha=0.5)).fit(texts, labels)
for msg in ["claim your cash now", "report for the monday meeting"]:
    print(f"{msg!r:34} -> {'spam' if pipe.predict([msg])[0] else 'ham'}")
print("number of features (words and word pairs):", len(pipe[0].get_feature_names_out()))

Output:

'claim your cash now'              -> spam
'report for the monday meeting'    -> ham
number of features (words and word pairs): 47

Even on 8 training messages the pipeline classifies both new ones correctly, using 47 features (words plus word pairs). On real datasets with thousands of documents, this kind of pipeline trains in seconds and is a hard baseline to beat without much more expensive models. Try a linear SVM or logistic regression on the same TF-IDF features too; on text, they're often slightly more accurate. Modern alternatives replace TF-IDF with learned embeddings or a fine-tuned transformer (Lesson 19).

Generative vs discriminative models

Naive Bayes is a generative model: it learns $P(\mathbf{x}\mid y)$ and $P(y)$, a story of how each class produces data, and then uses Bayes' theorem to get $P(y\mid\mathbf{x})$. Logistic regression is discriminative: it models $P(y\mid\mathbf{x})$ directly and never describes $\mathbf{x}$ itself. The two can be exact counterparts. Gaussian naive Bayes with a shared variance per feature produces a log-odds that is linear in $\mathbf{x}$, the same form as logistic regression.

Generative (naive Bayes, LDA, mixture models)Discriminative (logistic regression, SVM, neural nets)
LearnsHow each class generates featuresThe boundary between classes
With little dataOften reaches its best accuracy soonerNeeds more data
With lots of dataLimited by wrong assumptionsUsually more accurate
Missing featuresHandled naturally (leave them out of the product)Need imputation
Can generate new examplesYesNo
ProbabilitiesOften badly calibrated (Lesson 8's "Going deeper")Usually better calibrated

A well-known analysis (Ng and Jordan, 2001) showed that naive Bayes approaches its own best error with far fewer examples (roughly logarithmic in the number of features), while logistic regression needs more (roughly linear) but ends lower when the independence assumption is wrong. In practice: with very few labelled examples, or as a quick baseline, try naive Bayes; with plenty of data, a discriminative model usually wins. Today's generative AI (Lesson 19) is the generative idea at enormous scale: models of $P(\mathbf{x})$ that can produce new text or images.

Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Naive Bayes vs logistic regression for text: how do you choose?

The trap: Saying one is always better.

Naive Bayes trains by counting, needs very little data to reach its best accuracy, and handles huge vocabularies cheaply, but its independence assumption double-counts correlated words, so its probabilities are over-confident and its final accuracy is often lower. Logistic regression (or a linear SVM) on the same TF-IDF features usually wins with enough data and gives better-calibrated probabilities. Try both: they're cheap. NB is great as a baseline, for tiny datasets, or for streaming updates.

What is TF-IDF and why use it instead of raw counts?

The trap: Only giving the acronym.

Term frequency × inverse document frequency: a word's count in a document, multiplied by $\log(N/\text{df})$, where df is the number of documents containing it (implementations add smoothing). Very common words get weights near 0; distinctive words get more. Vectors are usually normalised to unit length, so long documents don't dominate. It gives linear models and kNN a much better representation than raw counts.

Why is the smoothing parameter α a regularization hyperparameter?

The trap: Thinking it only avoids division by zero.

It pulls every class's word distribution towards uniform, like a prior. A large α means estimates trust the prior more, giving simpler, less confident models (more bias, less variance); a tiny α trusts sparse counts, giving extreme, overfit probabilities. So it's tuned by cross-validation like any regularization strength.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. Laplace smoothing in naive Bayes is the same as…

It's the posterior mean under a symmetric Dirichlet prior.

2. What does TF-IDF do to a word that appears in almost every document?

The inverse-document-frequency factor $\log(N/\text{df})$ is near 0 for very common words.

3. Multinomial naive Bayes's decision rule is…

The log-odds is a constant plus a sum of (log-ratio × count) over words.

4. Which model is generative?

It models $P(\mathbf{x}\mid y)$ for each class, then applies Bayes' theorem.

5. With only 30 labelled examples and 1,000 word features, a quick strong baseline is…

Generative models like naive Bayes typically reach their best accuracy with far fewer examples.

15.Practice exercises

Work each exercise on paper (or in the lesson notebook), type your answer into the box to check it, and open the solution to compare your working. Answers can be decimals (round to 3 places), fractions like 2/3 or percentages like 75%. Every answer has been checked with Python. For hands-on coding practice, the lesson notebook ends with two coding challenges: fill in one missing line and an automatic check tells you whether it's right.

Exercise 1By hand

With add-one smoothing, a word never seen in the ham class, ham total word count 50, vocabulary size 100. What is $P(\text{word} \mid \text{ham})$?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$(0 + 1)/(50 + 100) = 1/150 \approx 0.0067$ — small, but not zero.
Exercise 2By hand

Priors: spam 0.5, ham 0.5. $P(\text{cheap} \mid \text{spam}) = 0.2$, $P(\text{cheap} \mid \text{ham}) = 0.02$; $P(\text{meeting} \mid \text{spam}) = 0.01$, $P(\text{meeting} \mid \text{ham}) = 0.1$. Classify "cheap meeting".

Check your answer:

Show solution
Spam: $0.5\times0.2\times0.01 = 0.001$. Ham: $0.5\times0.02\times0.1 = 0.001$. A perfect tie: $P(\text{spam}) = 0.5$. The two words' evidence (×10 for spam, ×10 for ham) cancels out.
Exercise 3By hand

Gaussian NB, one feature. Class A: $\mu = 10$, $\sigma = 2$. Class B: $\mu = 14$, $\sigma = 2$. Equal priors. Classify $x = 11.5$.

Check your answer:

Show solution
Same $\sigma$, so compare $e^{-z^2/2}$. A: $z = 0.75$ → $e^{-0.281} \approx 0.755$. B: $z = -1.25$ → $e^{-0.781} \approx 0.458$.
$P(A \mid x) = 0.755/(0.755 + 0.458) \approx 0.62$ → class A.
Exercise 4Concepts

Why does Naive Bayes often classify well even though its probabilities are over-confident?

Show solution
Classification only needs the right class to score highest. Violated independence distorts the size of the probabilities more than their ranking.
Exercise 5Intermediate

A word appears 3 times in spam emails, which contain 200 words in total. The vocabulary has 1,000 words. With $\alpha = 1$, what is $P(\text{word}\mid\text{spam})$? What would it be for a word never seen in spam?

Check your answers:

Show solution
$(3 + 1)/(200 + 1000) = 4/1200 \approx 0.00333$. An unseen word: $1/1200 \approx 0.000833$, small but not zero.
Exercise 6Intermediate

A word appears in 10 of 1,000 documents. Using $\text{idf} = \ln(N/\text{df})$, compute its IDF. A word in all 1,000 documents gets what IDF?

Check your answers:

Show solution
$\ln(1000/10) = \ln 100 \approx 4.605$. In every document: $\ln 1 = 0$.
Exercise 7Intermediate

The spam log-odds starts at the log prior ratio $\ln(0.4/0.6)$. A message contains one word with log-ratio $+1.5$ and two copies of a word with log-ratio $-0.3$. What are the final log-odds and $P(\text{spam})$?

Check your answers:

Show solution
$\ln(0.4/0.6) = -0.405$. Total: $-0.405 + 1.5 - 0.6 = 0.495$. $P(\text{spam}) = 1/(1 + e^{-0.495}) \approx 0.621$.
