Lesson 17: Dimensionality Reduction & PCA

Compress many features into a few: variance, principal components and t-SNE.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Explain why reducing dimensions helps
  • Compute a covariance matrix and its eigenvalues by hand for 2D data
  • Find principal components, explained variance and projections
  • Choose the number of components and read t-SNE plots safely
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 2: Vectors & Matrices — A vector is a list of numbers; a dataset $X$ is a matrix with one row per example. The dot product $\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} = \sum w_ix_i$ is how linear models predict, and $\|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\|$ is the distance between two examples.
  • Lesson 4: Probability & Statistics — Probabilities run from 0 to 1. Bayes' theorem turns $P(B\mid A)$ into $P(A\mid B)$. Mean and standard deviation summarise data; the z-score $(x-\mu)/\sigma$ standardises it.
  • Lesson 16: Clustering — Clustering groups unlabelled data. k-means alternates assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving each centroid to the mean of its points.

Where this fits: The second unsupervised tool: compressing many features into a few, for visualisation, speed and noise reduction.

1.Too many features

Picture itA photo of a teapot from its best angle tells you almost everything about its shape; a photo straight down the spout tells you very little. PCA finds the "best angles" to look at your data from, so that a few of them show nearly everything.

A small 8×8 image of a handwritten digit is 64 numbers. A 1-megapixel photo is 3 million. A customer record might have hundreds of columns. Lots of features cause real problems:

  • The curse of dimensionality (Lesson 11): in many dimensions, data is sparse and distances lose meaning.
  • Overfitting: more features means more parameters to fit noise (Lesson 10).
  • Slowness and memory use grow with the number of features.
  • We can't see it: humans can plot 2 or 3 dimensions, not 64.

Fortunately, real features are often redundant. Height in cm and height in inches carry the same information; neighbouring pixels in an image are strongly correlated. Dimensionality reduction compresses many features into a few new ones while keeping most of the information. The most important method is principal component analysis (PCA).

Analogy: photographing a teapot

You have to describe a 3D teapot with a single 2D photo. Some angles (straight down from the top) lose almost everything — you just see a circle. The best angle, from the side, shows the spout, handle and lid: the photo keeps the most "spread-out" view of the object. PCA finds the best camera angle for your data: the directions in which the data varies the most.

2.The key idea: keep the directions with the most variance

Imagine points in 2D that lie roughly along a diagonal line. Two numbers $(x_1, x_2)$ describe each point, but really the points differ mainly in one way: how far along the line they are. If we rotate our axes so the first axis runs along the line, then:

  • the first new coordinate captures almost all the differences between points;
  • the second new coordinate (perpendicular) is nearly the same for every point — mostly noise.

Dropping the second coordinate loses very little. That's PCA: find new axes, ordered by how much of the data's variance they capture, and keep only the first few.

Principal components

The first principal component (PC1) is the direction along which the data has the largest variance. The second (PC2) is the direction of largest remaining variance that is perpendicular to PC1, and so on. With $d$ features there are $d$ principal components; we keep the first $k$.

3.Try it: find the best direction

Rotate the orange line. Each point is projected (dropped at a right angle) onto the line, and the readout shows the variance of those projected positions — how much "spread" this 1D view keeps. Find the angle that maximises it: that's PC1. Press Snap to PC1 to check, and notice that the best direction also minimises the total squared length of the projection lines (the information lost).

4.Measuring how features vary together: covariance

In plain wordsCovariance measures whether two features rise and fall together. PCA uses it to find the directions in which the data is most spread out.

To find directions of maximum variance, we need to know how features vary together. The covariance of two features (after subtracting their means) is the average product of their deviations:

$$\text{cov}(x_1, x_2) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i1} - \bar{x}_1)(x_{i2} - \bar{x}_2)$$
  • Positive: they tend to be above average together (like height and weight).
  • Negative: when one is above average, the other tends to be below.
  • Near zero: no linear relationship.

The covariance of a feature with itself is its variance (Lesson 4). Putting all the pairs in a table gives the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ ($d \times d$, symmetric). For centred data matrix $X_c$ it's simply

$$\Sigma = \frac{1}{n-1}X_c^\top X_c$$

5.Eigenvectors: the directions PCA finds

In plain wordsThe directions PCA finds are called eigenvectors; how spread out the data is along each one is its eigenvalue. Bigger eigenvalue = more important direction.

Here's the central fact (proved in linear algebra courses): the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and the variance along each one is its eigenvalue.

An eigenvector of a matrix $\Sigma$ is a special direction $\mathbf{v}$ that the matrix only stretches, without turning:

$$\Sigma\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$$

The stretch factor $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue. For a covariance matrix, eigenvectors are perpendicular to each other and eigenvalues are never negative. Sorting the eigenvectors by eigenvalue, largest first, gives PC1, PC2, …

The fraction of the total variance captured by component $j$ is the explained variance ratio:

$$\text{explained}_j = \frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \dots + \lambda_d}$$
For 2×2 matrices there's a formula

For $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ b & c\end{bmatrix}$ the eigenvalues are $\lambda = \frac{a+c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{a-c}{2}\right)^2 + b^2}$. Bigger matrices are handled by software (scikit-learn computes PCA with the singular value decomposition, an equivalent and more numerically stable method).

Step-by-step derivationWhy the best direction is the top eigenvector
  1. $$z_i = \mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{x}_i, \qquad \|\mathbf{u}\| = 1$$

    Project each centred point onto a unit direction $\mathbf{u}$.

  2. $$\text{Var}(z) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{x}_i)^2 = \mathbf{u}^\top\Big(\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i \mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^\top\Big)\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}^\top\Sigma\,\mathbf{u}$$

    The variance along $\mathbf{u}$ is a simple expression in the covariance matrix.

  3. $$\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}_j \Rightarrow \mathbf{u}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}_j^\top\lambda_j\mathbf{v}_j = \lambda_j$$

    Along an eigenvector, the variance is its eigenvalue.

  4. $$\mathbf{u} = \sum_j c_j\mathbf{v}_j \Rightarrow \mathbf{u}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{u} = \sum_j \lambda_j c_j^2, \quad \sum_j c_j^2 = 1$$

    Any unit direction is a mix of the (perpendicular) eigenvectors.

  5. $$\max_{\mathbf{u}} \mathbf{u}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{u} = \lambda_1 \ \text{ at } \ \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}_1$$

    A weighted average of eigenvalues is largest when all the weight is on the biggest one: PC1.

Read the formulaExplained variance ratio
$$\text{explained}_j = \frac{\htmlClass{fd-1}{\lambda_j}}{\htmlClass{fd-2}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \dots + \lambda_d}}$$
  • λⱼ — variance along component j (its eigenvalue)
  • λ₁ + … + λ_d — total variance in the data

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

6.Worked example: PCA by hand

Worked example — five points in 2D

Data: $(1, 2),\ (2, 3),\ (3, 5),\ (4, 4),\ (5, 6)$.

Step 1 — centre. Means: $\bar{x}_1 = 3$, $\bar{x}_2 = 4$. Subtract them:

$$(-2, -2),\ (-1, -1),\ (0, 1),\ (1, 0),\ (2, 2)$$

Step 2 — covariance matrix (dividing by $n - 1 = 4$):

$\text{var}(x_1) = \frac{4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4}{4} = 2.5$, $\ \text{var}(x_2) = \frac{4 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 4}{4} = 2.5$,
$\text{cov}(x_1, x_2) = \frac{4 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 4}{4} = 2.25$.

$$\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 2.5 & 2.25 \\ 2.25 & 2.5\end{bmatrix}$$

Step 3 — eigenvalues: $\lambda = 2.5 \pm \sqrt{0 + 2.25^2} = 2.5 \pm 2.25$, so $\lambda_1 = 4.75$ and $\lambda_2 = 0.25$.

Step 4 — eigenvectors: PC1 $= \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)$, the diagonal. Check: $\Sigma\,(1, 1) = (2.5 + 2.25,\ 2.25 + 2.5) = (4.75, 4.75) = 4.75\,(1, 1)$ ✓. PC2 $= \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1)$, perpendicular.

Step 5 — explained variance: PC1 keeps $\frac{4.75}{4.75 + 0.25} = 95\%$ of the variance. One number per point instead of two, losing only 5%.

Step 6 — project: each point's new coordinate is the dot product of its centred vector with PC1. For $(-2, -2)$: $\frac{-2 - 2}{\sqrt2} \approx -2.83$. All five: $-2.83,\ -1.41,\ 0.71,\ 0.71,\ 2.83$.

Make sense of it

The situation: Two exam scores per student — maths and physics — that rise and fall together. Could one number describe each student almost as well?

What the result tells you: PC1 is the diagonal direction "good at both". It holds 95% of the variation, so a single score per student keeps nearly all the information. PC2, "better at one than the other", holds only 5%.

What if…?

  • Points exactly on a line (1, 1), (2, 2), …: the second eigenvalue is 0 and PC1 keeps 100%. One number loses nothing.
  • Weakly related scores (1, 4), (2, 2), (3, 6), (4, 4), (5, 4): PC1 keeps only 62%. Dropping PC2 would throw away a lot.
  • Measure the second score in different units (×10): PC1 now keeps 99.8% and points almost entirely along that feature (0.996). Nothing about the students changed — PCA simply chases the feature with the biggest numbers.

Why it matters in ML: PCA finds the directions of greatest variance, so it works best when features are correlated — and it must be run on standardised features, or the units decide the answer. Check the explained-variance ratio before deciding how many components to keep.

7.PCA step by step

In plain wordsIn practice: standardise the features, let the library find the components, keep the first few that explain most of the variance (for example 95%), and use those as your new features.

  1. Centre the data (subtract each feature's mean). Usually also standardise (divide by the standard deviation) if features are in different units — otherwise a feature measured in large numbers dominates the variance.
  2. Compute the covariance matrix (or use the SVD directly).
  3. Find its eigenvectors and eigenvalues, sorted by eigenvalue.
  4. Choose $k$ and keep the top $k$ eigenvectors as the columns of a matrix $W_k$ ($d \times k$).
  5. Project: $Z = X_c W_k$, giving $n \times k$ new features.

You can also approximately reconstruct the original data from the compressed version: $\hat{X} = Z W_k^\top + \bar{\mathbf{x}}$. The reconstruction error is exactly the variance you threw away.

Advanced · optionalDeriving PCA — from maximum variance and from the SVD

Maximum variance. For centred data with covariance $C$, the variance along a unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ is $\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u}$. Maximise it subject to $\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u} = 1$ with a Lagrange multiplier: $\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\big[\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u} - \lambda(\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u}-1)\big] = 2C\mathbf{u} - 2\lambda\mathbf{u} = 0$, so $C\mathbf{u} = \lambda\mathbf{u}$: $\mathbf{u}$ must be an eigenvector, and the variance it captures is $\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u} = \lambda$. The best direction is the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue.

Via the SVD (how libraries actually do it). Write the centred $n\times d$ data matrix as $X = U\Sigma V^\top$, with $U$, $V$ orthogonal and $\Sigma$ diagonal with singular values $s_1 \ge s_2 \ge \dots$. Then

$$C = \frac{X^\top X}{n-1} = \frac{V\Sigma U^\top U\Sigma V^\top}{n-1} = V\,\frac{\Sigma^2}{n-1}\,V^\top.$$

This is an eigendecomposition of $C$: the columns of $V$ are the principal components and the eigenvalues are $\lambda_i = s_i^2/(n-1)$. The projected data is $XV = U\Sigma$. The SVD is preferred because it never forms $X^\top X$, which would square the condition number and lose numerical precision.

8.How many components?

  • Explained variance threshold: keep enough components to explain, say, 95% of the variance. In scikit-learn: PCA(n_components=0.95).
  • Scree plot: plot eigenvalues in order and look for an elbow, as with k-means.
  • For a downstream model: treat $k$ as a hyperparameter and choose it by cross-validation.
  • For visualisation: $k = 2$ or $3$.

9.Uses and limitations

Good forWatch out for
Visualising high-dimensional data in 2DComponents are mixtures of features — harder to interpret
Speeding up and regularizing other modelsOnly finds linear structure (straight directions)
Removing noise (drop low-variance components)High variance ≠ useful for prediction; a low-variance direction may matter for the label
Compressing dataSensitive to feature scale — standardise first

10.Beyond PCA: t-SNE and UMAP for visualisation

When structure is curved (like the moons in Lesson 16), a linear projection can squash different groups on top of each other. t-SNE is a non-linear method designed purely for visualisation: it places points in 2D so that points that were neighbours in the original space stay neighbours. Its main setting, perplexity, roughly controls how many neighbours each point pays attention to. UMAP is a newer, faster method with a similar goal.

Reading t-SNE plots safely

t-SNE pictures are easy to over-interpret. The authors of the guide "How to Use t-SNE Effectively" show that cluster sizes in a t-SNE plot mean nothing, distances between well-separated clusters may not mean anything either, and with a low perplexity even pure random noise can appear to form clusters. Different runs can give different pictures. Use t-SNE to explore, never as proof — and unlike PCA, it can't transform new data for a model.

11.In Python

The digits dataset: 1,797 images of handwritten digits, each 8×8 = 64 pixel features.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
pca = PCA().fit(X)
cum = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
for k in [2, 10, 20, 30]:
    print(f"{k:2d} components keep {cum[k-1]:.1%} of the variance")
print("components needed for 95%:", np.argmax(cum >= 0.95) + 1)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)
for k in [5, 10, 20, 40, 64]:
    model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=k), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(f"{k:2d} components: test accuracy {model.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}")

Output:

 2 components keep 28.5% of the variance
10 components keep 73.8% of the variance
20 components keep 89.4% of the variance
30 components keep 95.9% of the variance
components needed for 95%: 29
 5 components: test accuracy 0.820
10 components: test accuracy 0.867
20 components: test accuracy 0.956
40 components: test accuracy 0.971
64 components: test accuracy 0.969

29 of the 64 pixel features hold 95% of the variance. With 40 components the classifier is as accurate as with all 64 (slightly better, in fact), using under two-thirds of the features. Even 20 components give 95.6%. To plot the digits in 2D, use PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X) — or sklearn.manifold.TSNE for a non-linear picture.

12.Running example: Chennai Homes

PCA on the four standardised features: the first component captures 61.5% of the variance. Its weights are all positive — it measures "big, far and older" all at once — and four components can be squeezed into two while keeping about 82.5% of the information.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
cols = ["size_m2", "bedrooms", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
pca = PCA().fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(df[cols]))
print("explained variance ratio:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_.round(3))
print("PC1 weights:", {c: round(float(v), 2) for c, v in zip(cols, pca.components_[0])})

Output:

explained variance ratio: [0.615 0.21  0.165 0.01 ]
PC1 weights: {'size_m2': 0.61, 'bedrooms': 0.57, 'dist_km': 0.42, 'age_yrs': 0.34}

⇄ Compare side by side: PCA vs t-SNE

Where this is used
  • Visualising high-dimensional data in 2D
  • Compressing features before another model
  • Removing noise from signals and images

Choose it when: Many correlated features, or you need a 2D picture.

Think twice when: Interpretability of individual original features matters, or structure is strongly non-linear.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythPCA picks the most important original features.

RealityEach component is a mixture of all the original features.

MythDistances in a t-SNE picture are meaningful.

RealityCluster sizes and gaps between clusters in t-SNE plots can be misleading; it's for exploration only.

Responsible AI · Reducing dimensions does not anonymise

Compressing or transforming data does not make it anonymous. Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) re-identified users in the "anonymised" Netflix Prize dataset by matching a handful of their movie ratings with public reviews. A few dimensions, or a few rare values, can be enough to single someone out; treat derived features of personal data as personal data.

13.Questions beginners often ask

Does PCA throw away information?

Yes, the variance in the dropped components — by design, usually a small amount. The explained-variance ratio tells you how much you kept.

Should I always use PCA before a model?

No. It helps with many correlated features, visualisation or speed. With few features, or when interpretability matters, it's often unnecessary.

PCA or t-SNE?

PCA for compression and as input to models; t-SNE (or UMAP) only for exploring a 2D picture.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Running PCA on unstandardised features measured in different units.
  • Fitting PCA on all data before the train/test split.
  • Reading cluster sizes or gaps in a t-SNE plot as real distances.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • PCA vs t-SNE — PCA to compress; t-SNE to look.
  • Feature selection vs feature extraction — Choose columns vs make new ones.
  • Eigenvector vs eigenvalue — Direction vs amount.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Should you standardise before PCA?

The trap: Running PCA on raw features.

Almost always. PCA chases variance, so a feature in large units dominates. In Lesson 17, measuring one score ×10 made PC1 keep 99.8% of the variance and point almost entirely along that feature.

PCA keeps 95% of the variance. Can it still remove the feature that best predicts the target?

The trap: Assuming high variance means useful.

Yes. PCA ignores the target. A low-variance direction can be the most predictive one, and PCA might discard it. If prediction is the goal, compare with supervised selection, or tune the number of components by cross-validated performance.

You fit PCA on the full dataset, then split into train and test. Problem?

The trap: Thinking unsupervised steps can't leak.

Yes, a mild leak: the components were shaped by the test data. Fit PCA on the training data only (inside a Pipeline) and apply that transformation to the test data.

In a t-SNE plot, two clusters are far apart. Are they very different?

The trap: Reading t-SNE like a map.

Not necessarily. t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods, not global distances or cluster sizes, and its picture changes with the perplexity setting. Use it to explore, not to measure.

All 9 hidden questions for this lesson →

14.Key takeaways

  • Dimensionality reduction compresses many correlated features into a few new ones.
  • PCA finds perpendicular directions of maximum variance: the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by eigenvalue.
  • Explained variance ratio $= \lambda_j / \sum\lambda$; keep enough components for e.g. 95%.
  • Centre (and usually standardise) first; project with $Z = X_c W_k$.
  • PCA is linear; t-SNE/UMAP give non-linear pictures for exploration only.

15.Check your understanding

1. What is the first principal component?

PC1 is the direction of maximum variance — the eigenvector of the covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalue.

2. Eigenvalues are 6, 3 and 1. What fraction of the variance do the first two components explain?

$(6 + 3)/(6 + 3 + 1) = 9/10 = 90\%$.

3. Why standardise features before PCA?

PCA maximises variance; a feature in millimetres has far more raw variance than the same feature in metres.

4. $\Sigma\mathbf{v} = 3\mathbf{v}$. What is $\mathbf{v}$ and what is 3?

The matrix only stretches $\mathbf{v}$ by the factor 3, so $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3.

5. A t-SNE plot shows one big cluster and one small one. What can you conclude about their real sizes?

t-SNE expands dense clusters and contracts sparse ones, so visual sizes aren't trustworthy.

16.Going deeper: choosing components, and non-linear maps

In plain wordsHow to decide how many components to keep (variance kept and reconstruction error), kernel PCA for curved structure, and t-SNE and UMAP maps: what they keep (neighbourhoods), what they don't (distances between clusters, cluster sizes), and why they're for looking at data rather than for model features.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

PCA finds the best flat summary of the data. This section shows how to decide how many components to keep, what reconstruction error tells you, and what to do when the structure is curved: kernel PCA for features, and t-SNE and UMAP for pictures, including how to read those pictures without being misled.

You'll need: this lesson, and eigenvectors and the SVD from Lesson 2's "Going deeper".

How many components?

Keeping $k$ components has an exact cost: the reconstruction error, how far each point is from its projection back into the original space, equals the variance in the components you dropped. Projecting onto the top $k$ principal components gives the smallest possible error of any $k$-dimensional flat subspace (the Eckart–Young result from Lesson 2's "Going deeper"). On the 8×8 handwritten digits (64 pixel features):

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits, make_circles
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, KernelPCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# How many components? Variance kept and reconstruction error on the digits (64 pixels)
X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
pca = PCA().fit(X)
cum = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
for k in [2, 10, 20, 30, 40]:
    p = PCA(k).fit(X)
    rec = p.inverse_transform(p.transform(X))
    err = np.mean((X - rec) ** 2) / np.mean((X - X.mean(0)) ** 2)
    print(f"{k:2d} components: variance kept {cum[k - 1]:.3f}   relative reconstruction error {err:.3f}")
print("components needed for 95% of the variance:", int(np.searchsorted(cum, 0.95) + 1))

Output:

 2 components: variance kept 0.285   relative reconstruction error 0.715
10 components: variance kept 0.738   relative reconstruction error 0.262
20 components: variance kept 0.894   relative reconstruction error 0.106
30 components: variance kept 0.959   relative reconstruction error 0.041
40 components: variance kept 0.988   relative reconstruction error 0.012
components needed for 95% of the variance: 29

Two components keep only 28.5% of the variance; 29 components are needed to keep 95%, and the relative reconstruction error is exactly 1 minus the variance kept (0.041 at 30 components, where 0.959 is kept). Common ways to choose $k$:

  • A variance target, such as 90–99%. Scikit-learn accepts it directly: PCA(0.95).
  • An "elbow" in the plot of explained variance against component number.
  • Best of all, when PCA feeds a model: treat $k$ as a hyperparameter and choose it by cross-validation of the whole pipeline.

Reconstruction error has a useful side job: anomaly detection. Points that the main components can't reconstruct well don't follow the usual pattern.

Kernel PCA: principal components in a curved space

PCA can only find flat directions. When classes sit on concentric circles, no straight direction separates them. Kernel PCA applies the kernel trick (Lesson 15's "Going deeper") to PCA: it finds principal components in a high-dimensional feature space, computed entirely through the kernel matrix.

# Kernel PCA: a non-linear version that can "unroll" circles
Xc, yc = make_circles(n_samples=400, factor=0.3, noise=0.05, random_state=0)
for name, emb in [("ordinary PCA", PCA(1)), ("kernel PCA (RBF)", KernelPCA(1, kernel="rbf", gamma=5))]:
    z = emb.fit_transform(Xc)
    acc = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), z, yc, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{name:17}: a linear classifier on the 1 new feature scores {acc:.3f}")

Output:

ordinary PCA     : a linear classifier on the 1 new feature scores 0.450
kernel PCA (RBF) : a linear classifier on the 1 new feature scores 1.000

Ordinary PCA's single component is useless for separating the inner and outer circles (0.450, worse than guessing). With an RBF kernel, the first kernel principal component separates them perfectly (1.000): in the kernel's feature space, "distance from the centre" becomes a straight direction. Kernel PCA needs the $n\times n$ kernel matrix, so like kernel SVMs it doesn't scale to very large datasets, and its components are hard to interpret.

t-SNE and UMAP: maps for looking, not features

t-SNE builds a 2-D map that keeps neighbourhoods: points that are close in the original space should stay close on the map. It turns distances into probabilities of being neighbours (in the original space using a normal curve whose width is set by the perplexity, roughly "how many neighbours to care about"; on the map using a heavier-tailed $t$-distribution), then moves the map points to make the two sets of probabilities match. UMAP has a similar goal, is faster, and keeps more of the global layout.

from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

# Compare 2-D maps: how well do a point's map neighbours share its digit label?
maps = {"PCA, 2-D": PCA(2).fit_transform(X),
        "t-SNE, 2-D": TSNE(2, perplexity=30, random_state=0, init="pca").fit_transform(X)}
for name, Z in maps.items():
    acc = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(5), Z, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{name:10}: 5-nearest-neighbour accuracy in the map {acc:.3f}")

Output:

PCA, 2-D  : 5-nearest-neighbour accuracy in the map 0.603
t-SNE, 2-D: 5-nearest-neighbour accuracy in the map 0.976

How well does each 2-D map keep similar digits together? A point's 5 nearest map neighbours share its label 97.6% of the time for t-SNE, against 60.3% for PCA's flat 2-D projection. That's why t-SNE pictures of the digits show ten neat islands. But read such maps carefully:

  • Distances between clusters mean little. t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods, not global distances. Two islands far apart are not necessarily very different.
  • Cluster sizes mean little. t-SNE expands dense clusters and shrinks sparse ones.
  • Perplexity and the random seed change the picture. Try several values before trusting a pattern. Random noise can look clustered at low perplexity.
  • It's for looking, not for modelling. t-SNE has no transform for new points, and its axes have no meaning. Use PCA (or UMAP, which can transform new data) when you need features for a model.

Practical PCA notes

  • Fit PCA inside the pipeline, on training data only, so test data doesn't leak into the components (Lesson 5).
  • Standardise first when features have different units; otherwise the component directions are dominated by the features with the biggest numbers.
  • Whitening (PCA(whiten=True)) rescales each component to variance 1. It helps some models but also amplifies noise in the small components.
  • For huge or sparse data, use TruncatedSVD (works on sparse matrices, like TF-IDF text, where it's called latent semantic analysis), IncrementalPCA (in batches) or randomized SVD.
  • Autoencoders (Lesson 19) are a neural-network generalisation: an encoder squeezes the data through a small middle layer and a decoder reconstructs it. A linear autoencoder with squared error learns the same subspace as PCA.
Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

How do you choose the number of principal components?

The trap: "Always keep 95%."

Look at the cumulative explained-variance curve and the reconstruction error (they're the same information: error = variance dropped). A variance threshold (90–99%) or an elbow is a reasonable start. When PCA feeds a model, the best answer is to treat $k$ as a hyperparameter and pick it by cross-validating the whole pipeline. For visualisation, 2 or 3 components, accepting that much variance is lost.

What are the main pitfalls of interpreting t-SNE plots?

The trap: Reading cluster distances and sizes as meaningful.

t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods, so between-cluster distances and cluster sizes are unreliable; results depend on perplexity and the random seed; noise can look clustered at low perplexity; and the axes mean nothing. Try several settings, colour by known labels, and confirm structure with other methods. It has no out-of-sample transform, so don't use it to create model features.

How can PCA be used for anomaly detection?

The trap: Only mentioning dimensionality reduction.

Fit PCA on normal data and keep enough components to describe typical variation. For each new point, project and reconstruct it; the reconstruction error measures how badly it fits the usual pattern. A threshold on that error (chosen on validation data) flags anomalies. It works well when normal data really does lie near a lower-dimensional subspace.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. PCA with $k$ components keeps 93% of the variance. What is the relative reconstruction error?

The reconstruction error equals the variance in the dropped components: $1 - 0.93 = 0.07$.

2. Why can kernel PCA separate concentric circles when PCA can't?

It's PCA plus the kernel trick.

3. In a t-SNE map, two clusters are far apart. You can conclude that…

Global distances and cluster sizes on a t-SNE map are not reliable.

4. What does t-SNE's perplexity roughly control?

Low perplexity focuses on very local structure; high perplexity on broader structure.

5. Which method should you use to create features for a downstream model?

PCA has a transform for new data and stable, meaningful axes; t-SNE is for visualisation.

Part 5 · Neural networks & real projects · ~70 min

Lesson 18: Neural Networks from Scratch

Neurons, layers, activations and backpropagation — built by hand in NumPy.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Explain neurons, layers and why activation functions are needed
  • Run a forward pass through a small network by hand
  • Run backpropagation by hand and update the weights
  • Implement and train a neural network from scratch in NumPy
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 3: Derivatives & Gradients — A derivative is a slope; the gradient $\nabla L$ collects all partial derivatives and points uphill. Gradient descent steps the other way: $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\nabla L$. The chain rule differentiates functions inside functions.
  • Lesson 7: Gradient Descent — Gradient descent trains almost any model: compute the gradient of the loss, step against it, repeat. The learning rate controls the step size; too large diverges. Mini-batches make it fast on big data.
  • Lesson 8: Logistic Regression — Logistic regression outputs a probability $p = \sigma(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b)$, is trained with log loss, and classifies with a threshold (often 0.5), giving a straight decision boundary.

Where this fits: Starts Part 5. Neural networks combine everything so far — dot products, activations like the sigmoid, losses, the chain rule and gradient descent.

1.Why neural networks?

Every model so far has a fixed shape: a straight line, a set of boxes, a kernel. Neural networks learn their own internal features. Stack enough simple units together and the network can represent extremely complicated relationships — recognising faces, translating languages, generating text. Modern AI is built on them.

The good news: you already know every ingredient. A neuron is logistic regression (Lesson 8). Training is gradient descent (Lesson 7). And the famous backpropagation algorithm is the chain rule (Lesson 3), applied carefully. In this lesson you'll compute a full forward and backward pass by hand, then write a working network in about 20 lines of NumPy.

2.The artificial neuron

Picture itDeciding whether to go for a run, you weigh the weather, how tired you are and whether a friend is coming, then decide yes or no. A neuron does the same: weigh the inputs, add them up, and squash the total into a decision.

A neuron takes inputs $x_1, \dots, x_d$, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function $g$:

$$z = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b, \qquad a = g(z)$$

With $g = $ sigmoid, a single neuron is logistic regression. It draws one straight boundary. To learn more complex shapes, we connect many neurons in layers.

Loosely inspired by the brain

A biological neuron receives signals from other neurons, and "fires" if the combined signal is strong enough. The artificial version is a very simplified mathematical cartoon of that: weighted inputs, summed, then squashed. Don't take the analogy too far — what matters is the maths.

Read the formulaOne neuron
$$\htmlClass{fd-1}{a} = \htmlClass{fd-2}{g}\big(\htmlClass{fd-3}{\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}} + \htmlClass{fd-4}{b}\big)$$
  • a — the neuron's output (activation)
  • g — activation function, e.g. ReLU — adds the non-linearity
  • w · x — weighted sum of the inputs
  • b — bias — shifts the threshold

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

3.Why one neuron isn't enough: XOR

The XOR ("exclusive or") function outputs 1 when exactly one input is 1:

x1x2XOR
000
011
101
110

Plot the four points: the 1s sit on one diagonal, the 0s on the other. No single straight line separates them, so no single neuron (and no logistic regression) can learn XOR. But two neurons can each draw one line, and a third neuron can combine their answers — "above line A and below line B". That's the power of hidden layers: they create new features that make the problem easy for the next layer.

4.Layers: the multilayer perceptron

A multilayer perceptron (MLP), or feed-forward network, has:

  • an input layer — the features (no computation);
  • one or more hidden layers — neurons whose outputs feed the next layer;
  • an output layer — the prediction.

Each layer does a matrix multiplication (Lesson 2) followed by an activation:

$$\mathbf{h} = g\big(W^{[1]}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{[1]}\big), \qquad \hat{y} = \sigma\big(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{h} + c\big)$$

Here $W^{[1]}$ is a matrix with one row of weights per hidden neuron. With $d$ inputs and $m$ hidden neurons it has shape $m \times d$, plus $m$ biases.

Why activation functions are essential

Without $g$, two layers collapse into one: $V(W\mathbf{x}) = (VW)\mathbf{x}$, still a linear model. The non-linear activation is what lets depth add power.

5.Activation functions

NameFormulaRangeTypical use
ReLU$\max(0, z)$$[0, \infty)$Default for hidden layers
Sigmoid$\frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$$(0, 1)$Output for binary classification
tanh$\frac{e^z - e^{-z}}{e^z + e^{-z}}$$(-1, 1)$Hidden layers (zero-centred)
Softmax$\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}$probabilities summing to 1Output for multi-class

Their derivatives, needed for training: ReLU′ is 1 if $z > 0$ else 0; $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$; $\tanh'(z) = 1 - \tanh^2(z)$. ReLU is popular because it's cheap and its gradient doesn't shrink for positive inputs, which helps deep networks train (Lesson 19).

6.Worked example: a forward pass

Worked example — a 2-2-1 network

Inputs $\mathbf{x} = (1, 0)$, true label $y = 1$. Two sigmoid hidden neurons, one sigmoid output, all biases 0.

Hidden weights: neuron 1 has $(0.5,\ 0.3)$, neuron 2 has $(-0.5,\ 0.8)$. Output weights $\mathbf{v} = (1,\ -1)$.

Hidden layer:
$z_1 = 0.5\cdot1 + 0.3\cdot0 = 0.5 \Rightarrow h_1 = \sigma(0.5) \approx 0.6225$
$z_2 = -0.5\cdot1 + 0.8\cdot0 = -0.5 \Rightarrow h_2 = \sigma(-0.5) \approx 0.3775$

Output: $z = 1\cdot0.6225 - 1\cdot0.3775 = 0.2449 \Rightarrow p = \sigma(0.2449) \approx 0.5609$.

Loss (log loss, Lesson 8): $L = -\ln 0.5609 \approx 0.578$. The network gives only a 56% chance to the correct answer. Let's teach it.

Make sense of it

The situation: A tiny network decides whether to approve something from two yes/no signals. Each hidden neuron is a small feature detector; the output neuron weighs their opinions.

What the result tells you: Neuron 1 likes input 1 (output 0.62); neuron 2 dislikes it (0.38). The output adds them with weights +1 and −1, giving 0.56 — barely leaning towards "yes".

What if…?

  • Other input $\mathbf{x} = (0, 1)$: the hidden outputs become 0.57 and 0.69, and $p$ drops to 0.47 — the network now leans "no" (loss 0.75 if the truth is 1).
  • ReLU hidden neurons instead of sigmoid: $h = (0.5, 0)$ and $p = 0.62$ — neuron 2 is switched off entirely for this input.
  • All weights 0: both hidden neurons output exactly 0.5 and $p = 0.5$. Worse, both neurons get identical gradients forever, so they never become different — which is why weights start random.

Why it matters in ML: A forward pass is just repeated dot products (Lesson 2) followed by a non-linear function. Stacking layers lets the network build complex features out of simple ones.

7.Backpropagation: the chain rule, backwards

In plain wordsBackpropagation works out, for every weight, how much it contributed to the error — starting at the output and passing the blame backwards layer by layer. Then each weight is nudged to reduce the error.

To update every weight we need $\partial L/\partial(\text{weight})$. The loss depends on the weights through a chain: weight → hidden $z$ → hidden $h$ → output $z$ → $p$ → $L$. The chain rule multiplies the local derivatives along this path. Backpropagation organises it efficiently: compute an "error signal" $\delta$ at the output, then pass it backwards layer by layer, reusing each result.

  1. Output error. For sigmoid + log loss, Lesson 8 showed the derivative w.r.t. the output's $z$ simplifies to $\delta_{\text{out}} = p - y$.
  2. Output weights. $\frac{\partial L}{\partial v_j} = \delta_{\text{out}}\cdot h_j$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = \delta_{\text{out}}$.
  3. Pass the error back. Each hidden neuron gets the output error times the weight connecting it, times its own activation derivative: $\delta_j = \delta_{\text{out}}\cdot v_j\cdot g'(z_j)$.
  4. Hidden weights. $\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{jk}} = \delta_j\cdot x_k$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_j} = \delta_j$.
  5. Update all weights with gradient descent: $w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}$.

Every gradient has the same pattern: (error signal arriving at a neuron) × (input that came into it).

Worked example — backward pass and one update

Continuing from the forward pass ($p = 0.5609$, $y = 1$, $h = (0.6225, 0.3775)$).

1. Output error: $\delta_{\text{out}} = 0.5609 - 1 = -0.4391$.

2. Output weights: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial v_1} = -0.4391\times0.6225 \approx -0.2733$, $\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial v_2} = -0.4391\times0.3775 \approx -0.1658$, $\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = -0.4391$.

3. Hidden errors (sigmoid derivative $h(1-h) = 0.6225\times0.3775 \approx 0.2350$ for both):
$\delta_1 = -0.4391\times(1)\times0.2350 \approx -0.1032$
$\delta_2 = -0.4391\times(-1)\times0.2350 \approx +0.1032$

4. Hidden weights: multiply by the inputs $(1, 0)$: neuron 1's gradients are $(-0.1032,\ 0)$, neuron 2's are $(0.1032,\ 0)$. (Weights from $x_2 = 0$ get zero gradient — that input contributed nothing.)

5. Update with $\eta = 1$:
$v = (1 + 0.2733,\ -1 + 0.1658) = (1.2733,\ -0.8342)$, $\ c = 0.4391$
neuron 1: $(0.5 + 0.1032,\ 0.3) = (0.6032,\ 0.3)$; neuron 2: $(-0.5 - 0.1032,\ 0.8) = (-0.6032,\ 0.8)$

Check: running the forward pass again gives $p \approx 0.7245$ and loss $\approx 0.322$ (down from 0.578). One step of backpropagation made the network noticeably more confident in the right answer.

Make sense of it

The situation: The network gave 56% to the right answer. Backpropagation works out how much each weight was to blame, and nudges each one.

What the result tells you: The output error −0.44 says "too low". It flows back through each weight: weights that pushed the wrong way get the biggest corrections. After one step the network gives 72%.

What if…?

  • Learning rate 0.1: $p$ rises only to 0.579 (loss 0.547) — a small, safe step.
  • Learning rate 5: $p$ jumps to 0.98 in one step — great on this one example, but steps this big usually make training on many examples unstable.
  • If the truth were 0: every gradient flips sign; one step ($\eta = 1$) lowers $p$ to 0.34 and the loss from 0.82 to 0.41.

Why it matters in ML: Every deep-learning framework does exactly this, automatically, for millions of weights: forward pass, loss, backward pass (the chain rule, Lesson 3), update (gradient descent, Lesson 7).

Why it's efficient

Backpropagation computes the gradients for all weights in roughly the same time as one forward pass, by reusing the $\delta$ values. That's what makes training networks with millions or billions of weights possible. It was popularised for neural networks by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in 1986.

Step-by-step derivationDerive the gradient for one hidden weight
  1. $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{jk}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z}\cdot\frac{\partial z}{\partial h_j}\cdot\frac{\partial h_j}{\partial z_j}\cdot\frac{\partial z_j}{\partial W_{jk}}$$

    Chain rule along the path $W_{jk} \to z_j \to h_j \to z \to L$.

  2. $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = p - y$$

    Sigmoid output with log loss (Lesson 8).

  3. $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial h_j} = v_j$$

    Because $z = \sum_j v_jh_j + c$.

  4. $$\frac{\partial h_j}{\partial z_j} = g'(z_j)$$

    The hidden activation's derivative.

  5. $$\frac{\partial z_j}{\partial W_{jk}} = x_k$$

    Because $z_j = \sum_k W_{jk}x_k + b_j$.

  6. $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{jk}} = \underbrace{(p - y)\,v_j\,g'(z_j)}_{\delta_j}\cdot x_k$$

    Multiply: error signal × input — exactly the backprop rule.

Advanced · optionalThe softmax + cross-entropy gradient

With $K$ classes, the output layer computes $p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$ and the loss for a one-hot label $\mathbf{y}$ is $\ell = -\sum_k y_k\ln p_k$. The softmax derivative is $\partial p_k/\partial z_j = p_k(\mathbb{1}[k=j] - p_j)$. Therefore

$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_j} = -\sum_k \frac{y_k}{p_k}\,p_k(\mathbb{1}[k=j]-p_j) = -y_j + p_j\sum_k y_k = p_j - y_j.$$

Exactly the same "prediction minus target" error signal as the sigmoid + log loss in this lesson — which is why softmax and cross-entropy are always paired, and why frameworks fuse them into one numerically stable operation.

8.The same thing with matrices

In plain wordsThe same calculations are written with matrices so that the computer can process many examples at once.

For a batch of $n$ examples (rows of $X$), with tanh hidden units and a sigmoid output:

$$H = \tanh(XW_1 + \mathbf{b}_1), \qquad P = \sigma(HW_2 + b_2)$$

Backward:

$$\Delta_2 = \tfrac{1}{n}(P - Y), \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_2} = H^\top\Delta_2, \quad \Delta_1 = (\Delta_2W_2^\top)\odot(1 - H^2), \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_1} = X^\top\Delta_1$$

($\odot$ means element-wise multiplication; $1 - H^2$ is tanh's derivative.) These four lines are exactly what the NumPy code below does.

9.Try it: train a neural network

A small network with one hidden layer of tanh neurons learns to separate two classes. Pick a dataset — XOR, circle or spiral — and a number of hidden neurons, then press Train. The background shows the network's predicted probability. With 1 hidden neuron it can only draw a straight line; add neurons and watch it bend the boundary. The spiral needs the most neurons — and the most training: press Train again if it hasn't finished.

10.Training in practice

  • Initialisation: start weights as small random numbers, never all equal. If every weight is the same, every hidden neuron computes the same thing and gets the same gradient — they'd never become different.
  • Scale inputs (standardise), as with any gradient-descent model.
  • Mini-batches and epochs (Lesson 7): update on small random batches; one epoch is one pass over the data.
  • Watch the validation loss and stop when it starts rising (early stopping); use L2 regularization (Lesson 10).
  • Size: more neurons and layers give more capacity — and more risk of overfitting.
Universal approximation

A famous result says that a network with just one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any reasonable continuous function as closely as you like. It doesn't say how many neurons you'd need, or that training will find the right weights — in practice, deeper networks with fewer neurons per layer usually learn much more efficiently.

11.In Python: a network from scratch

A 2-4-1 network learning XOR with NumPy — every line corresponds to an equation above:

import numpy as np

X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
Y = np.array([[0], [1], [1], [0]], dtype=float)

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
W1 = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 4)); b1 = np.zeros(4)     # input -> 4 hidden neurons
W2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (4, 1)); b2 = np.zeros(1)     # hidden -> output
lr = 0.5

for step in range(5001):
    # forward pass
    H = np.tanh(X @ W1 + b1)
    P = sigmoid(H @ W2 + b2)
    loss = -np.mean(Y * np.log(P) + (1 - Y) * np.log(1 - P))
    # backward pass (backpropagation)
    dZ2 = (P - Y) / len(X)
    dW2 = H.T @ dZ2;  db2 = dZ2.sum(axis=0)
    dZ1 = (dZ2 @ W2.T) * (1 - H ** 2)          # tanh'(z) = 1 - tanh(z)^2
    dW1 = X.T @ dZ1;  db1 = dZ1.sum(axis=0)
    # gradient descent update
    W1 -= lr * dW1;  b1 -= lr * db1
    W2 -= lr * dW2;  b2 -= lr * db2
    if step in (0, 1000, 5000):
        print(step, round(loss, 4))

print(P.round(3).ravel())

Output:

0 0.6712
1000 0.0051
5000 0.0009
[0.    0.999 0.999 0.002]

The loss falls from 0.67 (guessing) to almost 0, and the predictions for $(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$ are essentially $0, 1, 1, 0$ — XOR, solved by a hidden layer.

With scikit-learn, on the 8×8 handwritten digits (64 inputs, 10 classes):

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)

mlp = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64,), max_iter=500, random_state=0))
mlp.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(round(mlp.score(X_train, y_train), 3), round(mlp.score(X_test, y_test), 3))

Output: 1.0 0.973. One hidden layer of 64 ReLU neurons (scikit-learn's default activation) — $64\times64 + 64 + 64\times10 + 10 = 4{,}810$ parameters — reaches 97.3% on unseen digits, a little above logistic regression on the same split (96.9%). The 100% training score hints at mild overfitting; increasing alpha (L2) or using early_stopping=True are the usual remedies.

12.Running example: Chennai Homes

A tiny neural network (one hidden layer of 4 neurons) learns to predict fast sales from size, distance and age, getting every house right even in leave-one-out evaluation. On such small, simple data, though, the decision tree's rule works just as well and is far easier to explain.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, LeaveOneOut
cols = ["size_m2", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
mlp = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(4,), max_iter=5000, random_state=0))
print("training accuracy:", mlp.fit(df[cols], df["sold_fast"]).score(df[cols], df["sold_fast"]))
print("leave-one-out accuracy:", round(cross_val_score(mlp, df[cols], df["sold_fast"], cv=LeaveOneOut()).mean(), 2))

Output:

training accuracy: 1.0
leave-one-out accuracy: 1.0

⇄ Compare side by side: Classical machine learning vs deep learning

Where this is used
  • Handwriting and image recognition
  • The foundation of every modern deep learning system

Choose it when: Large datasets with complex patterns, especially images, audio and text.

Think twice when: Small tabular datasets — gradient boosting or logistic regression are usually better and simpler.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythNeural networks work like the human brain.

RealityThey're loosely inspired by neurons, but they are mathematical functions trained by gradient descent.

MythDeeper networks are always better.

RealityMore depth needs more data and careful training; on small tabular data, simple models often win.

Responsible AI · Fragile and opaque

Neural networks can be fooled by tiny, deliberately chosen changes to their input: Szegedy et al. (2014) and Goodfellow et al. (2015) showed images altered imperceptibly to humans that networks misclassify with high confidence. Their reasoning is also hard to inspect. For safety-critical uses, test robustness, monitor behaviour after deployment, and don't treat confidence as correctness.

13.Questions beginners often ask

How many layers and neurons should I use?

Start small (one or two hidden layers), check for underfitting or overfitting, and grow or regularise from there.

Why ReLU instead of sigmoid in hidden layers?

ReLU is cheap and its gradient doesn't shrink for positive inputs, so deep networks train much better.

Is a neural network always better?

No. On small tabular datasets, gradient boosting or logistic regression is often more accurate and far simpler.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Initialising all weights to the same value (usually zero).
  • Forgetting non-linear activations between layers.
  • Not scaling inputs, which slows or stalls training.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Activation function vs loss function — Inside the network vs at the end.
  • Forward pass vs backward pass — Predict, then assign blame.
  • Dropout vs batch normalisation — Random silence vs steady scaling.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Why does a neural network need non-linear activation functions?

The trap: "To make outputs between 0 and 1."

Without them, stacked layers collapse into a single linear layer: $W_2(W_1\mathbf{x}) = (W_2W_1)\mathbf{x}$. However deep, the network could only draw straight boundaries. The non-linearity is what lets depth build complex functions.

What happens if you initialise all weights to zero?

The trap: "Training just starts slowly."

Every neuron in a layer computes the same output and receives the same gradient, so they stay identical forever — the layer behaves like a single neuron. Random initialisation breaks this symmetry. (Biases can start at zero.)

Why did sigmoid hidden layers make deep networks hard to train?

The trap: Blaming the data.

The sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, and nearly 0 for large inputs. Backpropagation multiplies one such factor per layer, so gradients shrink exponentially in early layers: the vanishing-gradient problem. ReLU (slope 1 for positive inputs), careful initialisation, batch normalisation and residual connections fixed it.

What is a "dying ReLU"?

The trap: Thinking ReLU has no downsides.

If a neuron's input becomes negative for every example (often after a large update), it outputs 0 and gets zero gradient, so it never recovers. Lower learning rates, careful initialisation or Leaky ReLU help.

All 11 hidden questions for this lesson →

14.Key takeaways

  • A neuron computes $g(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b)$; layers of neurons are matrix multiplications plus activations.
  • Non-linear activations (ReLU, tanh, sigmoid) are what make hidden layers useful — they let networks solve problems like XOR.
  • Backpropagation is the chain rule: compute $\delta_{\text{out}} = p - y$, pass errors backwards ($\delta_j = \delta_{\text{out}}v_jg'(z_j)$), and each gradient = error × input.
  • Training = forward pass, loss, backward pass, gradient-descent update, repeated over mini-batches.
  • Initialise randomly, scale inputs, and watch validation loss to avoid overfitting.

15.Check your understanding

1. Why can't a single neuron learn XOR?

The 1s and 0s lie on opposite diagonals; separating them needs at least two lines combined, i.e. a hidden layer.

2. What happens if you remove all activation functions from a deep network?

A chain of linear maps is still linear: $V(W\mathbf{x}) = (VW)\mathbf{x}$.

3. What is ReLU(−3)?

$\max(0, -3) = 0$.

4. Output $p = 0.8$, label $y = 0$, hidden activation $h_1 = 0.5$. What is $\partial L/\partial v_1$ (sigmoid + log loss)?

$\delta_{\text{out}} = p - y = 0.8$; $\partial L/\partial v_1 = 0.8\times0.5 = 0.4$. Positive, so $v_1$ will decrease.

5. Why must weights be initialised randomly rather than all zeros?

Random initialisation "breaks the symmetry" so each hidden neuron can specialise.

16.Going deeper: making deep networks trainable

In plain wordsWhy very deep networks are hard to train, with measurements: signals shrink or explode through the layers and gradients vanish on the way back. The standard fixes are careful starting weights (Xavier and He), ReLU, batch normalisation and dropout, plus a sensible default recipe for training a new network.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

A network with one hidden layer, as in this lesson, trains easily. Stack 20 layers and it often won't train at all. This section shows why, with measurements: signals that shrink or explode as they pass through layers, gradients that vanish on the way back, and the standard fixes that made deep learning work: careful initialisation, ReLU, batch normalisation and dropout.

You'll need: backpropagation from this lesson, and variance from Lesson 4.

Initialisation: keeping the signal alive

Each layer computes $\mathbf{h}_{\text{new}} = \sigma(W\mathbf{h})$. If each of the $n$ inputs to a unit has variance 1 and each weight has variance $s^2$, the sum $W\mathbf{h}$ has variance about $n s^2$. If $n s^2$ is bigger than 1 the signal grows layer after layer; if smaller, it shrinks. Two classic choices keep it steady:

  • Xavier (Glorot) initialisation, weight variance $1/n$, for tanh-like activations.
  • He initialisation, weight variance $2/n$, for ReLU, which sets half its inputs to zero and so needs twice the variance.

Here a batch passes through 20 layers of width 256 with different setups:

import numpy as np

# Push a batch through 20 layers of width 256 and watch the activations' spread
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x0 = rng.normal(size=(500, 256))
relu = lambda z: np.maximum(z, 0)
setups = {"tanh, weights std 1":           (np.tanh, 1.0),
          "tanh, weights std 0.01":        (np.tanh, 0.01),
          "tanh, Xavier std 1/sqrt(n)":    (np.tanh, 1 / np.sqrt(256)),
          "ReLU, Xavier std 1/sqrt(n)":    (relu, 1 / np.sqrt(256)),
          "ReLU, He std sqrt(2/n)":        (relu, np.sqrt(2 / 256))}
for name, (act, std) in setups.items():
    h = x0; spreads = []
    for layer in range(20):
        h = act(h @ rng.normal(0, std, size=(256, 256)))
        spreads.append(h.std())
    print(f"{name:27}: activation std after layers 1, 10, 20: {spreads[0]:.3f}, {spreads[9]:.3g}, {spreads[19]:.3g}")

# With weights of std 1, tanh is saturated: almost every unit sits near −1 or +1, where its slope is ~0
h = x0
for _ in range(20): h = np.tanh(h @ rng.normal(0, 1.0, size=(256, 256)))
print("tanh with std 1: share of units with |activation| > 0.99:", round(np.mean(np.abs(h) > 0.99), 3))

Output:

tanh, weights std 1        : activation std after layers 1, 10, 20: 0.975, 0.974, 0.974
tanh, weights std 0.01     : activation std after layers 1, 10, 20: 0.157, 1.06e-08, 1.12e-16
tanh, Xavier std 1/sqrt(n) : activation std after layers 1, 10, 20: 0.627, 0.221, 0.163
ReLU, Xavier std 1/sqrt(n) : activation std after layers 1, 10, 20: 0.581, 0.0212, 0.000893
ReLU, He std sqrt(2/n)     : activation std after layers 1, 10, 20: 0.829, 0.665, 0.674
tanh with std 1: share of units with |activation| > 0.99: 0.866

Weights that are too small (std 0.01) make the signal vanish: its spread falls to $10^{-16}$ by layer 20, so every input produces the same output. Weights that are too big (std 1) push tanh into saturation: the spread looks healthy (0.974), but 86.6% of units sit beyond $\pm 0.99$, where tanh's slope is almost 0, so almost no gradient flows back. Xavier keeps tanh in a usable range. Xavier with ReLU slowly dies away (0.000893 by layer 20), while He initialisation keeps ReLU steady (0.674). Frameworks build in scaled defaults like these (PyTorch's layers scale their random starting weights by the number of inputs), so you rarely set them by hand, but they explain why defaults matter, and why you may want torch.nn.init.kaiming_normal_ for a very deep ReLU network.

Vanishing gradients, measured

Backpropagation multiplies by each layer's activation slope on the way back. The sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so over 20 layers the gradient can shrink by up to $0.25^{20} \approx 10^{-12}$. ReLU's slope is exactly 1 wherever a unit is active:

# Backpropagate through 20 sigmoid layers vs 20 ReLU layers: how big is the gradient at the first layer?
def grad_norms(act, dact, std):
    h, cache, Ws = x0[:100], [], []
    for _ in range(20):
        W = rng.normal(0, std, size=(256, 256)); z = h @ W
        cache.append(z); Ws.append(W); h = act(z)
    g = np.ones_like(h)                                  # pretend dLoss/dOutput is all ones
    norms = []
    for z, W in zip(reversed(cache), reversed(Ws)):
        g = (g * dact(z)) @ W.T                          # chain rule, one layer back
        norms.append(np.linalg.norm(g))
    return norms[0], norms[-1]

sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
for name, act, dact, std in [("sigmoid", sig, lambda z: sig(z) * (1 - sig(z)), 1 / np.sqrt(256)),
                             ("ReLU", relu, lambda z: (z > 0).astype(float), np.sqrt(2 / 256))]:
    last, first = grad_norms(act, dact, std)
    print(f"{name:7}: gradient size at the last layer {last:.3g}, at the first layer {first:.3g}")

Output:

sigmoid: gradient size at the last layer 40.4, at the first layer 3.5e-11
ReLU   : gradient size at the last layer 186, at the first layer 658

With sigmoid, the gradient reaching the first layer is $4\times 10^{-11}$, about a trillionth of its size at the last layer, so the early layers essentially never learn. With ReLU and He initialisation, it stays the same order of magnitude (197 at the end, 524 at the start). That single change, together with good initialisation, is a big part of why deep networks became trainable around 2010–2012. The other big fixes are below, and residual connections (Lesson 19), which add a shortcut $\mathbf{h} + f(\mathbf{h})$ so gradients can skip layers.

Batch normalisation

Batch normalisation standardises each unit's values across the current mini-batch (mean 0, variance 1), then rescales them with two learned numbers per unit, $\gamma$ and $\beta$:

$$\hat{z} = \frac{z - \mu_{\text{batch}}}{\sqrt{\sigma^2_{\text{batch}} + \epsilon}}, \qquad \text{output} = \gamma\,\hat{z} + \beta$$

It keeps every layer's inputs in a steady range however the earlier weights change, which allows larger learning rates and makes training much less sensitive to initialisation. At prediction time it uses running averages of $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ collected during training, not the current batch. Layer normalisation standardises across the units of a single example instead; it doesn't depend on the batch, and it's the standard choice in transformers.

Dropout

Dropout randomly switches off each hidden unit with probability $p$ at every training step, so the network can't rely on any single unit and has to spread knowledge out. It works like training a huge ensemble of thinned networks that share weights, and averaging them at the end. Modern implementations use inverted dropout: scale the surviving units by $1/(1-p)$ during training, so nothing needs to change at prediction time, when dropout is switched off.

# Inverted dropout: drop units with probability p during training and scale the rest by 1/(1−p)
p = 0.5
h = np.ones(100000)
mask = rng.random(h.shape) > p
train_out = h * mask / (1 - p)
print("share of units kept:", round(mask.mean(), 3), "  average activation, training:", round(train_out.mean(), 3), "  at prediction time (no dropout):", h.mean())

# Batch normalisation: standardise each feature over the batch, then rescale with learned gamma and beta
z = rng.normal(5, 3, size=(64, 4))
gamma, beta = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5]), np.array([0.0, 1.0, -1.0, 0.0])
bn = gamma * (z - z.mean(0)) / np.sqrt(z.var(0) + 1e-5) + beta
print("after batch norm, per-feature mean:", (bn.mean(0).round(3) + 0.0), " std:", bn.std(0).round(3))

Output:

share of units kept: 0.499   average activation, training: 0.997   at prediction time (no dropout): 1.0
after batch norm, per-feature mean: [ 0.  1. -1.  0.]  std: [1.  2.  1.  0.5]

With $p = 0.5$, about half the units survive (0.498), and thanks to the $1/(1-p)$ scaling the average activation stays about 1 (0.995), matching prediction time exactly. The batch-norm example shows each feature leaving with exactly the mean $\beta$ and spread $\gamma$ chosen for it. In PyTorch, model.train() and model.eval() switch both dropout and batch norm between their training and prediction behaviour. Forgetting model.eval() before predicting is a classic bug.

A training recipe for a new network

ChoiceSensible default
ActivationReLU (or GELU in transformers)
InitialisationThe framework default (He or Xavier variants)
NormalisationBatch norm for CNNs; layer norm for transformers
OptimiserAdamW, learning rate about $10^{-3}$, warm-up then decay (Lesson 7's "Going deeper")
RegularizationWeight decay, dropout 0.1–0.5, early stopping, data augmentation
First checkOverfit a tiny batch (say 10 examples) to near-zero loss. If you can't, there's a bug.
Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Explain vanishing and exploding gradients and three ways to fix them.

The trap: Naming the problem without the mechanism.

Backprop multiplies, layer by layer, by each layer's weights and activation slopes. If those factors are typically below 1 the gradient shrinks exponentially with depth (vanishing); if above 1 it grows (exploding). Fixes: ReLU-family activations (slope 1 when active); variance-preserving initialisation (Xavier for tanh, He for ReLU); normalisation layers (batch or layer norm); residual connections that give gradients a shortcut; gradient clipping for explosions; and, for sequences, gated units (LSTM, GRU) or attention.

How does batch normalisation behave differently in training and inference, and what goes wrong if you forget?

The trap: Not knowing there's a difference.

In training it standardises with the current mini-batch's mean and variance and updates running averages. In inference it uses those running averages, so predictions don't depend on the batch. Forgetting to switch to evaluation mode (model.eval() in PyTorch) makes predictions depend on batch composition and size, often badly for batch size 1. Very small training batches also make batch statistics noisy, which is one reason layer or group norm are used instead.

Why does dropout reduce overfitting, and why scale by $1/(1-p)$?

The trap: "It removes neurons."

Randomly dropping units prevents co-adaptation (units relying on specific partners) and acts like training an exponential ensemble of thinned subnetworks that share weights; prediction with the full network approximates averaging them. Scaling survivors by $1/(1-p)$ during training keeps each unit's expected input the same as at test time, when nothing is dropped, so no adjustment is needed at prediction.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. He initialisation uses weight variance $2/n$ rather than $1/n$ because…

Doubling the variance compensates for the half of the signal ReLU throws away.

2. A deep sigmoid network's first layers barely learn. The most likely reason is…

Over 20 layers the product of slopes can be around $10^{-12}$.

3. At prediction time, batch normalisation uses…

So a single example gets the same output whatever else is in the batch.

4. With inverted dropout and $p = 0.2$, surviving units during training are multiplied by…

$1/(1 - p) = 1/0.8 = 1.25$, so the expected activation is unchanged.

5. Weights drawn with standard deviation 1 in a 256-wide tanh network mostly cause…

The pre-activations are huge (variance about 256), so tanh is flat almost everywhere it's evaluated.

Exercise 1By hand

Inputs $\mathbf{x} = (2, 1)$. Hidden ReLU neurons with weights $(1, -1)$ and $(-1, 2)$, biases 0. Output sigmoid with weights $(2, 3)$, bias $-1$. Compute the output.

Check your answer:

Show solution
$h_1 = \text{ReLU}(2 - 1) = 1$; $h_2 = \text{ReLU}(-2 + 2) = 0$. $z = 2\cdot1 + 3\cdot0 - 1 = 1$; $p = \sigma(1) \approx 0.731$.
Exercise 2By hand

Continue exercise 1 with label $y = 0$. Compute $\partial L/\partial v_1$ and $\partial L/\partial v_2$ (sigmoid + log loss).

Check your answers:

Show solution
$\delta_{\text{out}} = p - y = 0.731$. $\partial L/\partial v_1 = 0.731\times h_1 = 0.731$; $\partial L/\partial v_2 = 0.731\times0 = 0$ (neuron 2 was inactive).
Exercise 3By hand

How many parameters has a network with 10 inputs, hidden layers of 32 and 16 neurons, and 3 outputs?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$(10\cdot32 + 32) + (32\cdot16 + 16) + (16\cdot3 + 3) = 352 + 528 + 51 = 931$.
Exercise 4Code

In the XOR code, change the hidden size from 4 to 1 ((2, 1) and (1, 1)) and run it. Can it learn XOR? Why?

Show solution
No — the loss stays high and at least one point is misclassified. One hidden neuron draws one line, and XOR needs two.
Exercise 5Intermediate

A layer has 512 inputs. What weight standard deviation does Xavier ($\text{var} = 1/n$) give, and what does He ($\text{var} = 2/n$) give?

Check your answers:

Show solution
Xavier: $\sqrt{1/512} \approx 0.0442$. He: $\sqrt{2/512} = 0.0625$.
Exercise 6Intermediate

Each layer of a 10-layer network multiplies the gradient by about 0.25. By what factor has it shrunk at the first layer? And if each factor is 1.3?

Check your answers:

Show solution
$0.25^{10} \approx 9.5\times 10^{-7}$ (vanishing). $1.3^{10} \approx 13.79$ (exploding, and much worse with more layers).
Exercise 7Intermediate

Batch norm receives values $(2, 4, 6, 8)$ for one unit, with $\gamma = 2$, $\beta = 1$ and $\epsilon \approx 0$. What are the outputs? (Use the population variance.)

Check your answer — for several numbers, separate them with commas:

Show solution
Mean $5$; variance $(9 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 5$; std $\approx 2.236$. Standardised: $(-1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342)$. Output $= 2\hat{z} + 1$: $(-1.683, 0.106, 1.894, 3.683)$.
