Part 5 · Neural networks & real projects · ~70 min

Lesson 20: Feature Engineering, Pipelines & Final Project

Clean and encode data, build leak-proof pipelines, and complete an end-to-end project.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Scale, transform and encode features correctly
  • Handle missing values without leaking information
  • Build leak-proof pipelines with ColumnTransformer
  • Complete an end-to-end ML project from raw data to a saved model
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 5: Data, Features & Generalization — Always judge a model on data it hasn't seen: split into train / validation / test, or use k-fold cross-validation. Overfitting = low training error but high test error. Never let test data leak into training.
  • Lesson 9: Evaluating Models — Accuracy can mislead. Precision $= TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $= TP/(TP+FN)$, and F1 balances them. Moving the threshold trades one for the other; ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds.
  • Lesson 10: Overfitting, Regularization & Bias–Variance — Error = bias² + variance + noise. Regularization adds a penalty on weight size (L2 ridge shrinks weights; L1 lasso zeros some) to reduce variance; its strength is chosen by cross-validation.

Where this fits: Brings everything together into a real project: preparing messy data, building leak-proof pipelines, choosing and evaluating a model, and deploying it.

1.Data beats algorithms

Every model in this course expects a neat table of numbers: no gaps, no text, sensible scales. Real data is never like that. It has missing values, categories like "Chennai" or "two-year contract", amounts that range from 5 to 5 million, and dates. Turning raw data into good model inputs is called feature engineering, and in practice it often matters more than which algorithm you choose.

This final lesson covers the essential techniques, then shows how to package every step into a pipeline that is safe from data leakage. It ends with a complete project — from raw data to a saved, tested model — that puts the whole course together.

2.Numeric features

Scaling

From Lessons 7, 10, 11 and 15: distance-based and gradient-based models (kNN, SVMs, linear and logistic regression, neural networks) need features on similar scales. Tree models (Lessons 13–14) don't.

  • Standardisation (StandardScaler): $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ — mean 0, standard deviation 1. The usual default.
  • Min–max scaling (MinMaxScaler): $x' = (x - x_{\min})/(x_{\max} - x_{\min})$ — squeezes into $[0, 1]$.
  • Robust scaling (RobustScaler): uses the median and interquartile range, so outliers don't distort it.
Worked example — standardising tenure

Three customers have been with the company 3, 12 and 24 months. Mean $\mu = 13$. Standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{(-10)^2 + 1^2 + 11^2}{3}} = \sqrt{74} \approx 8.60$.

z-scores: $\frac{3-13}{8.60} \approx -1.16$, $\ \frac{12-13}{8.60} \approx -0.12$, $\ \frac{24-13}{8.60} \approx 1.28$.

Crucially, $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are computed on the training set only, then reused unchanged on the test set and on new data.

Make sense of it

The situation: A telecom company's churn model uses tenure (months with the company). It must be put on a standard scale before training.

What the result tells you: The z-scores say how many standard deviations each customer is from the average: −1.16 is short tenure, +1.28 is long.

What if…?

  • A new customer with 60 months: $z = (60 - 13)/8.60 = 5.46$ — far outside anything seen in training. Worth flagging: the model is extrapolating.
  • One long-standing customer (120 months) in the training data: the mean becomes 39.75 and the standard deviation 46.9, so the original three get z-scores −0.78, −0.59 and −0.34. One outlier squashes everyone else together — robust scaling (median and IQR) avoids this.

Why it matters in ML: Compute the mean and standard deviation on the training data only and reuse them — otherwise information from the test set leaks into training and your scores are over-optimistic.

Transforming skewed values

Amounts like income, prices or total spending are often skewed: most values are small, a few are huge. A log transform compresses the range so the huge values don't dominate: 100, 1,000 and 10,000 become 2, 3 and 4 with $\log_{10}$. In code, np.log1p(x) computes $\ln(1 + x)$, which also handles zeros safely.

Binning

Sometimes it helps to turn a number into ranges (age 18–25, 26–40, …) — useful when the effect isn't smooth, or for readability. It throws away detail, so use it deliberately.

Read the formulaStandardising with training statistics
$$z = \frac{\htmlClass{fd-1}{x} - \htmlClass{fd-2}{\mu_{\text{train}}}}{\htmlClass{fd-3}{\sigma_{\text{train}}}}$$
  • x — any value — training, test or a new customer
  • μ_train — mean learned from the training set only
  • σ_train — standard deviation learned from the training set only

Hover over (or tap) a part to highlight it in the formula.

3.Categorical features

Picture itGiving cities numbers like house numbers on a street would imply Delhi lives "between" Chennai and Mumbai. One-hot encoding gives each city its own light switch instead: on or off.

Models need numbers, but you can't just number the categories (Chennai = 1, Mumbai = 2, Delhi = 3): the model would think Delhi is "three times" Chennai, and that Mumbai lies "between" them.

One-hot encoding

Create one 0/1 column per category; exactly one is 1 for each row.

Worked example
city→city_Chennaicity_Delhicity_Mumbai
Chennai100
Mumbai001
Delhi010

All categories are now equally different from each other. In scikit-learn: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") — the option means a category never seen in training (say "Kolkata") becomes all zeros instead of an error.

Make sense of it

The situation: City is a category, not a number. Coding Chennai = 1, Delhi = 2, Mumbai = 3 would tell a linear model that Mumbai is "three times" Chennai.

What the result tells you: One-hot encoding gives each city its own 0/1 column, so no city is "bigger" or "between" others.

What if…?

  • A new city (Kolkata) appears after deployment: with handle_unknown="ignore" it becomes all zeros — the model treats it as "none of the known cities".
  • 1,000 different cities: 1,000 new columns, most almost always 0. Group rare categories into "other", or use target or frequency encoding.

Why it matters in ML: Tree models can cope with simple integer codes; linear models, kNN and neural networks need one-hot (or learned embeddings, Lesson 19).

Ordinal encoding

When categories have a natural order (small < medium < large; month-to-month < one-year < two-year), mapping them to 0, 1, 2 keeps that order in one column (OrdinalEncoder). Fine for trees; for linear models it assumes equal steps between levels.

Many categories

A feature like "postcode" may have thousands of values, which would create thousands of columns. Options include grouping rare categories into "other", or target encoding (replacing each category by the average label for that category — computed carefully inside cross-validation, or it leaks).

4.Missing values

Most scikit-learn models refuse missing values (HistGradientBoosting is an exception). Choices:

  • Drop rows — only if very few are missing and missingness is random. Otherwise you lose data and may bias the sample.
  • Impute — fill in a value with SimpleImputer: the median (robust for numbers), mean, most frequent (for categories), or a constant like "unknown". KNNImputer fills values from similar rows.
  • Add a "was missing" indicator (add_indicator=True). Missingness itself can carry information: a customer who didn't give a phone number may behave differently.
Imputation can leak too

The median used for filling gaps must be computed from the training data only — just like scaling statistics. Pipelines handle this automatically.

5.Creating new features

Often the most valuable features are ones you build from domain knowledge:

  • Ratios and differences: price per m², debt-to-income, monthly charge per support call.
  • Dates: from a timestamp, extract day of week, month, hour, "is weekend", or "days since last purchase". Raw timestamps are rarely useful directly.
  • Interactions: products of features (e.g. PolynomialFeatures) let linear models capture combined effects.
  • Aggregates: a customer's average order value, number of orders in the last 30 days.
  • Text: word counts (CountVectorizer, Lesson 12) or TF-IDF weights, which down-weight words common to every document.
Think like the model

Ask: "If I were predicting this by hand, what would I want to know?" A model predicting late payments benefits from "days until due date" far more than from two separate raw dates.

6.Feature selection

More features isn't always better (Lessons 10, 11, 17). Ways to keep only useful ones: remove near-constant features (VarianceThreshold), keep the best by a statistical test (SelectKBest), keep features a model rates as important (SelectFromModel, e.g. with Lasso), or let L1 regularization zero out the rest. Like all preprocessing, do it inside the pipeline.

7.Try it: a preprocessing pipeline, step by step

Edit the raw customer table (left) — try deleting a monthly charge or changing a city. On the right is the matrix the model actually receives: missing charge filled with the training median, numbers standardised, and the contract one-hot encoded. The statistics shown are "learned" from these rows, exactly what fit does on a training set.

8.Pipelines: preprocessing done right

A Pipeline chains steps into a single model object. A ColumnTransformer applies different steps to different columns. Together they give you three huge benefits:

  1. No leakage. Calling fit learns imputation values, scaling statistics and encodings from the training data only. During cross-validation, they're re-learned inside every fold.
  2. One object to tune. Grid search can tune preprocessing and model settings together (e.g. model__C).
  3. One object to deploy. Raw data in, prediction out — exactly the same transformations in training and production. Mismatches between the two ("training/serving skew") are a classic source of silent bugs.

9.Final project: predicting customer churn

The problem: a telecom company wants to know which customers are likely to cancel ("churn") so it can offer them a deal first. The table has numbers, categories and missing values — like real data. So that you can run everything yourself without downloading anything, the code first generates a realistic dataset of 2,000 customers. (It's synthetic: the patterns were built in, so they illustrate the workflow rather than real customer behaviour.)

Step 1 — Load and explore the data

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 2000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "tenure_months": rng.integers(1, 73, n),
    "monthly_charge": rng.normal(65, 20, n).clip(15, 130).round(2),
    "support_calls": rng.poisson(1.5, n),
    "contract": rng.choice(["month-to-month", "one-year", "two-year"], n, p=[0.55, 0.25, 0.20]),
    "payment": rng.choice(["card", "bank", "check"], n, p=[0.4, 0.35, 0.25]),
    "city": rng.choice(["Chennai", "Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune"], n),
})
df["total_spent"] = (df["tenure_months"] * df["monthly_charge"] * rng.normal(1, 0.05, n)).round(2)
score = (-2.0 + 1.6 * (df["contract"] == "month-to-month") - 0.035 * df["tenure_months"]
         + 0.018 * df["monthly_charge"] + 0.45 * df["support_calls"] + 0.5 * (df["payment"] == "check"))
df["churned"] = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-score))).astype(int)
for col, frac in [("monthly_charge", 0.05), ("payment", 0.04)]:     # real data has gaps
    df.loc[rng.random(n) < frac, col] = np.nan

print(df.shape)
print(df.head(3).to_string())
print("churn rate:", round(df["churned"].mean(), 3))
print(df.isna().sum()[df.isna().sum() > 0].to_dict())
(2000, 8)
   tenure_months  monthly_charge  support_calls        contract payment     city  total_spent  churned
0              7           50.16              2        one-year    bank     Pune       316.79        0
1             56           83.49              0  month-to-month     NaN    Delhi      4578.37        1
2             48           65.69              2  month-to-month    card  Chennai      3111.67        1
churn rate: 0.403
{'monthly_charge': 105, 'payment': 86}

2,000 customers, 7 features plus the label. 40% churned, so the classes are only mildly imbalanced. Two columns have gaps (105 and 86 missing values), and three columns are text categories.

Step 2 — Split before anything else

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = df.drop(columns="churned")
y = df["churned"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=0)

The test set (400 customers) is now locked away until Step 6 (Lesson 5).

Step 3 — Feature engineering and preprocessing

from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, FunctionTransformer

def add_features(X):
    X = X.copy()
    X["charge_per_call"] = X["monthly_charge"] / (X["support_calls"] + 1)   # a ratio feature
    X["log_total_spent"] = np.log1p(X["total_spent"])                       # tame the skew
    return X

numeric = ["tenure_months", "monthly_charge", "support_calls", "total_spent",
           "charge_per_call", "log_total_spent"]
categorical = ["contract", "payment", "city"]

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                      ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"))]), categorical),
])

Numbers: fill gaps with the median, then standardise. Categories: fill gaps with the most common value, then one-hot encode. Nothing is fitted yet — that happens inside cross-validation.

Step 4 — Start with a baseline, then compare models

from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

candidates = {
    "baseline (majority)": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "logistic regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
    "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0),
    "gradient boosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
}
for name, clf in candidates.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("features", FunctionTransformer(add_features)),
                     ("prep", preprocess), ("model", clf)])
    s = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
    print(f"{name:22s} ROC-AUC {s.mean():.3f} ± {s.std():.3f}")
baseline (majority)    ROC-AUC 0.500 ± 0.000
logistic regression    ROC-AUC 0.771 ± 0.008
random forest          ROC-AUC 0.756 ± 0.010
gradient boosting      ROC-AUC 0.739 ± 0.008

We use ROC-AUC (Lesson 9) because we'll want to rank customers by risk. The baseline scores 0.5 — pure guessing — so everything above it is real signal. Interesting: logistic regression beats the ensembles here. The relationships in this data are close to linear on the log-odds scale (Lesson 8), so the simpler model fits them best and the flexible models only add variance. Always compare — don't assume the fanciest model wins.

Step 5 — Tune the best model

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

pipe = Pipeline([("features", FunctionTransformer(add_features)), ("prep", preprocess),
                 ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
search = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"model__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]}, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print("best C:", search.best_params_["model__C"], " CV ROC-AUC:", round(search.best_score_, 3))
best C: 0.1  CV ROC-AUC: 0.772

Slightly stronger regularization ($C = 0.1$, Lesson 10) helps a little.

Step 6 — Evaluate once on the test set

from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, classification_report

best = search.best_estimator_
proba = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
print("test ROC-AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(y_test, proba), 3))
print(classification_report(y_test, (proba >= 0.5).astype(int), target_names=["stayed", "churned"]))
test ROC-AUC: 0.765
              precision    recall  f1-score   support

      stayed       0.73      0.82      0.77       239
     churned       0.67      0.55      0.61       161

    accuracy                           0.71       400
   macro avg       0.70      0.68      0.69       400
weighted avg       0.71      0.71      0.70       400

Test ROC-AUC 0.765 is close to the cross-validated 0.772, so our estimate was honest. At the default threshold the model catches 55% of churners (recall) and is right 67% of the time when it flags someone (precision). If a retention offer is cheap, the company could lower the threshold to catch more churners at the cost of more false alarms (Lesson 9).

Step 7 — Interpret the model

names = best.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out()
coefs = best.named_steps["model"].coef_[0]
for name, c in sorted(zip(names, coefs), key=lambda t: -abs(t[1]))[:5]:
    print(f"{name:32s} {c:+.2f}")
cat__contract_month-to-month     +0.85
num__tenure_months               -0.59
num__support_calls               +0.45
cat__contract_one-year           -0.43
cat__contract_two-year           -0.42

Because features were standardised, the coefficients are comparable (Lesson 6). Month-to-month contracts and more support calls push towards churn; longer tenure and annual contracts push away. These match the patterns built into the data — a good sanity check. Remember: these describe associations, not proven causes.

Step 8 — Save, reload and predict

import joblib

joblib.dump(best, "churn_model.joblib")
reloaded = joblib.load("churn_model.joblib")       # only ever load files you trust!

new_customer = pd.DataFrame([{"tenure_months": 3, "monthly_charge": 95.0, "support_calls": 4,
                              "contract": "month-to-month", "payment": "check", "city": "Pune",
                              "total_spent": 285.0}])
print("churn probability:", round(reloaded.predict_proba(new_customer)[0, 1], 3))
churn probability: 0.958

The whole pipeline — feature creation, imputation, scaling, encoding and model — is saved as one file. Raw customer data goes in, a probability comes out. A new, expensive, month-to-month customer with 4 support calls is flagged as very high risk.

One practical detail

The saved file stores a reference to the add_features function, not its code. To load the model in a different script or server, that function must be importable there too — for example, put it in a small module file (features.py) and import it in both places.

Security: loading model files

scikit-learn's documentation warns that pickle-based formats (pickle, joblib) can execute arbitrary code when loaded. Never load a model file from a source you don't trust. Safer formats include skops.io (which lets you inspect untrusted types before loading) and ONNX. Pickle-based files also need the same library versions that were used to save them.

10.After deployment: monitoring

A model's performance can quietly decay because the world changes (Lesson 5's distribution shift). Google's Rules of Machine Learning warns to "watch for silent failures" — for example, a feature that used to be filled in for 90% of rows dropping to 60% because an upstream system changed. In practice:

  • Log inputs and predictions; track the distribution of each feature and of the predicted probabilities over time.
  • When true outcomes arrive (did the customer actually leave?), keep measuring real-world metrics.
  • Check for training/serving skew: is production data processed exactly like training data?
  • Retrain regularly on recent data, and evaluate on data from later than the training period.

11.The complete ML workflow — a checklist

  1. Define the problem, the label and the metric that reflects real costs.
  2. Collect and explore the data: types, gaps, imbalance, oddities.
  3. Split off a test set immediately (by time, if the data is time-ordered).
  4. Build a pipeline: feature engineering, imputation, encoding, scaling.
  5. Score a trivial baseline.
  6. Compare several model families with cross-validation.
  7. Tune the best one or two.
  8. Evaluate once on the test set; choose a decision threshold.
  9. Interpret and sanity-check the model.
  10. Save the whole pipeline, deploy, and monitor.

12.Congratulations — and where to go next

You've gone from "what is a model?" to building, evaluating and saving complete machine learning systems — and you understand the maths underneath: vectors, gradients, probability, loss functions, regularization, and backpropagation. Ideas to explore next:

  • Practice on real datasets: the scikit-learn documentation's example gallery is full of complete, runnable examples.
  • Deep learning in depth: install PyTorch and build the CNN from Lesson 19; the free Deep Learning book by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville goes much further.
  • Stronger maths: Mathematics for Machine Learning (Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong) is free online and builds directly on Lessons 2–4.
  • Revisit the demos: re-reading a lesson after the later ones often makes things click.

13.Running example: Chennai Homes

A complete pipeline: impute a missing age, scale the numbers, one-hot encode the area, then ridge regression. Adding the area feature didn't help here (MAE 6.9 → 7.2 lakh) — distance already carries most of that information, and with 12 houses every extra column adds noise.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
df.loc[3, "age_yrs"] = np.nan                     # pretend one value is missing
num = ["size_m2", "bedrooms", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
numeric = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())])
with_area = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, num), ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["area"])])
numbers_only = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, num)])
for name, prep in [("numbers only", numbers_only), ("numbers + area", with_area)]:
    model = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=1.0))])
    mae = -cross_val_score(model, df, df["price_lakh"], cv=4, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()
    print(f"{name:15s} cross-validated MAE: {mae:.1f} lakh")

Output:

numbers only    cross-validated MAE: 6.9 lakh
numbers + area  cross-validated MAE: 7.2 lakh
Where this is used
  • Every real-world ML system: churn prediction, demand forecasting, risk scoring…

Choose it when: Always.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythFeature engineering is obsolete now that we have deep learning.

RealityFor tabular data, good features and careful preprocessing are still among the biggest drivers of performance.

MythOnce a model is deployed, the work is done.

RealityData changes over time; models need monitoring and retraining.

Responsible AI · Responsible deployment

A model in production makes decisions at scale, so document it: model cards (Mitchell et al., 2019) record what the model is for, how it was evaluated, for which groups, and its known limits. Monitor for drift and for unequal error rates, watch for feedback loops (a model's decisions changing the data it later learns from), and make sure people affected can question a decision and reach a human.

14.Questions beginners often ask

How much time goes into data preparation?

In real projects, usually more than into modelling. Clean, well-understood data matters more than the choice of algorithm.

Should I always build new features?

Only if they add new information. Test each one with cross-validation — Exercise 4 in this lesson shows a feature that doesn't help.

What should I learn next?

Practise on real datasets end to end, then go deeper into whichever area interests you: deep learning, time series, or the maths.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Fitting any preprocessing step on the full dataset before splitting.
  • Label-encoding unordered categories as 1, 2, 3 for linear or distance-based models.
  • Deploying without monitoring, so silent data changes go unnoticed.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Normalisation vs standardisation — Squeeze into a range vs centre and scale.
  • One-hot vs label vs ordinal encoding — Switches, ID numbers, or ranks.
  • Data drift vs concept drift — New questions vs new answers to old questions.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Where should the mean and standard deviation for scaling come from?

The trap: "From the whole dataset."

From the training data only, then reused unchanged for validation, test and production data. Computing them on everything leaks information about the test set.

When you one-hot encode a category for linear regression, why drop one column?

The trap: Keeping all columns by habit.

With an intercept, the one-hot columns always sum to 1, the same as the intercept column — perfect collinearity (the "dummy variable trap"). Dropping one column fixes it. Regularised models and trees don't need this.

Why is target encoding risky, and how is it done safely?

The trap: Replacing each category with its average target on the full data.

Each row's own label contributes to its encoded value, so rare categories leak the answer and the model looks unrealistically good. Compute encodings out of fold (from other folds' data only) and add smoothing towards the overall mean.

You oversample the minority class (e.g. SMOTE), then split into train and test. What's wrong?

The trap: Thinking resampling is just preprocessing.

Synthetic or duplicated minority examples end up on both sides, inflating the test score. Resample the training data only, inside cross-validation, and evaluate on untouched, naturally imbalanced data.

All 11 hidden questions for this lesson →

15.Key takeaways

  • Good features often matter more than the choice of algorithm.
  • Scale numbers for distance/gradient models, log-transform skewed amounts, one-hot encode categories, and impute missing values (optionally with an indicator).
  • Create features from domain knowledge: ratios, date parts, aggregates.
  • Put everything in a Pipeline + ColumnTransformer so it's fitted on training data only and deployed as one object.
  • Workflow: split → baseline → compare with CV → tune → test once → interpret → save → monitor.

16.Check your understanding

1. Why not encode cities as Chennai = 1, Mumbai = 2, Delhi = 3 for a linear model?

Arbitrary numbers impose a fake order and spacing. One-hot encoding treats categories as equally different.

2. Where should the median used to fill missing values come from?

Like all learned preprocessing statistics, it must come from training data to avoid leakage.

3. A column holds account balances from 0 to 5,000,000, mostly under 10,000. A sensible transformation is…

The log compresses the huge range so a few extreme values don't dominate. log1p also handles zeros.

4. What is the main advantage of putting preprocessing inside a Pipeline?

Pipelines prevent leakage and guarantee identical processing in training and deployment.

5. Your new model scores ROC-AUC 0.52 and the baseline scores 0.50. What does that tell you?

Always compare with a baseline; a tiny improvement over random ranking means little useful signal has been captured.

17.Going deeper: leak-proof pipelines and efficient tuning

In plain wordsHow much a single leaky feature can fake (73% accuracy on pure noise), how to process numbers, categories and text in one leak-proof pipeline, why random search usually beats grid search for the same budget, and how teams keep track of their experiments.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

The lesson above builds features and a pipeline for a full project. This section shows, with numbers, how much a single leaky encoding can fake, how to handle numbers, categories and text in one leak-proof pipeline, why random search usually beats grid search, and how teams keep track of hundreds of experiments. (A later intermediate lesson covers hyperparameter tuning in full.)

You'll need: this lesson, leakage from Lesson 5 and nested cross-validation from Lesson 5's "Going deeper".

Target encoding: how much leakage can fake

Target encoding replaces each category with the average target for that category. It's powerful for categories with many levels (postcodes, product IDs), but if the averages are computed using the rows you then evaluate on, each row's own target leaks into its feature. Here a category with 2,000 levels has no real relationship with the target, so the honest accuracy is 50%:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder

# A category with 2,000 levels (like a postcode) that has NO real link to the target
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 5000
code = rng.integers(0, 2000, n)
y = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)

# Wrong: encode with each level's average target computed on ALL the data, then cross-validate
means = pd.Series(y).groupby(code).mean()
leaky = means[code].to_numpy()[:, None]
print("naive target encoding, CV accuracy:", round(cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), leaky, y, cv=cv).mean(), 3))

# Right: TargetEncoder inside the pipeline (it also uses internal cross-fitting when training)
pipe = make_pipeline(TargetEncoder(cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)), LogisticRegression())
print("target encoding inside the pipeline, CV accuracy:", round(cross_val_score(pipe, code[:, None], y, cv=cv).mean(), 3))

Output:

naive target encoding, CV accuracy: 0.731
target encoding inside the pipeline, CV accuracy: 0.497

The naive encoding reports 73.1% accuracy on pure noise: with about 2.5 rows per level, each level's average is dominated by the rows' own labels. Inside the pipeline, scikit-learn's TargetEncoder is refitted on each training fold, and also uses cross-fitting during training (each training row is encoded using averages from the other internal folds), so the estimate drops to the honest 49.7%. Two further safeguards it applies: smoothing towards the overall average for rare levels, much like the Bayesian shrinkage in Lesson 4's "Going deeper", and handling of unseen levels.

One pipeline for mixed data

Real tables mix numbers, categories and text, each needing different preprocessing. ColumnTransformer applies the right steps to the right columns, and putting it inside a pipeline means every step is fitted on training folds only:

from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

# One pipeline for mixed data: numbers, a category and free text (Chennai Homes)
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")
df.loc[2, "age_yrs"] = np.nan                              # pretend one value is missing
prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler()), ["size_m2", "bedrooms", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["area"]),
    ("txt", TfidfVectorizer(), "description"),
])
model = make_pipeline(prep, Ridge(alpha=1.0))
scores = cross_val_score(model, df, df["price_lakh"], cv=KFold(4, shuffle=True, random_state=0), scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
print("columns after preprocessing:", prep.fit_transform(df).shape[1])
print("4-fold mean absolute error:", round(-scores.mean(), 1), "lakh")

Output:

columns after preprocessing: 30
4-fold mean absolute error: 7.0 lakh

Four numeric columns (one with a missing value, imputed with the training median and standardised), one-hot encoded areas and a TF-IDF of the descriptions give 30 columns, fed to ridge regression. Cross-validated on the 12 Chennai homes the mean error is about 7.0 lakh, which with so few homes is only an illustration. The important point is structural: the whole object can be cross-validated, tuned with GridSearchCV (parameter names such as columntransformer__num__simpleimputer__strategy) and saved as one file, so training and serving can't drift apart.

Grid search vs random search

A grid tries every combination of a few values per setting. Random search samples settings from ranges you specify. With the same budget it usually does as well or better, because typically only one or two settings really matter: a 3×3×2 grid tests just 3 distinct values of each, whereas 18 random draws test 18 different values of every setting (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012). Sample learning rates and penalties on a log scale (loguniform), since they matter by orders of magnitude.

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from scipy.stats import loguniform, randint

Xb, yb = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
gb = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0)
grid = GridSearchCV(gb, {"learning_rate": [0.03, 0.1, 0.3], "max_leaf_nodes": [7, 15, 31],
                         "l2_regularization": [0.0, 1.0]}, cv=5).fit(Xb, yb)
rand = RandomizedSearchCV(gb, {"learning_rate": loguniform(0.01, 0.5), "max_leaf_nodes": randint(4, 64),
                               "l2_regularization": loguniform(1e-3, 10)}, n_iter=18, cv=5, random_state=0).fit(Xb, yb)
print(f"grid search:   {len(grid.cv_results_['params'])} settings, best CV accuracy {grid.best_score_:.3f}")
print(f"random search: {len(rand.cv_results_['params'])} settings, best CV accuracy {rand.best_score_:.3f}")

Output:

grid search:   18 settings, best CV accuracy 0.975
random search: 18 settings, best CV accuracy 0.972

Here, with 18 settings each, both reach about the same best cross-validated accuracy (0.975 and 0.972, a difference well within noise). The advantage of random search grows with the number of settings: the grid's size multiplies, the random budget doesn't. Beyond random search, Bayesian optimisation (for example Optuna's TPE sampler) uses past results to choose promising settings next, and successive halving (HalvingRandomSearchCV) gives every candidate a little data and only the best ones more.

Keeping track of experiments

After a few weeks a project has hundreds of runs. Without records, nobody can say which data, code and settings produced the model in production. Good practice:

  • Log every run: parameters, metrics, the code version (a git commit), the data version, the random seed and the library versions. Tools such as MLflow and Weights & Biases do this with a few lines.
  • Version the data as well as the code (for example with DVC, or by storing immutable dated snapshots).
  • Save the whole pipeline, not just the model, together with a model card: intended use, training data, metrics by subgroup (Lesson 21) and known limitations.
  • Keep the test set out of the loop. Every decision taken by looking at test results makes them optimistic (Lesson 4's "Going deeper" on multiple testing).
Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

How would you build a pipeline for a table with numeric, categorical and text columns, so it can't leak?

The trap: Preprocessing the whole dataframe first, then splitting.

Use a ColumnTransformer inside a Pipeline: imputation and scaling for numbers, one-hot or target encoding (with cross-fitting) for categories, TF-IDF or embeddings for text, then the model. Cross-validate and tune the whole pipeline, so every statistic is learned from training folds only, and save it as one artifact so serving uses identical transformations.

Grid search, random search or Bayesian optimisation: which would you use?

The trap: Always grid search.

Grid search only for one or two settings with few values. Random search as a strong default: with the same budget it explores far more values of the settings that matter, and it parallelises trivially. Bayesian optimisation (e.g. Optuna/TPE) when each run is expensive, since it uses earlier results to pick the next settings. Add early stopping or successive halving to drop bad candidates cheaply. Report the final score with nested CV or a held-out test set.

Six months later, you need to reproduce the model in production exactly. What should have been recorded?

The trap: "The notebook."

The exact code version (commit), the data snapshot or version and how it was split, every parameter and random seed, library versions (requirements or lock file), the full preprocessing pipeline, and the evaluation metrics, ideally in an experiment tracker or model registry. Without the data version and the preprocessing, the same code can produce a different model.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. Target-encoding a category using averages computed on all the data, then cross-validating, gives…

On pure noise it reported 73% instead of 50%.

2. What does ColumnTransformer do?

Numbers, categories and text each get their own steps, all fitted on training folds only.

3. Why does random search often beat grid search with the same number of tries?

A grid wastes tries repeating the same few values of the important settings.

4. How should a learning rate between 0.001 and 1 be sampled?

Each order of magnitude should get similar attention; uniform sampling would mostly try values above 0.1.

5. Which should be logged with every training run?

Reproducing a model needs all of them.

18.Practice exercises

Work each exercise on paper (or in the lesson notebook), type your answer into the box to check it, and open the solution to compare your working. Answers can be decimals (round to 3 places), fractions like 2/3 or percentages like 75%. Every answer has been checked with Python. For hands-on coding practice, the lesson notebook ends with two coding challenges: fill in one missing line and an automatic check tells you whether it's right.

Exercise 1By hand

Training values of a feature are $10, 20, 30$. Standardise the new value 40 (divide by $n$).

Check your answer:

Show solution
$\mu = 20$, $\sigma = \sqrt{(100 + 0 + 100)/3} \approx 8.165$. $z = (40 - 20)/8.165 \approx 2.45$. Training statistics are reused — never recomputed on new data.
Exercise 2By hand

One-hot encode the sizes small, large, medium, small (categories in alphabetical order: large, medium, small).

Show solution
small → $(0, 0, 1)$; large → $(1, 0, 0)$; medium → $(0, 1, 0)$; small → $(0, 0, 1)$.
Exercise 3Concepts

What's wrong? X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), then train_test_split(X, y), then cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train).

Show solution
The scaler was fitted on all data (including test rows) — leakage. Split first and put the scaler inside a Pipeline so it's re-fitted on each fold.
Exercise 4Project

Extend the churn project: add a feature is_new_customer (tenure ≤ 6 months) inside add_features, add it to the numeric list, and re-run Steps 4–6. Did it help?

Show solution
Add X["is_new_customer"] = (X["tenure_months"] <= 6).astype(int). Compare the cross-validated ROC-AUC with the earlier 0.771. When we ran it, logistic regression stayed at exactly 0.771 — no gain. Tenure is already a feature, and the new column only repeats part of it. A useful lesson: a new feature must add new information. Any change smaller than the ± spread (about 0.01) isn't a real improvement.
Exercise 5Intermediate

A category level appears in 4 training rows with targets $1, 1, 0, 1$. The overall average is $0.3$. Using the smoothed encoding $\frac{n\,\bar{y}_{\text{level}} + m\,\bar{y}}{n + m}$ with $m = 6$, what is the level's encoding?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$\bar{y}_{\text{level}} = 0.75$. Encoding $= (4 \times 0.75 + 6 \times 0.3)/(4 + 6) = (3 + 1.8)/10 = 0.48$. The rare level is pulled strongly towards the overall average.
Exercise 6Intermediate

A grid search over 4 learning rates, 5 depths and 3 penalties, with 5-fold CV. How many model fits is that? How many different learning rates does it try?

Check your answers:

Show solution
$4 \times 5 \times 3 = 60$ settings $\times\ 5 = 300$ fits, but only 4 distinct learning rates. A random search with 60 settings would try 60.
Exercise 7Intermediate

Sampling learning rates log-uniformly between 0.001 and 1, what fraction of draws fall below 0.01?

Check your answer:

Show solution
The range covers 3 orders of magnitude, and 0.001 to 0.01 is one of them, so $1/3 \approx 0.333$. (Uniform sampling would give only 0.009.)

Lesson 21: Ethics & Fairness in Machine Learning

Where bias comes from, how to measure fairness per group, why the criteria conflict, and what to do about it.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Name the main kinds of harm and the places where bias enters an ML system
  • Compute selection rate, TPR, FPR and precision for each group from confusion-matrix counts
  • Explain demographic parity, equal opportunity, equalised odds and predictive parity, and the four-fifths rule
  • Explain why the fairness criteria conflict when base rates differ, and choose mitigations
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 5: Data, Features & Generalization — Always judge a model on data it hasn't seen: split into train / validation / test, or use k-fold cross-validation. Overfitting = low training error but high test error. Never let test data leak into training.
  • Lesson 8: Logistic Regression — Logistic regression outputs a probability $p = \sigma(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b)$, is trained with log loss, and classifies with a threshold (often 0.5), giving a straight decision boundary.
  • Lesson 9: Evaluating Models — Accuracy can mislead. Precision $= TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $= TP/(TP+FN)$, and F1 balances them. Moving the threshold trades one for the other; ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds.

Where this fits: Steps back from building models to ask who they affect. It reuses the confusion matrix from Lesson 9 and the threshold idea from Lesson 8 to measure and reduce unfairness.

1.Why fairness is a machine-learning problem

Imagine a bank that replaces its loan officers with a model trained on ten years of past decisions. The model is 88% accurate, fast and consistent. Is it fair? Accuracy alone can't tell you. If past officers turned down qualified applicants from one neighbourhood, the model has learned to do the same — automatically, at scale, and with an air of objectivity that makes it harder to challenge.

Machine learning finds patterns in data, and data records the world as it was, including its unfairness. A model doesn't need to be told anyone's ethnicity or gender to discriminate: other features — a postcode, a first name, a gap in employment — can act as proxies. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, the numbers and the habits to notice and reduce these problems.

The core idea

A model can be accurate on average while making very different kinds of mistakes for different groups of people. Fairness work means measuring those differences, deciding which ones matter for the situation, and acting on them — a job for people, informed by numbers.

2.What can go wrong: kinds of harm

  • Allocation harms: a resource or opportunity — a loan, a job interview, a medical referral — is withheld from some groups more than others.
  • Quality-of-service harms: the system simply works worse for some people, like face recognition or speech recognition with higher error rates for some groups.
  • Representation harms: outputs reinforce stereotypes or erase groups, such as image search or text generation that reproduces biased associations.
  • Privacy and autonomy harms: people are profiled, re-identified or manipulated using data they never agreed to share for that purpose.

3.Where bias comes from

Bias can enter at every step of the workflow you learned in Lesson 5:

  1. Historical bias: the world itself was unequal, so even a perfect record of it teaches the model those patterns (the Amazon hiring model, Lesson 1).
  2. Representation (sampling) bias: some groups are under-represented in the training data, so the model is less accurate for them.
  3. Measurement and label bias: the label is a proxy for what you care about. Using healthcare cost to stand for health need under-served Black patients (Obermeyer et al., 2019; Lesson 5).
  4. Aggregation bias: one model for everyone ignores real differences between groups — for example, a medical threshold that suits one population but not another.
  5. Evaluation bias: the test set or benchmark doesn't reflect the people the model will actually be used on.
  6. Deployment and feedback loops: the model's decisions change the future data. Police sent where a model predicts crime record more crime there, which "confirms" the prediction.

4.Measuring fairness with group metrics

Split your test set by group and compute the confusion matrix (Lesson 9) for each group separately. From those counts come the standard fairness measures:

MeasureFormula (per group)"Fair" means equal…Name of the criterion
Selection rate$\frac{TP + FP}{\text{all}}$share of people approvedDemographic parity
True-positive rate (recall)$\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$chance a qualified person is approvedEqual opportunity
TPR and false-positive rate$\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$ and $\frac{FP}{FP+TN}$both kinds of errorEqualised odds
Precision (PPV)$\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$how reliable an approval isPredictive parity

A common summary is the demographic-parity ratio: the lower selection rate divided by the higher one. In US employment law the "four-fifths rule" of thumb treats a ratio below 0.8 as evidence of possible adverse impact that needs explaining.

Worked example — one loan model, two groups

A bank tests its model on 100 applicants from each of two groups. In group A, 50 would repay; in group B, 20 would.

GroupTPFPFNTN
A4051045
B124876

Selection rate: A $= 45/100 = 0.45$; B $= 16/100 = 0.16$. Ratio $0.16/0.45 \approx 0.36$ — far below 0.8.

True-positive rate: A $= 40/50 = 0.80$; B $= 12/20 = 0.60$. A qualified applicant from B is approved less often.

False-positive rate: A $= 5/50 = 0.10$; B $= 4/80 = 0.05$.

Precision: A $= 40/45 \approx 0.89$; B $= 12/16 = 0.75$.

Accuracy: A $= 85/100 = 0.85$; B $= 88/100 = 0.88$ — the model is more accurate for group B even though it fails B's qualified applicants more often. Accuracy alone hides the problem.

Make sense of it

The situation: A bank's compliance officer audits the loan model before it goes live, comparing two groups of applicants.

What the result tells you: Group B is approved far less often (16% vs 45%), and qualified B applicants are approved less often (60% vs 80%) — yet B's accuracy is higher. Each metric answers a different fairness question.

What if…?

  • Lower group B's threshold so it approves 32 people (16 who would repay, 16 who wouldn't): selection 0.32 (ratio 0.71), TPR 0.80 (now equal to A), but FPR doubles to 0.20 and precision falls to 0.50.
  • A smaller audit: if group B had only 10 people, one applicant would move B's selection rate by 10 points. Small groups need confidence intervals before conclusions.

Why it matters in ML: Fairness metrics are the confusion matrix (Lesson 9) computed per group. Changing a threshold for one group moves all its metrics at once — the trade-offs are unavoidable, so decide which matters most with the people affected.

5.Try it: one threshold or two?

Two groups, A (half would repay) and B (one in five would repay), each get a score from the same model. Move the thresholds and watch the per-group rates. Try to make the selection rates equal; then try to make the true-positive rates equal; then notice what happens to precision and accuracy.

6.You can't have everything: the impossibility result

Why not just make every rate equal? Because, when the groups' base rates differ (here 50% vs 20%), it is mathematically impossible except for a perfect classifier. For any group, the four quantities are tied together by an identity (Chouldechova, 2017):

$$\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR},$$

where $p$ is the group's base rate. If two groups have the same PPV and the same TPR but different $p$, their FPRs must differ.

Worked example — checking the identity

Group A: $p = 0.5$, PPV $= 40/45$, TPR $= 0.8$: $\ \frac{0.5}{0.5}\cdot\frac{5/45}{40/45}\cdot 0.8 = 1\times0.125\times0.8 = 0.10$ ✓ (the FPR we computed).

Group B: $p = 0.2$, PPV $= 0.75$, TPR $= 0.6$: $\ \frac{0.2}{0.8}\cdot\frac{0.25}{0.75}\cdot0.6 = 0.25\times0.333\times0.6 = 0.05$ ✓.

Now suppose we tuned group B to match A's PPV (0.889) and TPR (0.8). The identity forces B's FPR to be $0.25\times0.125\times0.8 = 0.025$ — no longer equal to A's 0.10. Equal precision and equal opportunity together rule out equal false-positive rates.

Make sense of it

The situation: A regulator asks: "Can't you just make every error rate equal for both groups?"

What the result tells you: The identity links FPR, precision, TPR and the base rate. Because the groups' base rates differ (50% vs 20%), fixing two of the rates forces the third apart.

What if…?

  • Insist B's FPR equals A's 0.10 while keeping TPR 0.8: B's precision must drop to 0.67 (vs A's 0.89).
  • If both groups had the same base rate, the factor $\frac{p}{1-p}$ would be the same and all three rates could match.

Why it matters in ML: This is why fairness is a choice, not a setting. The impossibility comes from the data's base rates, not from a bad algorithm.

So choosing a fairness criterion is a value judgement. In lending, a bank may care most that qualified applicants are treated alike (equal opportunity). In criminal justice, critics of the COMPAS risk score (ProPublica, 2016) focused on unequal false-positive rates, while its makers pointed to equal predictive value — and both were right about their own measure. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2016) proved a closely related result for calibrated scores.

7.What you can do about it

  • Fix the data (before training): collect more data for under-represented groups, check that labels measure what you care about, remove or rethink proxy features, re-weight examples so groups count fairly.
  • Constrain the model (during training): add a fairness penalty or constraint to the loss, just as regularisation adds a penalty (Lesson 10). Libraries such as Fairlearn and AIF360 implement several methods.
  • Adjust decisions (after training): choose thresholds per group to equalise a chosen rate, as in the demo. This is effective but can be legally restricted, because it treats groups differently explicitly — get legal advice.
  • Change the system, not just the model: keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions, give people an explanation and a way to appeal, monitor outcomes after deployment, and be willing not to deploy.
"Fairness through unawareness" doesn't work

Deleting the protected attribute does not remove bias when other features are correlated with it — and it makes the bias harder to measure, because you can no longer compute group metrics. Most practitioners keep the attribute out of the model's inputs but use it for auditing.

8.Beyond fairness: privacy, transparency and accountability

  • Privacy: collect only the data you need, with consent. Models can leak training data (membership inference, Lesson 10); differential privacy adds carefully calibrated random noise during training so that no single person's record changes the result much.
  • Transparency: prefer interpretable models for high-stakes decisions, and explain outputs to the people affected. Document data with datasheets (Gebru et al.) and models with model cards (Mitchell et al., 2019).
  • Accountability: someone must be responsible for a model's decisions, and there must be a route to contest them. Laws such as the EU AI Act (see Recent developments) now require risk management, documentation and human oversight for high-risk uses such as hiring and credit.
  • Wider impact: energy use, effects on workers, and misuse (deepfakes, surveillance) are part of the responsibility too.

9.A practical checklist before you deploy

  1. Purpose: who is affected, what decision does the model inform, and is ML appropriate at all?
  2. Data: who is missing or under-represented? Is the label a fair proxy for the real goal?
  3. Metrics: compute the confusion matrix, selection rate, TPR, FPR and PPV for every relevant group — and the uncertainty when groups are small.
  4. Choose: decide with stakeholders which errors matter most here, and which fairness criterion you will hold the model to.
  5. Document: write a model card: intended use, evaluation by group, known limitations.
  6. Monitor: after deployment, track group metrics over time and watch for feedback loops; provide explanations and appeals.

10.In Python: a fairness report from scratch

Everything above is just the confusion matrix computed per group. Here is a small report on a synthetic loan dataset in which group B has a lower base rate:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# A synthetic loan dataset: two groups with different base rates of repayment
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
group = rng.choice(["A", "B"], size=n, p=[0.6, 0.4])
base = np.where(group == "A", 0.5, 0.2)              # share who would repay
repay = (rng.random(n) < base).astype(int)
score = np.clip(0.5 + 0.25 * (repay - 0.5) * 2 + rng.normal(0, 0.18, n), 0, 1)  # model's score
df = pd.DataFrame({"group": group, "repay": repay, "score": score})

def group_report(df, threshold):
    d = df.assign(approve=(df["score"] >= threshold).astype(int))
    rows = {}
    for g, s in d.groupby("group"):
        tp = ((s.approve == 1) & (s.repay == 1)).sum(); fp = ((s.approve == 1) & (s.repay == 0)).sum()
        fn = ((s.approve == 0) & (s.repay == 1)).sum(); tn = ((s.approve == 0) & (s.repay == 0)).sum()
        rows[g] = {"selection rate": (tp + fp) / len(s), "TPR": tp / (tp + fn), "FPR": fp / (fp + tn), "PPV": tp / (tp + fp)}
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)

r = group_report(df, threshold=0.6)
print(r)
print("demographic-parity ratio:", round(r.loc["B", "selection rate"] / r.loc["A", "selection rate"], 3))
   selection rate    TPR    FPR    PPV
A           0.430  0.799  0.039  0.956
B           0.178  0.801  0.025  0.887
demographic-parity ratio: 0.414

Read it like a fairness auditor: with one shared threshold, qualified applicants are treated alike — the true-positive rates are both 0.80 (equal opportunity holds). But group B is approved far less often (ratio 0.41, well below 0.8) and an approval is less reliable for B (PPV 0.89 vs 0.96) — both consequences of B's lower base rate, exactly as the impossibility result predicts.

11.Running example: Chennai Homes

Does the Lesson 8 model treat areas differently? It only sees distance and age, never the area name — yet distance is a near-perfect proxy for area. Every Central house is flagged as a fast seller (4 of 4), including the one that didn't sell fast (FPR 1.00); elsewhere only 3 of 8 are flagged and none wrongly. With 4 and 8 houses these rates are extremely noisy — one house moves a rate by 25 points — which is itself a fairness lesson: small groups need far more data before you trust their numbers.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
cols = ["dist_km", "age_yrs"]                 # the model never sees "area"
clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())
df["pred"] = cross_val_predict(clf, df[cols], df["sold_fast"], cv=4)   # honest out-of-fold predictions
df["group"] = np.where(df["area"] == "Central", "Central", "Not central")
for g, s in df.groupby("group"):
    tp = ((s.pred == 1) & (s.sold_fast == 1)).sum(); fp = ((s.pred == 1) & (s.sold_fast == 0)).sum()
    pos, neg = (s.sold_fast == 1).sum(), (s.sold_fast == 0).sum()
    print(f"{g:12s} n={len(s):2d}  base rate {s.sold_fast.mean():.3f}  flagged {s.pred.mean():.3f}  "
          f"TPR {tp / pos:.2f}  FPR {fp / neg if neg else float('nan'):.2f}")

Output:

Central      n= 4  base rate 0.750  flagged 1.000  TPR 1.00  FPR 1.00
Not central  n= 8  base rate 0.375  flagged 0.375  TPR 1.00  FPR 0.00
Where this is used
  • Auditing credit, hiring, insurance and healthcare models before deployment
  • Model cards and impact assessments required by regulators
  • Monitoring deployed models for unequal error rates

Choose it when: Always, whenever a model's decisions affect people.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythAlgorithms are objective because they are maths.

RealityThe maths is objective about the data it's given; the data, the label, the features and the threshold all carry human choices.

MythA model that's accurate overall is fair.

RealityOverall accuracy can hide very different error rates for different groups, as the worked example shows (88% accuracy for B, yet B's qualified applicants are approved less often).

MythWe can satisfy every fairness definition if we try hard enough.

RealityWhen base rates differ, it is mathematically impossible (except for a perfect model). You must choose which criterion matters most.

Responsible AI · Fairness is a process, not a number

No single metric certifies a model as fair. Fairness work means involving the people affected, documenting choices and their reasons, and keeping the ability to question, override and switch off the system. Metrics are evidence for that conversation, not a replacement for it.

12.Questions beginners often ask

If I remove gender and ethnicity from the data, is my model fair?

Not necessarily. Other features (postcode, school, first name) can act as proxies, and without the attribute you can no longer measure group differences. Keep it for auditing.

Which fairness metric is the right one?

There is no universal answer. Ask which mistake hurts people most in this situation: missing qualified people (compare TPR), wrongly flagging people (compare FPR), or unequal access overall (compare selection rates). Decide with the people affected.

Isn't the model just reflecting reality?

It reflects the data, which records past decisions and unequal access as well as reality. A model used to make future decisions can lock those patterns in, so 'it's in the data' is a reason to look closer, not a defence.

Are fairness rules the same everywhere?

No. Laws differ by country and by domain (lending, employment, housing). The four-fifths rule is a US guideline for employment, not a universal law. Get legal advice for real deployments.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Reporting only overall accuracy and never splitting the metrics by group.
  • Treating a tiny subgroup's rates as precise — with a handful of people, one person changes the rate a lot.
  • Deleting the protected attribute and assuming the problem is solved.
  • Choosing a fairness metric without involving the people the decisions affect.
Interview corner

Don't confuse

  • Demographic parity vs equal opportunity vs equalised odds — Equal approvals, equal chances for the qualified, or equal errors of both kinds.
  • Disparate treatment vs disparate impact — Intent in the rule vs effect in the outcome.

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

If you remove gender and ethnicity from the data, is the model fair?

The trap: "Yes, it can't see them."

Not necessarily. Other features (postcode, school, first name) act as proxies, and without the attribute you can't even measure group differences. Keep it out of the inputs if appropriate, but use it for auditing.

Can a model have equal precision, equal TPR and equal FPR across two groups?

The trap: "Just tune the thresholds."

Not if the groups' base rates differ (unless the model is perfect). The identity $\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR}$ forces at least one to differ. In Lesson 21's loan example, equalising FPR at 0.10 drops group B's precision to 0.67.

Group B's accuracy is higher than group A's. Does that show the model treats B fairly?

The trap: Using accuracy as the fairness measure.

No. In Lesson 21's example B had higher accuracy (0.88 vs 0.85) yet qualified B applicants were approved less often (TPR 0.60 vs 0.80). Compare the specific error rates that matter for the decision.

Is the four-fifths rule a law that defines fairness?

The trap: Treating it as universal.

It's a US employment-selection rule of thumb for spotting possible adverse impact, not a definition of fairness and not a law everywhere. Rules differ by country and domain.

All 8 hidden questions for this lesson →

13.Key takeaways

  • Models learn the unfairness in their data; proxies let them discriminate without seeing protected attributes.
  • Bias can enter through history, sampling, labels, aggregation, evaluation and feedback loops.
  • Fairness is measured by comparing per-group rates: selection rate (demographic parity), TPR (equal opportunity), TPR and FPR (equalised odds), precision (predictive parity).
  • When base rates differ, these criteria cannot all hold at once — choosing one is a value judgement to make with the people affected.
  • Mitigation happens in the data, the training, the thresholds and, above all, the surrounding system: documentation, human oversight, appeal and monitoring.
You've finished the course

That was the last lesson. To turn what you've learned into real skill, see What next: your learning plan — directions, a 12-week plan, project ideas and free resources.

14.Check your understanding

1. A model never receives applicants' ethnicity. Can it still discriminate by ethnicity?

Features like postcode or school are often correlated with protected attributes, so a model can reproduce group differences without the attribute itself.

2. Group A's selection rate is 0.50 and group B's is 0.30. What is the demographic-parity ratio, and does it pass the four-fifths rule of thumb?

$0.30/0.50 = 0.6$, which is below 0.8, so it would be flagged for possible adverse impact.

3. "Equal opportunity" asks which rate to be the same for every group?

Equal opportunity (Hardt, Price & Srebro, 2016) requires that qualified people — the true positives — are approved at the same rate in every group.

4. Two groups have different base rates. A model has equal precision and equal TPR for both. What must be true?

By the identity $\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR}$, different base rates $p$ force different FPRs.

5. A hospital model predicts healthcare spending to decide who gets extra care. What kind of bias is the biggest risk?

This is the Obermeyer et al. (2019) case: groups with less access to care spend less at the same level of need, so the label understates their need.

15.Going deeper: the impossibility result, measured

In plain wordsWhy fairness metrics conflict, with the one-line identity that proves it, a perfectly calibrated model that still has very different error rates for two groups, what group-specific thresholds gain and cost, and why fairness numbers for small groups need error bars.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

The lesson above introduces the main fairness metrics and states that they can conflict. This section proves why with one line of algebra, shows it happening to a model that is perfectly calibrated for both groups, measures what a common fix (group-specific thresholds) gains and costs, and shows why small groups make fairness numbers unreliable unless you report their uncertainty.

You'll need: this lesson, the confusion matrix from Lesson 9, calibration from Lesson 8's "Going deeper", and the bootstrap from Lesson 4's.

The identity behind the conflict

For any classifier and any group with base rate $p$ (the share of actual positives), the error rates are tied together by a simple identity, which follows from writing out the confusion matrix:

$$\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1 - \text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR}$$

Now suppose two groups have different base rates $p$. If the model has equal precision (PPV) in both groups and equal TPR, the identity forces their FPRs to differ. Equal PPV, equal TPR and equal FPR can hold together only if the base rates are equal or the classifier is perfect. This is the result of Chouldechova (2017); Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2016) proved a similar one for calibration. It's not a flaw of a particular model: it is arithmetic.

A perfectly calibrated model can still have unequal error rates

Below, every person's score is their true probability of the outcome, so the model is calibrated in both groups by construction: among people scored 0.6–0.7, about 63–65% have the outcome in either group. Group A's base rate is 0.287 and group B's is 0.500. With one threshold of 0.5 for everyone:

import numpy as np

# Two groups with different base rates; a model whose scores are perfectly calibrated in both groups
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def make_group(n, a, b):
    risk = rng.beta(a, b, n)                 # each person's true probability
    return risk, (rng.random(n) < risk).astype(int)
groups = {"group A": make_group(20000, 2, 5), "group B": make_group(20000, 4, 4)}

print("group     base rate   calibration (pred 0.6–0.7: actual)   TPR     FPR     PPV")
for g, (score, y) in groups.items():
    flag = score >= 0.5
    sel = (score >= 0.6) & (score < 0.7)
    tpr = flag[y == 1].mean(); fpr = flag[y == 0].mean(); ppv = y[flag].mean()
    print(f"{g:8}   {y.mean():9.3f}   {y[sel].mean():33.3f}   {tpr:.3f}   {fpr:.3f}   {ppv:.3f}")

Output:

group     base rate   calibration (pred 0.6–0.7: actual)   TPR     FPR     PPV
group A        0.287                               0.629   0.232   0.060   0.607
group B        0.500                               0.654   0.631   0.362   0.636

Precision is similar (0.607 and 0.636), but group A's true-positive rate is 0.232 against group B's 0.631, and its false-positive rate 0.060 against 0.362. A person in group A who truly has the outcome is far less likely to be flagged; a person in group B who doesn't is far more likely to be wrongly flagged. Which of those matters more depends entirely on what being flagged means: a loan refused, an extra medical test, a police stop. That's a decision for people, not for the metric.

Group-specific thresholds: what they buy and what they cost

One common mitigation is to choose a separate threshold for each group so that a chosen metric matches, here the true-positive rate ("equal opportunity"):

# Equalise true-positive rates with group-specific thresholds, and see what it costs
def rates(score, y, t):
    flag = score >= t
    return flag[y == 1].mean(), flag[y == 0].mean(), (flag == y).mean()

sA, yA = groups["group A"]; sB, yB = groups["group B"]
target_tpr = rates(sB, yB, 0.5)[0]
ts = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 181)
tA = ts[np.argmin([abs(rates(sA, yA, t)[0] - target_tpr) for t in ts])]
for name, t_A in [("one threshold 0.5 for both", 0.5), (f"threshold {tA:.3f} for group A", tA)]:
    tprA, fprA, accA = rates(sA, yA, t_A); tprB, fprB, accB = rates(sB, yB, 0.5)
    print(f"{name:28}: TPR A {tprA:.3f} / B {tprB:.3f}   FPR A {fprA:.3f} / B {fprB:.3f}   accuracy A {accA:.3f}")

Output:

one threshold 0.5 for both  : TPR A 0.232 / B 0.631   FPR A 0.060 / B 0.362   accuracy A 0.736
threshold 0.305 for group A : TPR A 0.634 / B 0.631   FPR A 0.320 / B 0.362   accuracy A 0.667

Lowering group A's threshold to about 0.305 brings its TPR to 0.634, matching group B's 0.631. The FPRs come closer too (0.320 and 0.362). But group A's accuracy falls from 0.736 to 0.667, because many more of its negatives are now flagged, and precision equality is lost. Every option moves along this trade-off; none removes it. In some countries and domains, using a protected attribute to set different thresholds is also legally restricted, so check before deploying. Alternatives include improving the data for under-served groups, adding features that are informative for them, or changing the decision itself (for example offering a review rather than a refusal).

Small groups: put error bars on fairness metrics

Fairness audits often compare metrics for small groups, and small groups make noisy estimates. Here group A's TPR is measured on just 400 people (106 actual positives):

# Small groups make fairness metrics noisy: bootstrap interval for a TPR measured on just 400 people
yS, sS = yA[:400], sA[:400]
pos = np.flatnonzero(yS == 1)
boot = [np.mean(sS[rng.choice(pos, len(pos))] >= 0.5) for _ in range(5000)]
print("positives in the small sample:", len(pos), "  TPR:", round(np.mean(sS[pos] >= 0.5), 3),
      "  95% interval:", np.round(np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5]), 3))

Output:

positives in the small sample: 106   TPR: 0.226   95% interval: [0.151 0.311]

The TPR is 0.226, but the 95% bootstrap interval runs from 0.151 to 0.311, wider than many gaps people report as unfair (or as fixed). Report intervals for every group's metrics; check intersections (for example older women, not just "women" and "older people"), where groups are smaller still; and treat large gaps on small groups as a reason to collect more evidence, not as a final verdict.

An audit checklist

StepQuestion
Decide what harm mattersIs a missed positive or a false alarm worse for the people affected?
Pick the metric before lookingEqual TPR, equal FPR, equal precision, calibration within groups, or demographic parity?
Measure every group and intersectionWith bootstrap intervals, on held-out data
Check calibration within each groupDo scores mean the same thing for everyone?
Compare mitigations with their costsThresholds, reweighting, better data, a different decision process
Document and monitorA model card, plus re-checks as data and base rates drift (Lesson 5's "Going deeper")
Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Prove that equal precision, equal TPR and equal FPR can't all hold across groups with different base rates.

The trap: Only citing the paper.

From the confusion matrix, $\text{FP} = \text{TP}(1 - \text{PPV})/\text{PPV}$, and $\text{FPR} = \text{FP}/N$, $\text{TPR} = \text{TP}/P$. So $\text{FPR} = \frac{P}{N}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR}$. If PPV and TPR are equal in both groups, FPR is proportional to $p/(1-p)$, which differs when base rates differ. Only a perfect classifier (PPV = 1, so FPR = 0) or equal base rates escape it.

Your audit shows a 6-point TPR gap between two groups. Is the model unfair?

The trap: Answering yes or no from the point estimate.

First, is the gap real? Compute bootstrap intervals; for small groups a 6-point gap can be noise. Second, is it the gap that matters for this decision (would a missed positive or a false positive cause the harm)? Third, look at calibration within groups and at intersections. Then compare mitigations (better data, thresholds, reweighting, changing the decision) with their costs, and document the choice.

What are group-specific thresholds, and what are their downsides?

The trap: Presenting them as a free fix.

Choosing a different decision threshold per group so that a target metric (for example TPR) matches. Downsides: other metrics (precision, FPR, accuracy) move, sometimes worse for the same group; it requires knowing the protected attribute at decision time; it may be legally restricted in some domains; and it treats the symptom, while the underlying data or feature gap remains.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. Two groups have different base rates. A model has equal precision and equal TPR in both. Its FPRs must be…

From $\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR}$, different $p$ forces different FPR.

2. A model is perfectly calibrated in both groups. Does that guarantee equal true-positive rates?

In the example, calibrated scores gave TPR 0.232 vs 0.631.

3. Lowering one group's threshold to equalise TPR typically…

More people are flagged, including more true negatives: in the example FPR rose from 0.060 to 0.320.

4. A group's TPR is 0.23 measured on 100 positives. What should you report?

With about 100 positives the 95% interval spans roughly ±0.08.

5. Who should decide which fairness metric matters most?

The metrics encode different values; choosing between them is not a technical question.

Work each exercise on paper (or in the lesson notebook), type your answer into the box to check it, and open the solution to compare your working. Answers can be decimals (round to 3 places), fractions like 2/3 or percentages like 75%. Every answer has been checked with Python. For hands-on coding practice, the lesson notebook ends with two coding challenges: fill in one missing line and an automatic check tells you whether it's right.

Exercise 1By hand

Group A: 60 of 200 applicants approved. Group B: 30 of 150 approved. Compute both selection rates and the demographic-parity ratio. Does it pass the four-fifths rule of thumb?

Check your answers:

Show solution
A: $60/200 = 0.30$. B: $30/150 = 0.20$. Ratio $= 0.20/0.30 \approx 0.667$, below 0.8, so it would be flagged for possible adverse impact.
Exercise 2By hand

In group C, 40 people would repay a loan; the model approves 30 of them. Of the 60 who would not repay, it approves 6. Compute TPR, FPR and precision.

Check your answers:

Show solution
TPR $= 30/40 = 0.75$. FPR $= 6/60 = 0.10$. Precision $= 30/(30+6) = 30/36 \approx 0.833$.
Exercise 3By hand

A group has base rate $p = 0.25$, precision 0.8 and TPR 0.6. Use the identity $\text{FPR} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\text{PPV}}{\text{PPV}}\cdot\text{TPR}$ to find its FPR.

Check your answer:

Show solution
$\frac{0.25}{0.75}\cdot\frac{0.2}{0.8}\cdot 0.6 = 0.3333\times0.25\times0.6 = 0.05$.
Exercise 4Concepts

A university admissions model is trained on past admissions decisions. List two ways bias could enter, and one check you would run before using it.

Show solution
Historical bias: past decisions may have favoured some schools or groups, and the model copies them. Measurement bias: 'admitted' is a proxy for 'would succeed'. Representation bias: some groups have few past applicants. Check: compute selection rate and TPR (using later student success as the outcome) per group, with uncertainty for small groups.
Exercise 5Project

Take the synthetic loan data from the Python section. Choose a separate threshold for group B so that its selection rate is within 0.8 of group A's. What happens to B's TPR, FPR and precision?

Show solution
Lowering B's threshold raises its selection rate; TPR and FPR both rise and precision falls. Equalising one rate moves the others — the trade-off from the impossibility result. The exact numbers depend on the threshold you pick.
Exercise 6Intermediate

A group has base rate $p = 0.2$, precision $0.6$ and TPR $0.75$. Use the identity to find its FPR.

Check your answer:

Show solution
$\text{FPR} = \frac{0.2}{0.8}\cdot\frac{0.4}{0.6}\cdot 0.75 = 0.25 \times 0.6667 \times 0.75 = 0.125$.
Exercise 7Intermediate

Another group has the same precision ($0.6$) and TPR ($0.75$) but base rate $p = 0.5$. What is its FPR?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$\frac{0.5}{0.5}\cdot\frac{0.4}{0.6}\cdot 0.75 = 1 \times 0.6667 \times 0.75 = 0.5$: four times the first group's, as the identity predicts.
Exercise 8Intermediate

A TPR of 0.25 is measured on 100 positives. Using the normal approximation $\pm 1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, give the 95% interval.

Check your answer — for several numbers, separate them with commas:

Show solution
$\sqrt{0.25 \times 0.75/100} = 0.0433$; $\pm 1.96 \times 0.0433 = \pm 0.0849$. Interval about $[0.165,\ 0.335]$.
