Part 6 · Intermediate topics · ~60 min

Lesson 24: Interpretability & Explainable ML

Explain models globally and locally: standardised weights, permutation importance, partial dependence and ICE, SHAP values from scratch, LIME, and the traps.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Tell global from local explanations and choose a method for each question
  • Compute and read permutation importance and partial-dependence / ICE plots
  • Compute Shapley values by hand for a small model and explain their fairness properties
  • Spot misleading explanations: correlated features, unrealistic inputs and importance mistaken for causation
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 6: Linear Regression — Linear regression predicts $\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b$ and chooses the weights that minimise the mean squared error (least squares). $R^2$ measures the share of variance explained.
  • Lesson 13: Decision Trees — A decision tree asks a sequence of 'feature ≤ threshold?' questions chosen to reduce impurity (Gini or entropy). Deep trees overfit and are unstable.
  • Lesson 14: Random Forests & Boosting —

Where this fits: Opens up the models of Parts 2–5. It builds on standardised weights (Lesson 6), tree importances and their flaws (Lessons 13–14) and turns them into trustworthy explanations.

1.Why explain a model?

A bank's model refuses a loan. The applicant asks why. The regulator asks how the model decides. The data scientist wants to know whether it learned something real or a shortcut, such as a hospital's scanner model that "detects" pneumonia by reading the hospital's name printed on the X-ray. Accuracy answers none of these questions.

Interpretability methods answer two kinds of question:

  • Global: how does the model behave overall? Which features matter most, and how does the prediction change as a feature changes?
  • Local: why did the model make this prediction for this person?

This lesson covers the methods practitioners use most: reading linear weights properly, permutation importance, partial-dependence and ICE plots, SHAP values (built from scratch, so there's no mystery), and LIME-style local surrogates, along with the traps that make explanations misleading.

The core idea

An explanation is itself a simplified model of the model. Global methods summarise behaviour across all the data; local methods describe one prediction. Every method answers a specific, narrow question, and none of them says what causes the outcome in the real world: only what the model relies on.

2.Reading linear models properly

For linear and logistic regression the weights are the explanation, but only if the features are on comparable scales. A weight per millimetre and a weight per kilometre can't be compared. Standardise first (Lesson 10), and each weight becomes "the change in log-odds for a one-standard-deviation increase in the feature":

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

data = load_breast_cancer()
X, y, names = data.data, data.target, data.feature_names      # target 1 = benign
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)
lin = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=0.1, max_iter=5000)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
coef = pd.Series(lin[-1].coef_[0], index=names)
print("largest standardised weights (positive pushes towards benign):")
print(coef.reindex(coef.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index).head(5).round(3))

Output:

largest standardised weights (positive pushes towards benign):
worst texture          -0.543
worst radius           -0.529
worst perimeter        -0.496
worst concave points   -0.469
worst area             -0.463
dtype: float64

On the breast-cancer data (target 1 = benign), the five largest standardised weights are all negative: larger "worst" tumour measurements push the prediction away from benign. Three cautions from earlier lessons apply. Correlated features share and swap weight (Lesson 6's "Going deeper": radius, perimeter and area are almost the same measurement here). Regularization shrinks weights. And a weight describes association in this model, not cause.

3.Permutation importance

For any model, permutation importance asks: how much worse does the model get if this feature's information is destroyed? Shuffle one column of the test data, which breaks its link to the target but keeps its distribution, and measure the drop in score. Repeat with several shuffles and average. Lesson 13's "Going deeper" showed why this is more honest than a tree's built-in impurity importance.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("test accuracy:", round(rf.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
perm = permutation_importance(rf, X_te, y_te, n_repeats=30, random_state=0)
imp = pd.Series(perm.importances_mean, index=names).sort_values(ascending=False)
print("permutation importance on test data (drop in accuracy):")
print(imp.head(5).round(4))

Output:

test accuracy: 0.953
permutation importance on test data (drop in accuracy):
worst radius            0.0211
worst area              0.0177
worst concave points    0.0156
worst texture           0.0131
worst perimeter         0.0131
dtype: float64

The random forest's accuracy falls most when "worst radius" is shuffled (by 0.021, about 2 percentage points). The drops are small because the features are highly correlated: when one is shuffled, the forest can lean on a near-copy. That's the main weakness of permutation importance; the fix is to shuffle groups of correlated features together, or to read the results as "unique information this feature adds".

4.Partial dependence and ICE plots

Importance says how much a feature matters, not how. A partial-dependence plot (PDP) shows the average prediction as one feature is varied: set the feature to a value $v$ for every row, predict, average, and repeat for a grid of values:

$$\text{PD}(v) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f\big(v,\ \mathbf{x}_{i,\text{other}}\big)$$

An ICE plot (individual conditional expectation) draws one such curve per row instead of their average, revealing whether different people respond differently.

from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence

d = load_diabetes()
Xd, yd = d.data, d.target
gbr = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(Xd, yd)
bmi = list(d.feature_names).index("bmi")
pd_res = partial_dependence(gbr, Xd, [bmi], grid_resolution=6, kind="both")
print("bmi (scaled):        ", np.round(pd_res["grid_values"][0], 3))
print("average prediction:  ", np.round(pd_res["average"][0], 1))
ice = pd_res["individual"][0]
print("ICE spread at each bmi value (std across patients):", np.round(ice.std(axis=0), 1))

Output:

bmi (scaled):         [-0.067 -0.036 -0.005  0.025  0.056  0.087]
average prediction:   [130.9 129.1 141.7 176.4 177.  209.7]
ICE spread at each bmi value (std across patients): [45.2 40.6 49.  42.6 45.4 45.8]

For a gradient-boosting model of diabetes progression, the average prediction rises from about 131 to 210 as BMI goes from low to high: a clear, mostly increasing effect, with a jump in the middle of the range. The ICE curves are spread out by about 40–49 units at every BMI value, so patients' baseline predictions differ a lot even though the BMI effect is similar. One warning: a PDP sets BMI to every value for every patient, including combinations that don't occur in real data (say, very high BMI with very low weight-related blood measures). With strongly correlated features, prefer ALE plots (accumulated local effects), which only use realistic nearby values.

5.SHAP values: fair credit for each feature

For one prediction, we'd like to split "prediction minus the average prediction" into a contribution from each feature. The fair way to do it comes from cooperative game theory: the Shapley value. Treat features as players and the prediction as the payout. A feature's Shapley value is its average extra contribution when it joins, averaged over every possible order in which the features could join:

$$\phi_j = \sum_{S \subseteq F \setminus \{j\}} \frac{|S|!\,(p - |S| - 1)!}{p!}\Big[v(S \cup \{j\}) - v(S)\Big]$$

Here $v(S)$ is the model's expected prediction when only the features in $S$ are known; the unknown ones are filled in from a background sample. Shapley values are the only way of splitting the credit that is fair in a precise sense:

  • Efficiency: the contributions add up exactly to prediction minus baseline.
  • Symmetry: two features that always contribute equally get equal credit.
  • Dummy: a feature that never changes the prediction gets 0.
Worked example — Shapley values by hand

A tiny model: $f = 2x_1 + 3x_2 + 4x_1x_3$, explained at $\mathbf{x} = (1, 0.5, 1)$ against the baseline $(0, 0, 0)$, where $f = 0$. So the total to share is $f(\mathbf{x}) = 2 + 1.5 + 4 = 7.5$.

$x_2$ enters the model on its own, so it adds $3 \times 0.5 = 1.5$ whenever it joins: $\phi_2 = 1.5$.

$x_1$ always adds its own $2$. It also adds the interaction $4$, but only if $x_3$ has already joined, which happens in half of the orderings. So $\phi_1 = 2 + 4 \times \tfrac12 = 4$.

$x_3$ has no effect of its own; it adds the interaction $4$ only if $x_1$ is already in (half the orderings): $\phi_3 = 2$.

Check: $4 + 1.5 + 2 = 7.5$ ✓. The interaction's credit is split equally between the two features that create it.

The same formula, computed exactly for a gradient-boosting model on four diabetes features and one patient:

from itertools import combinations
from math import factorial

# Exact Shapley values for a model on 4 features, for one patient
feats = ["bmi", "bp", "s5", "age"]
idx = [list(d.feature_names).index(f) for f in feats]
X4 = Xd[:, idx]
model4 = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X4, yd)
background = X4[:100]                    # "absent" features are filled in from these patients
x = X4[200]

def value(subset):
    """Average prediction when the features in `subset` take x's values and the others vary as in the background."""
    Z = background.copy()
    Z[:, list(subset)] = x[list(subset)]
    return model4.predict(Z).mean()

p = len(feats); shap = np.zeros(p)
for j in range(p):
    others = [k for k in range(p) if k != j]
    for size in range(p):
        for S in combinations(others, size):
            weight = factorial(size) * factorial(p - size - 1) / factorial(p)
            shap[j] += weight * (value(S + (j,)) - value(S))

base, pred = value(()), model4.predict(x[None, :])[0]
for f, v in zip(feats, shap):
    print(f"{f:4}: {v:+7.2f}")
print(f"baseline {base:.2f}, plus the contributions ({shap.sum():.2f}), gives {base + shap.sum():.2f}")
print(f"the model's actual prediction: {pred:.2f}")

Output:

bmi :  -11.11
bp  :   +2.11
s5  :  -13.74
age :   +5.26
baseline 136.35, plus the contributions (-17.47), gives 118.87
the model's actual prediction: 118.87

The baseline (average prediction over the background patients) is 136.35. For this patient, low s5 (a blood-serum measure) lowers the prediction by 13.74 and low BMI by 11.11, while age adds 5.26 and blood pressure 2.11. The four contributions add to −17.47, giving 118.87, exactly the model's prediction: the efficiency property in action.

The exact formula needs $2^p$ subsets, so with 4 features it's 16 evaluations, but with 40 features it's about a trillion. The shap library makes it practical with clever approximations: KernelSHAP (a weighted regression over sampled subsets, for any model) and TreeSHAP (an exact, fast algorithm for tree ensembles). Plotting many patients' SHAP values together gives global views too: a "beeswarm" plot shows each feature's contributions across the whole dataset.

6.Try it: Shapley values for a tiny model

The model is $f = 2x_1 + 3x_2 + 4x_1x_3$, explained against the baseline $(0, 0, 0)$. Move the sliders and watch the contributions. Set $x_3 = 0$ and see $x_1$'s share of the interaction disappear; set $x_1 = 0$ and $x_3$ gets nothing at all.

7.Local surrogates (LIME)

LIME (local interpretable model-agnostic explanations) explains one prediction by fitting a simple model, usually linear, that imitates the black box near that point: create many perturbed copies of the example, ask the black box to predict them, weight each copy by how close it is, and fit a weighted linear regression. Its slopes are the explanation:

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

# A LIME-style local explanation: fit a weighted linear model to the black box near one patient
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
scale = X4.std(axis=0)
Z = x + rng.normal(0, 0.5, size=(2000, 4)) * scale          # perturbed copies of the patient
w = np.exp(-np.sum(((Z - x) / scale) ** 2, axis=1) / 2)        # nearer copies count more
local = Ridge(alpha=1e-3).fit((Z - x) / scale, model4.predict(Z), sample_weight=w)
print("local slopes (prediction change per +1 standard deviation):")
for f, c in zip(feats, local.coef_):
    print(f"{f:4}: {c:+7.2f}")

Output:

local slopes (prediction change per +1 standard deviation):
bmi :   +9.25
bp  :   +7.68
s5  :  +21.64
age :   +8.76

Near this patient, the model's prediction rises by about 22 units per standard deviation of s5 and by 7.7–9.3 units for the others. Notice these are slopes ("what if s5 increased a little?"), while the SHAP values above were contributions ("how much did this patient's s5 move the prediction from average?"). Both are valid; they answer different questions. LIME's results depend on choices such as the neighbourhood width and the sampling, and can change from run to run, which is why SHAP, with its guarantees, is more widely used.

8.How explanations mislead

  • Importance is not causation. A model may lean on a feature because it's correlated with the true cause. Changing that feature in the real world won't change the outcome (Lesson 4: correlation vs causation).
  • Correlated features share, split or hide credit. Methods that perturb one feature at a time also create unrealistic inputs.
  • Explanations describe the model, including its mistakes. If the model learned a shortcut (a watermark, a hospital ID), a faithful explanation shows the shortcut. That's a feature, not a bug: it's how shortcuts are found.
  • Different methods answer different questions (weights, drops in score, average curves, contributions, local slopes). Say which one you're reporting.
  • Simple, interpretable models (a short tree, a sparse linear model, a scorecard) are sometimes nearly as accurate as a black box. When the stakes are high, consider them first rather than explaining a black box afterwards (Rudin, 2019).

9.In Python: an explanation workflow

A typical sequence for a tabular model: check global importance on test data, look at the effect shape of the top features, then explain individual predictions.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance, partial_dependence

d = load_diabetes()
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(d.data, d.target, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
model = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

# 1. Global: which features does the model rely on? (on test data)
perm = permutation_importance(model, X_te, y_te, n_repeats=20, random_state=0, scoring="r2")
top = np.argsort(perm.importances_mean)[::-1][:3]
print("top features:", [d.feature_names[i] for i in top], np.round(perm.importances_mean[top], 3))

# 2. Shape: how does the prediction change with the most important feature?
pdr = partial_dependence(model, X_tr, [top[0]], grid_resolution=5, method="brute")
print("partial dependence:", np.round(pdr["average"][0], 1))

Output:

top features: ['s5', 'bmi', 'bp'] [0.221 0.181 0.043]
partial dependence: [103.4 129.  155.  186.5 194.5]

Shuffling s5 lowers the test $R^2$ the most (by 0.221), followed by BMI (0.181) and blood pressure (0.043), and the predicted progression rises steadily with s5, from about 103 to 195. For step 3, local explanations, install the shap library: shap.TreeExplainer(model)(X_te) gives exact SHAP values for tree models in milliseconds, and shap.plots.waterfall draws one prediction's contributions like the bars in the demo.

10.Running example: Chennai Homes

For a linear model with standardised features, each feature's SHAP value is simply its weight times its centred value, so explanations are exact and cheap. House 5 (a new Suburb villa) starts from the average price, then gains for its size, loses a little for its distance, and gains for being new; the contributions add up exactly to the model's prediction.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
cols = ["size_m2", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df[cols])
lr = LinearRegression().fit(Xs, df["price_lakh"])
base = lr.intercept_                                  # average price (features are centred)
contrib = Xs * lr.coef_                               # for a linear model, SHAP = weight × centred value
h = 4                                                 # house id 5
print("baseline", round(base, 1), "| contributions:", {c: float(v) for c, v in zip(cols, contrib[h].round(1))})
print("prediction", round(base + contrib[h].sum(), 1), "| actual", df.price_lakh[h])

Output:

baseline 72.1 | contributions: {'size_m2': 2.4, 'dist_km': -0.2, 'age_yrs': 8.6}
prediction 82.9 | actual 88
Where this is used
  • Explaining credit, insurance and medical decisions to customers and regulators
  • Debugging models that learned shortcuts or leaked features
  • Building stakeholder trust and choosing which features to collect

Choose it when: Whenever a model's predictions affect people or must be justified, and always while debugging.

Think twice when: you could use a simple model that is interpretable by design and nearly as accurate.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythA feature with high importance causes the outcome.

RealityIt's what the model relies on. The feature may just be correlated with the true cause.

MythSHAP values tell you what would happen if you changed a feature.

RealityThey split one prediction into contributions relative to a baseline. What-if questions need the model's curve (ICE) or, for the real world, causal analysis.

MythDeep models can't be explained, so they can't be trusted.

RealityMany tools work for any model. But for high-stakes decisions, an interpretable model is often almost as accurate and is easier to trust.

Responsible AI · Explanations people can act on

Laws such as the EU's GDPR and AI Act, and lending rules in many countries, expect meaningful reasons for automated decisions. A useful explanation is one the affected person can understand and act on ("your debt-to-income ratio was the main factor"), not a list of 40 numbers. Check that explanations are faithful to the model, stable, and don't reveal other people's data.

11.Questions beginners often ask

Should I use SHAP or permutation importance?

Both, for different questions. Permutation importance gives a quick, honest global ranking on test data. SHAP explains individual predictions and, aggregated, also gives global views. For tree models, TreeSHAP is fast and exact.

Do I need the shap library?

For real projects, yes: it implements fast approximations and plots. This lesson computes exact Shapley values from scratch so you know what the library is doing, but the exact method needs 2^p evaluations and only works for a handful of features.

Can explanations prove a model is fair?

No. They show what a model uses, which helps you find proxies and shortcuts (Lesson 21), but fairness is judged by outcomes and error rates per group.

Why do different methods rank features differently?

They measure different things: weights, score drops on test data, impurity on training data, average contributions. Correlated features also share credit in method-dependent ways. Report which method you used.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Comparing raw linear weights of features measured in different units.
  • Computing permutation importance on training data, where overfitting inflates it.
  • Reading importance as causation.
  • Trusting a PDP when the feature is strongly correlated with others (use ALE or ICE).
  • Reporting a single LIME explanation without checking that it is stable.
Interview corner

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

What's the difference between permutation importance and a tree's built-in feature importance?

The trap: Treating them as the same number.

Built-in (impurity) importance sums how much each feature reduced impurity during training: it's computed on training data and favours features with many distinct values, so noise can rank highly. Permutation importance measures the drop in a held-out score when the feature is shuffled: model-agnostic and honest, though correlated features can hide each other. Prefer permutation importance (or SHAP) for reporting.

Explain Shapley values and the properties that make them attractive.

The trap: Calling SHAP "just feature importance".

A feature's Shapley value is its average marginal contribution to the prediction over all orders in which features could be revealed, with absent features filled in from a background. They satisfy efficiency (contributions sum to prediction minus baseline), symmetry, dummy (no effect, zero credit) and additivity, and are the unique attribution with these properties. Exact computation is exponential, so KernelSHAP samples and TreeSHAP exploits tree structure.

A PDP shows a strong effect of feature A, but A is highly correlated with B. What could go wrong?

The trap: Trusting the curve as-is.

A PDP sets A to every value for every row while keeping B as it is, creating unrealistic combinations (high A with low B) that the model never saw, so the curve may reflect extrapolation. Credit may also be split arbitrarily between A and B. Use ALE plots or conditional methods, check ICE curves, and interpret A and B together.

Your model's top feature is the patient's hospital ID. What do you do?

The trap: Celebrating the high accuracy.

Treat it as a red flag for a shortcut or leakage: the model may be learning which hospital treats sicker patients, or a data-collection artefact, which won't generalise to new hospitals. Remove or group the feature, validate on hospitals the model never saw (group split), and look for other proxies. Explanations are most valuable exactly for finding this.

All 6 hidden questions for this lesson →

12.Key takeaways

  • Global explanations describe overall behaviour; local ones explain one prediction.
  • Linear weights are explanations only after standardising, and correlated features share their weight.
  • Permutation importance: the drop in test score when one feature is shuffled. Model-agnostic, but correlated features hide each other.
  • PDP and ICE show how the prediction changes with a feature, on average and per row; use ALE when features are strongly correlated.
  • SHAP values split prediction minus baseline into fair contributions that add up exactly; TreeSHAP makes them fast for tree models.
  • Explanations describe the model, not the world: importance is not causation.

13.Check your understanding

1. Permutation importance measures…

Shuffling destroys the feature's information; a big drop means the model relied on it.

2. A model's baseline prediction is 100 and it predicts 130 for Priya. Her SHAP values must add up to…

Efficiency: contributions sum to prediction minus baseline.

3. In $f = 4x_1x_3$, explained at $x_1 = x_3 = 1$ against a baseline of 0, the SHAP value of $x_1$ is…

The interaction's credit is shared equally between the two features that create it.

4. A PDP shows predictions rising with "number of support calls". Can we conclude that more support calls cause customers to leave?

Unhappy customers call support and also leave; the calls may be a symptom, not a cause.

5. ICE curves for a feature are parallel lines at different heights. What does that suggest?

Parallel curves mean the same shape of effect for each row; crossing or diverging curves reveal interactions.

14.Going deeper: when features are correlated

In plain wordsWhen two features carry the same information, explanation methods disagree: permutation importance shows what the model uses, drop-column importance shows what is replaceable, and SHAP splits credit arbitrarily between near-copies. For linear models, a feature's SHAP value is simply its weight times how far the value is from average.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

Almost every real dataset has correlated features, and that's where explanation methods disagree most. This section puts two near-identical features into a model and compares how permutation importance, drop-column importance and SHAP share the credit, then shows the exact SHAP formula for linear models and how SHAP values become a global ranking.

You'll need: this lesson, and multicollinearity from Lesson 6's "Going deeper".

Three methods, three answers

Here the target depends on a (weight 3) and c (weight 1). Feature b is a near-copy of a that adds nothing new. Drop-column importance retrains the model without each feature and measures the loss; it answers "what would we lose if we didn't have this feature at all?"

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

# Two copies of the same signal: how do importance methods share the credit?
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
a = rng.normal(size=n); b = a + rng.normal(0, 0.05, n)        # b is almost a copy of a
c = rng.normal(size=n)
X = np.column_stack([a, b, c]); y = 3 * a + 1 * c + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
perm = permutation_importance(rf, X_te, y_te, n_repeats=10, random_state=0, scoring="r2").importances_mean
print("permutation importance (a, b, c):", perm.round(3))

# Drop-column importance: retrain without each feature and measure the loss
full = rf.score(X_te, y_te)
drop = [full - RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(np.delete(X_tr, j, 1), y_tr).score(np.delete(X_te, j, 1), y_te) for j in range(3)]
print("drop-column importance (a, b, c):", np.round(drop, 3))

Output:

permutation importance (a, b, c): [1.045 0.129 0.172]
drop-column importance (a, b, c): [0.004 0.    0.117]

Permutation importance says a matters most (1.045) and gives b some credit (0.129), because the forest happens to split on both. Drop-column importance says neither a nor b matters much (0.004 and 0): remove one and the model simply uses the other. Only c, which carries unique information, loses a lot when dropped (0.117). Neither answer is wrong: permutation asks "does this model use the feature?", drop-column asks "is the information replaceable?". When features are correlated, report them as a group, or shuffle or drop the whole group together.

Exact SHAP for linear models, and global SHAP

For a linear model $f(\mathbf{x}) = b + \sum_j w_jx_j$ with independent features, the Shapley value has a closed form: $\phi_j = w_j\,(x_j - \bar{x}_j)$, the weight times how far this row's value is from the average. Averaging $|\phi_j|$ over many rows gives a global importance in the units of the prediction:

# For a linear model the exact SHAP value of feature j is w_j * (x_j - mean_j); averaging |SHAP| gives a global ranking
lin = LinearRegression().fit(X_tr, y_tr)
shap_vals = lin.coef_ * (X_te - X_tr.mean(axis=0))
print("weights (a, b, c):            ", lin.coef_.round(2))
print("mean |SHAP| per feature:      ", np.abs(shap_vals).mean(axis=0).round(3))
print("check, first row: baseline + contributions", round(lin.predict(X_tr).mean() + shap_vals[0].sum(), 4), "vs prediction", round(lin.predict(X_te[:1])[0], 4))

Output:

weights (a, b, c):             [2.75 0.24 1.02]
mean |SHAP| per feature:       [2.31  0.202 0.791]
check, first row: baseline + contributions 3.9815 vs prediction 3.9815

The linear model split the effect of the near-duplicates as 2.75 for a and 0.24 for b; with different random noise the split could easily come out differently (Lesson 6's "Going deeper" on unstable weights). The mean absolute SHAP values (2.31, 0.20, 0.79) inherit that arbitrary split. And the efficiency check holds: baseline plus contributions equals the prediction exactly (3.9815). Two ways to explain with correlated features: interventional SHAP (the default in most tools) treats features as independent and explains the model; conditional SHAP respects the correlations and explains the data-generating relationship more, but is harder to compute and can give credit to features the model never uses.

Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Permutation importance, drop-column importance and SHAP rank your features differently. How do you explain that to a stakeholder?

The trap: Picking whichever ranking looks most sensible.

They answer different questions. Permutation importance: how much does this trained model rely on the feature's information? Drop-column: how much would we lose if the feature didn't exist and we retrained (low for features with substitutes)? SHAP: how much does each feature move individual predictions from the baseline? Correlated features cause most of the disagreement, so report correlated groups together and say which question each number answers.

What's the closed-form SHAP value for a linear model, and what assumption does it rely on?

The trap: Saying the SHAP value equals the weight.

$\phi_j = w_j(x_j - E[x_j])$: the weight times the row's deviation from the feature's mean. It assumes features are independent (interventional SHAP), so with correlated features it explains the model's arithmetic rather than how the features move together in reality.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. Two near-identical features both have drop-column importance close to 0. The best conclusion is…

Dropping one lets the model use the other. Drop or shuffle them as a group to see their joint importance.

2. For a linear model with weight 2 on feature $x$, mean of $x$ 5 and a row with $x = 8$, the SHAP value of $x$ is…

$w(x - \bar{x}) = 2 \times 3 = 6$.

3. What does drop-column importance require that permutation importance doesn't?

That's why it's expensive, but it measures how replaceable each feature's information is.

4. Global SHAP importance is usually computed as…

Absolute values stop positive and negative contributions cancelling out.

5. Interventional SHAP treats features as…

It explains the model's behaviour; conditional SHAP respects correlations in the data instead.

15.Practice exercises

Work each exercise on paper (or in the lesson notebook), type your answer into the box to check it, and open the solution to compare your working. Answers can be decimals (round to 3 places), fractions like 2/3 or percentages like 75%. Every answer has been checked with Python. For hands-on coding practice, the lesson notebook ends with two coding challenges: fill in one missing line and an automatic check tells you whether it's right.

Exercise 1By hand

A model scores 0.90 accuracy on test data. Shuffling feature A gives 0.82, shuffling B gives 0.89 and shuffling C gives 0.90. Give the three permutation importances. Is C useless?

Check your answer — for several numbers, separate them with commas:

Show solution
A: 0.08, B: 0.01, C: 0. C adds no unique information to this model, but it may be correlated with A or B, so it isn't necessarily useless on its own.
Exercise 2By hand

For $f = 3x_1 + 2x_2 + 6x_1x_2$ explained at $(1, 1)$ against the baseline $(0, 0)$, compute both Shapley values.

Check your answers:

Show solution
$x_1$: own effect 3 plus half the interaction, 3, so 6. $x_2$: 2 plus 3, so 5. Check: $6 + 5 = 11 = f(1, 1) - f(0, 0)$.
Exercise 3By hand

With 3 features, what weight does the Shapley formula give to a coalition $S$ of size 1 when computing $\phi_j$? (Use $|S|!(p-|S|-1)!/p!$.)

Check your answer:

Show solution
$1! \times 1!/3! = 1/6 \approx 0.1667$. (Size 0 and size 2 coalitions each get $2/6 = 1/3$.)
Exercise 4By hand

A model's baseline prediction is 50 lakh. For one house the SHAP values are size +12, distance −8 and age −3. What does the model predict?

Check your answer:

Show solution
$50 + 12 - 8 - 3 = 51$ lakh.
Exercise 5Code

In the lesson's Shapley code, explain patient 0 instead of patient 200. Check that the contributions still add up exactly to prediction minus baseline.

Show solution
Change x = X4[200] to x = X4[0]. The printed baseline plus the sum of contributions equals the model's prediction to the second decimal, as the efficiency property guarantees.
Exercise 6Intermediate

A linear model is $f = 10 + 2x_1 - 3x_2$, with feature means $\bar{x}_1 = 4$, $\bar{x}_2 = 1$. For the row $(6, 2)$, compute both SHAP values and check that baseline + contributions = prediction.

Check your answers — for several numbers, separate them with commas:

Show solution
$\phi_1 = 2(6 - 4) = 4$; $\phi_2 = -3(2 - 1) = -3$. Baseline $f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) = 10 + 8 - 3 = 15$. $15 + 4 - 3 = 16$, and $f(6, 2) = 10 + 12 - 6 = 16$ ✓.
Exercise 7Intermediate

A model scores $R^2 = 0.80$. Retrained without feature A it scores 0.79; without feature B, 0.60. What are the drop-column importances?

Check your answer — for several numbers, separate them with commas:

Show solution
A: $0.01$ (largely replaceable). B: $0.20$ (unique, important information).

Part 6 · Intermediate topics · ~55 min

Lesson 25: Imbalanced Data & Anomaly Detection

Rare events: the right metrics, thresholds vs class weights vs resampling, SMOTE, and finding anomalies without labels with z-scores, Isolation Forest and LOF.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Explain why accuracy fails on rare classes and choose recall, precision, average precision or cost instead
  • Compare threshold moving, class weights, oversampling and SMOTE, and apply them without leakage
  • Detect anomalies without labels using z-scores, the IQR rule, Isolation Forest and Local Outlier Factor
  • Evaluate a detector with precision in the top k and plan how it runs in practice
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 8: Logistic Regression — Logistic regression outputs a probability $p = \sigma(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b)$, is trained with log loss, and classifies with a threshold (often 0.5), giving a straight decision boundary.
  • Lesson 9: Evaluating Models — Accuracy can mislead. Precision $= TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $= TP/(TP+FN)$, and F1 balances them. Moving the threshold trades one for the other; ROC-AUC summarises all thresholds.
  • Lesson 16: Clustering — Clustering groups unlabelled data. k-means alternates assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving each centroid to the mean of its points.

Where this fits: Applies the metrics of Lesson 9 and the calibration and imbalance ideas of Lesson 8 to rare events, and uses the density ideas of clustering (Lesson 16) to find anomalies without labels.

1.When the thing you care about is rare

Fraud is perhaps 1 transaction in 1,000. A machine failure, one reading in 10,000. A rare disease, one patient in 500. In these problems the class you care about is a tiny minority, and almost everything you learned about "accuracy" breaks: a model that never predicts the rare class is 99.9% accurate and completely useless.

This lesson covers the two situations you'll meet. When you have labels for some rare cases, it's an imbalanced classification problem: choose the right metrics, then fix the imbalance with thresholds, class weights or resampling. When you have few or no labels, it's anomaly detection: find points that don't look like the rest, with methods such as z-scores, Isolation Forest and Local Outlier Factor.

The core idea

With rare classes, judge models with precision, recall and average precision, never accuracy. Most of the "fixes" for imbalance (reweighting, oversampling, SMOTE) mainly move the decision threshold; often the simplest and best fix is a calibrated model plus a threshold chosen from the cost of each mistake.

2.Why accuracy fails, in numbers

A dataset with 1% positives, split in half, with a logistic regression and a "model" that always says normal:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, recall_score, precision_score, average_precision_score

# 1% positives, like fraud
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20000, n_features=10, n_informative=5, weights=[0.99],
                           class_sep=1.0, flip_y=0, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=0, stratify=y)
print("positives in the test set:", int(y_te.sum()), "of", len(y_te))
for name, m in [("always 'normal'", DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")), ("logistic regression", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]:
    m.fit(X_tr, y_tr); pr = m.predict(X_te)
    print(f"{name:20}: accuracy {accuracy_score(y_te, pr):.3f}   recall {recall_score(y_te, pr):.3f}")

Output:

positives in the test set: 100 of 10000
always 'normal'     : accuracy 0.990   recall 0.000
logistic regression : accuracy 0.995   recall 0.520

The do-nothing model is 99.0% accurate and catches none of the 100 positives. Logistic regression is 99.5% accurate, which sounds only slightly better, yet it catches 52% of them. Accuracy hides almost everything that matters here. Use (Lesson 9):

  • Recall: the share of positives you catch.
  • Precision: the share of your alerts that are real.
  • Average precision (PR-AUC): the threshold-free summary of the precision–recall trade-off, compared with its baseline, the positive rate (0.01 here).
  • Or a cost or business metric, such as rupees saved, or alerts per analyst per day.

3.Thresholds, class weights and resampling

Three families of fix, all aiming to make the model flag more of the rare class:

  • Move the threshold: keep the model, flag anything with probability above, say, 0.1 instead of 0.5 (Lesson 9's "Going deeper" shows how to choose it from costs).
  • Class weights: make each positive count more in the training loss (class_weight="balanced", Lesson 8's "Going deeper").
  • Resampling: train on a rebalanced copy of the training data, by oversampling positives (repeating them) or undersampling negatives (dropping some).
def report(name, scores, threshold=0.5):
    flag = scores >= threshold
    print(f"{name:32}: recall {recall_score(y_te, flag):.3f}  precision {precision_score(y_te, flag, zero_division=0):.3f}  "
          f"average precision {average_precision_score(y_te, scores):.3f}")

plain = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
weighted = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced").fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pos = np.flatnonzero(y_tr == 1)
extra = rng.choice(pos, size=(y_tr == 0).sum() - len(pos), replace=True)        # random oversampling
Xo, yo = np.vstack([X_tr, X_tr[extra]]), np.r_[y_tr, y_tr[extra]]
over = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(Xo, yo).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]

report("plain, threshold 0.5", plain)
report("plain, threshold 0.1", plain, 0.1)
report("class_weight='balanced'", weighted)
report("random oversampling", over)

Output:

plain, threshold 0.5            : recall 0.520  precision 0.912  average precision 0.746
plain, threshold 0.1            : recall 0.760  precision 0.490  average precision 0.746
class_weight='balanced'         : recall 0.900  precision 0.146  average precision 0.471
random oversampling             : recall 0.900  precision 0.146  average precision 0.470

Read the four rows carefully. Lowering the threshold to 0.1 raises recall from 0.52 to 0.76 at a precision of 0.49, with the same average precision (0.746), because the model's ranking hasn't changed. Class weights and oversampling reach recall 0.90 but with precision 0.146 (most alerts false), and here they even lower average precision to about 0.47: training on a distorted class balance made the ranking worse, not just the threshold different. That isn't always so, but it's common enough that the order to try things in is: first a good model and the right threshold; then weights or resampling if they improve average precision on validation data.

Worked example — what "balanced" weights mean

The training half has 9,900 negatives and 100 positives ($n = 10{,}000$, $k = 2$ classes). Scikit-learn's balanced weight for class $c$ is $n/(k\,n_c)$:

Negatives: $10{,}000/(2 \times 9{,}900) = 0.505$. Positives: $10{,}000/(2 \times 100) = 50$.

So each positive counts $50/0.505 = 99$ times as much as a negative: exactly the ratio of the class sizes. In total, positives and negatives now carry equal weight ($100 \times 50 = 5{,}000 \approx 9{,}900 \times 0.505$). Random oversampling to equal counts copies each positive about 99 times, which for logistic regression has almost the same effect, as the identical results above show.

4.SMOTE: synthetic minority examples

Copying the same positives many times can make a model memorise them. SMOTE (synthetic minority oversampling technique) creates new positives instead: pick a positive, pick one of its $k$ nearest positive neighbours, and place a new point at a random position on the line between them.

# SMOTE from scratch: new minority points on the line between a point and one of its minority neighbours
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

def smote(Xmin, n_new, k=5, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k + 1).fit(Xmin)
    _, nbrs = nn.kneighbors(Xmin)
    i = rng.integers(0, len(Xmin), n_new)
    j = nbrs[i, rng.integers(1, k + 1, n_new)]          # skip column 0 (the point itself)
    gap = rng.random((n_new, 1))
    return Xmin[i] + gap * (Xmin[j] - Xmin[i])

Xmin = X_tr[y_tr == 1]
new = smote(Xmin, (y_tr == 0).sum() - len(Xmin))
Xs, ys = np.vstack([X_tr, new]), np.r_[y_tr, np.ones(len(new), int)]
report("SMOTE", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(Xs, ys).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1])
print("synthetic minority points created:", len(new))

Output:

SMOTE                           : recall 0.900  precision 0.169  average precision 0.515
synthetic minority points created: 9800

SMOTE created 9,800 synthetic positives and gives the same recall as oversampling (0.900) with slightly better precision (0.169) and average precision (0.515), still well below the plain model with a tuned threshold. SMOTE can help flexible models (trees, boosting, kNN) more than linear ones, and it can also hurt, by inventing positives in regions that really belong to negatives. Two firm rules: resample only the training folds (never the validation or test data, and never before splitting), and judge it by average precision or cost on untouched data.

5.Anomaly detection without labels

Often you have almost no labelled anomalies, or new kinds keep appearing. Then you model what's normal and flag what isn't. Common methods, from simplest:

  • z-scores: flag values more than about 3 standard deviations from the mean. Simple, but assumes one bell-shaped cluster, and outliers inflate the very standard deviation used to find them (Lesson 4).
  • IQR rule: flag values beyond 1.5 × the interquartile range outside the middle half. Robust to outliers, but one feature at a time.
  • Isolation Forest: build random trees that split on random features at random values. Anomalies are few and different, so they get isolated in very few splits; the score is the average path length.
  • Local Outlier Factor (LOF): compare each point's local density with its neighbours' density. A point in a sparse spot next to a dense cluster stands out, even if another cluster elsewhere is sparse.
  • Reconstruction error: fit PCA (Lesson 17's "Going deeper") or an autoencoder on normal data, and flag points it can't reconstruct well.

Below, 980 normal points form two clusters and 20 anomalies are scattered around them. Each method scores every point, and we check how many of its top 20 are real anomalies:

from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score as roc_auc

# Unsupervised anomaly detection: 980 normal points in two clusters, 20 anomalies scattered around them
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
normal = np.vstack([rng.normal([0, 0], 0.6, (490, 2)), rng.normal([4, 4], 0.6, (490, 2))])
anomalies = rng.uniform(-3, 7, (20, 2))
Xa = np.vstack([normal, anomalies]); truth = np.r_[np.zeros(980), np.ones(20)]

def precision_at_20(score):          # higher score = more anomalous
    return truth[np.argsort(score)[::-1][:20]].mean()

z = np.abs((Xa - Xa.mean(0)) / Xa.std(0)).max(axis=1)        # largest per-feature z-score
iso = -IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(Xa).score_samples(Xa)
lof = -LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20).fit(Xa).negative_outlier_factor_
for name, s in [("z-score", z), ("Isolation Forest", iso), ("Local Outlier Factor", lof)]:
    print(f"{name:21}: share of true anomalies among the top 20 {precision_at_20(s):.2f}   ROC-AUC {roc_auc(truth, s):.3f}")

Output:

z-score              : share of true anomalies among the top 20 0.50   ROC-AUC 0.730
Isolation Forest     : share of true anomalies among the top 20 0.65   ROC-AUC 0.984
Local Outlier Factor : share of true anomalies among the top 20 0.80   ROC-AUC 0.991

The z-score catches only half (0.50 of its top 20; ROC-AUC 0.730): with two clusters, "far from the overall mean" isn't the same as "unusual", so points between the clusters look normal and the clusters' own edges look odd. Isolation Forest does much better (0.65, AUC 0.984), and LOF best (0.80, AUC 0.991), because it judges each point against its own neighbourhood. In practice anomaly scores are usually turned into a ranked list for people to review, so "precision in the top $k$" is often the metric that matters.

6.Try it: flag the most isolated points

Each point's score is its distance to its 5th nearest neighbour, a simple version of the idea behind LOF. Red points are the true anomalies. Increase the number of points flagged and watch recall rise while precision falls.

7.Evaluating and running a detector

  • Get some labels. Even a few hundred reviewed cases let you measure precision at the top of the list and compare methods.
  • Split by time. Fraud and failures change; validate on later data (Lesson 5's "Going deeper").
  • Combine approaches. A supervised model catches known patterns; an unsupervised detector watches for new ones. Analysts' decisions become labels for the next model.
  • Set the alert budget. If a team can review 200 cases a day, flag the 200 highest scores; the threshold follows from capacity.
  • Watch for feedback. You only learn the truth about cases you flagged and checked, so unflagged anomalies stay invisible. Randomly review a small sample of unflagged cases to estimate what you're missing.

8.In Python: a workflow for rare events

Train a calibrated model, choose the threshold on validation data to hit a target precision, and confirm on the test set.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve, precision_score, recall_score, average_precision_score

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=30000, n_features=10, n_informative=5, weights=[0.99],
                           class_sep=1.0, flip_y=0, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_rest, y_tr, y_rest = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.4, random_state=0, stratify=y)
X_val, X_te, y_val, y_te = train_test_split(X_rest, y_rest, test_size=0.5, random_state=0, stratify=y_rest)

model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
p_val, p_te = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1], model.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
print("average precision, validation:", round(average_precision_score(y_val, p_val), 3))

prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y_val, p_val)
t = thr[np.argmax(prec[:-1] >= 0.8)]                  # lowest threshold with precision of at least 0.8
flag = p_te >= t
print(f"threshold {t:.3f}: test precision {precision_score(y_te, flag):.3f}, recall {recall_score(y_te, flag):.3f}")

Output:

average precision, validation: 0.691
threshold 0.458: test precision 0.682, recall 0.500

Gradient boosting reaches a validation average precision of 0.691. The threshold chosen to give 80% precision on validation data (0.458) gives only 68.2% precision on the test set, with recall 0.500. That gap is the honest lesson: the validation set holds only about 60 positives, so a threshold tuned on it is noisy. With rare events, use as much validation data as you can (or cross-validated predictions), report the test result with a confidence interval (Lesson 9's "Going deeper"), and re-check the threshold once the model is live.

9.Running example: Chennai Homes

Which Chennai homes look least like the others? An Isolation Forest on size, price, distance and age ranks every house by how easily it can be isolated. The three Outskirts homes come out on top (scores 0.578, 0.558 and 0.546): they are the only houses more than 20 km from the centre. With 12 houses the scores are rough, but a ranked list like this is where an analyst starts checking for data errors or genuinely unusual properties.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
cols = ["size_m2", "price_lakh", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]
iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=500, random_state=0).fit(df[cols])
df["oddness"] = -iso.score_samples(df[cols])            # higher = more unusual
print(df.sort_values("oddness", ascending=False)[["id", "area", "description", "oddness"]].head(3).round(3).to_string(index=False))

Output:

 id      area                 description  oddness
 10 Outskirts  old house needs renovation    0.578
  9 Outskirts    quiet flat far from city    0.558
  8 Outskirts new large villa with garden    0.546
Where this is used
  • Fraud and money-laundering detection
  • Predictive maintenance and quality control (rare failures and defects)
  • Rare-disease screening, intrusion detection and monitoring data pipelines for bad records

Choose it when: Whenever the class you care about is rare, or when you need to find unusual cases nobody has labelled.

Think twice when: the classes are roughly balanced: then ordinary methods and metrics work.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythYou must balance the classes before training.

RealityMany models train fine on imbalanced data; what must change is the metric and the threshold. Rebalancing is optional and can hurt calibration and ranking.

MythA high ROC-AUC means the alerts will be useful.

RealityWith very rare positives, even a small false-positive rate floods analysts with false alarms. Check precision and average precision (Lesson 9's "Going deeper").

MythAnomalies are just points far from the average.

RealityWith several clusters, unusual points can sit near the overall average. Judge points against their local neighbourhood.

Responsible AI · Who pays for a false alarm?

In fraud and safety systems, false alarms are not free: a blocked card, a frozen account or an unnecessary investigation lands on a real person, and often unevenly across groups. Measure false-positive rates per group (Lesson 21), give people a fast way to contest a flag, and budget alerts so humans can review them properly rather than rubber-stamping.

10.Questions beginners often ask

How rare is "imbalanced"?

There's no hard line, but below about 10% positives accuracy starts to mislead, and below 1% the choice of metric and threshold dominates everything else.

Should I always use SMOTE?

No. It sometimes helps flexible models, but often a calibrated model with a tuned threshold does as well or better, and class-imbalance corrections can distort risk estimates. Compare on average precision or cost with untouched validation data.

Isolation Forest or LOF?

Isolation Forest is fast, scales to large data and works well in many dimensions. LOF judges each point against its local neighbourhood, so it's better when normal data has clusters of different densities, but it's slower on large datasets.

What's the difference between outlier detection and novelty detection?

Outlier detection finds unusual points inside a dataset that may contain them. Novelty detection trains on clean, normal data and flags new points that don't fit, as a one-class model would.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Reporting accuracy on a dataset with 1% positives.
  • Oversampling or applying SMOTE before splitting, so copies leak into the test set.
  • Using a class-weighted model's probabilities as if they were real risks.
  • Tuning the threshold on the test set.
  • Assuming unflagged cases are normal, without ever checking a sample of them.
Interview corner

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Why is accuracy a bad metric for fraud detection?

The trap: Saying it's "too high".

With 0.1% fraud, predicting "not fraud" for everything is 99.9% accurate and catches nothing. Accuracy is dominated by the majority class. Use recall, precision, average precision (PR-AUC) against its baseline, or a cost-based metric, at the threshold you will actually use.

Class weights, oversampling or threshold moving: how do you choose for an imbalanced problem?

The trap: Always reaching for SMOTE.

Start with a well-calibrated model and pick the threshold from costs or an alert budget: this keeps probabilities meaningful. Try class weights or resampling when they improve average precision or cost on validation data, which happens more for flexible models. Always resample inside training folds only, and recalibrate if you need real probabilities afterwards.

How does Isolation Forest work, and why does it suit anomaly detection?

The trap: Describing it as a random forest classifier.

It builds many random trees: each split picks a random feature and a random threshold between its min and max. Anomalies, being few and different, are separated from the rest in fewer splits, so their average path length is short; the score normalises that length. It needs no labels or distance computations, scales linearly, and handles many features.

You deploy an anomaly detector and only review flagged cases. What problem does this create?

The trap: Assuming recall can be measured from reviewed cases.

You never learn about anomalies the system missed, so recall is invisible and any retraining on reviewed cases only reinforces what the detector already finds (a feedback loop). Review a random sample of unflagged cases, track known incidents from other sources, and keep some exploration in what you flag.

All 5 hidden questions for this lesson →

11.Key takeaways

  • With rare classes, accuracy is misleading: use recall, precision, average precision (against its baseline) or cost.
  • Try a good model with a tuned threshold first; class weights and resampling mostly move the threshold, and can hurt the ranking.
  • SMOTE creates synthetic positives between neighbours; resample only the training folds.
  • Without labels, model normal behaviour: z-scores and IQR for simple cases, Isolation Forest and LOF for multi-dimensional, multi-cluster data.
  • Evaluate detectors with precision in the top k on some reviewed cases, split by time, and sample unflagged cases to see what you miss.

12.Check your understanding

1. 0.5% of transactions are fraud. A model that never flags fraud has accuracy…

It's right on every non-fraud case: 99.5%. That's why accuracy is the wrong metric here.

2. Lowering the threshold of a fixed model changes…

Average precision summarises all thresholds, so it depends only on the ranking of the scores.

3. When should SMOTE or oversampling be applied?

Resampling before splitting puts copies (or near-copies) of the same positives on both sides, which leaks.

4. Why does Isolation Forest give anomalies high scores?

Points that are few and different are separated from the rest quickly, so their average path length is short.

5. With two separate clusters of normal data, which detector is most likely to miss anomalies between the clusters?

Points between the clusters are close to the overall mean, so their z-scores look normal.

13.Going deeper: correcting probabilities and how isolation works

In plain wordsHow to turn a class-weighted model's inflated probabilities back into real risks with one formula, and why Isolation Forest works: a far-away point is cut off by random splits in about 2 steps, while a typical point needs about 15.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

Two details that matter in real rare-event systems: how to turn a class-weighted (or resampled) model's distorted probabilities back into real risks with one formula, and why random splits isolate anomalies so quickly, measured directly.

You'll need: this lesson, calibration from Lesson 8's "Going deeper", and decision trees from Lesson 13.

Undoing class weights: the prior correction

Balanced class weights (or oversampling to 50/50) make the model behave as if positives were as common as negatives, so its probabilities are far too high. If the real positive rate is $\pi$, the odds can be corrected with Bayes' theorem by multiplying by the real prior odds:

$$\text{odds}_{\text{real}} = \frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}, \qquad p_{\text{real}} = \frac{\text{odds}_{\text{real}}}{1 + \text{odds}_{\text{real}}}$$

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=40000, n_features=10, n_informative=5, weights=[0.98], flip_y=0, random_state=1)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=0, stratify=y)
pi = y_tr.mean()                                                    # true positive rate in training data
p_bal = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced").fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]

# Undo the reweighting: the model behaves as if positives were as common as negatives
odds = p_bal / (1 - p_bal) * (pi / (1 - pi))
p_fixed = odds / (1 + odds)
p_plain = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
for name, p in [("balanced weights", p_bal), ("balanced, corrected", p_fixed), ("plain model", p_plain)]:
    print(f"{name:20}: average predicted risk {p.mean():.3f} (true rate {y_te.mean():.3f})   Brier score {brier_score_loss(y_te, p):.4f}")

Output:

balanced weights    : average predicted risk 0.372 (true rate 0.020)   Brier score 0.1702
balanced, corrected : average predicted risk 0.017 (true rate 0.020)   Brier score 0.0178
plain model         : average predicted risk 0.020 (true rate 0.020)   Brier score 0.0169

The balanced model predicts an average risk of 0.372 when the true rate is 0.020, with a terrible Brier score of 0.1702. After the correction its average risk is 0.017 and its Brier score 0.0178, almost matching a model trained without weights (0.0169). So if you use weights or resampling to help a model learn the rare class, apply this correction (or recalibrate on held-out data with CalibratedClassifierCV) before using the outputs as probabilities: for pricing, ranking by expected loss, or telling a patient their risk.

Why random splits isolate anomalies

Isolation Forest grows each tree by choosing a random feature and a random split value between that feature's minimum and maximum, until every point sits alone. A point far from the crowd is very likely to be cut off by one of the first few random splits; a point deep inside a cluster needs many. Here we measure the average number of splits for one far-away point and for typical points among 500:


# Isolation Forest's intuition: average number of random splits needed to isolate a point
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pts = np.vstack([rng.normal(0, 1, (500, 2)), [[6, 6]]])            # 500 normal points and one far away
def splits_to_isolate(i, trials=200):
    total = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        idx = np.arange(len(pts)); depth = 0
        while len(idx) > 1:
            f = rng.integers(2); lo, hi = pts[idx, f].min(), pts[idx, f].max()
            t = rng.uniform(lo, hi)
            idx = idx[pts[idx, f] < t] if pts[i, f] < t else idx[pts[idx, f] >= t]
            depth += 1
        total += depth
    return total / trials
print("average splits to isolate the far point:   ", round(splits_to_isolate(500), 1))
print("average splits to isolate a typical point: ", round(np.mean([splits_to_isolate(i, 40) for i in range(10)]), 1))

Output:

average splits to isolate the far point:    2.3
average splits to isolate a typical point:  14.6

The far point is isolated in 2.3 splits on average, typical points in 14.6. Isolation Forest turns that path length into a score between 0 and 1, normalised by the average path length expected for $n$ points (about $2\ln n$). Because it never computes distances, it scales linearly with the data and copes with many features; its main settings are the number of trees and the subsample size per tree (256 by default, which is enough because anomalies stand out even in small samples).

Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

You trained on a 50/50 resampled dataset, but the real positive rate is 1%. How do you get calibrated probabilities?

The trap: Using the raw scores as risks.

Apply the prior correction: multiply the model's odds by $\pi/(1-\pi)$ divided by the training odds (1 for 50/50), then convert back to a probability. Equivalently, add $\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi} - \log\frac{\pi_{train}}{1-\pi_{train}}$ to the logit. Or recalibrate on a held-out set with the real class balance (Platt scaling or isotonic regression). Verify with a reliability table and the Brier score.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. A model trained with balanced weights gives $p = 0.5$. The real positive rate is 2%. What is the corrected probability?

Odds $1 \times 0.02/0.98 = 0.0204$, so $p \approx 0.020$.

2. Why do class weights inflate predicted probabilities?

Weighting positives up is equivalent to changing the prior class balance.

3. In Isolation Forest, a short average path length means…

Few, different points get separated after few random splits.

4. Why can Isolation Forest use small subsamples (such as 256 points) per tree?

Subsampling keeps it fast and often improves detection.

5. After oversampling to 50/50, the simplest fix for probabilities is…

Either restores realistic risk estimates.

1,000 transactions include 10 frauds. A model flags 25, of which 8 are fraud. Compute accuracy, recall and precision.

Check your answers:

Exercise 2By hand

A training set has 19,600 negatives and 400 positives. What balanced class weights does scikit-learn give each class, using $n/(k\,n_c)$?

$n = 20{,}000$, $k = 2$. Negatives: $20{,}000/39{,}200 \approx 0.510$. Positives: $20{,}000/800 = 25$.

SMOTE picks a positive at $(2, 4)$ and its neighbour $(6, 2)$, with random gap 0.25. Where is the new point?

In the anomaly code, change LocalOutlierFactor's n_neighbors to 5 and to 50. How does its precision in the top 20 change?

Show solution
Very small neighbourhoods make LOF noisy (a few close anomalies can look like a dense cluster); very large ones blur local structure towards a global view. Try both and compare with 20; the best value depends on cluster sizes and is worth tuning on labelled examples.

A balanced-weight model outputs $p = 0.8$. The true positive rate is 5%. Compute the corrected probability.

Check your answer:

Show solution
Model odds $= 0.8/0.2 = 4$. Prior odds $= 0.05/0.95 = 0.05263$. Corrected odds $= 0.2105$, so $p = 0.2105/1.2105 \approx 0.174$.
