Part 6 · Intermediate topics · ~55 min

Lesson 26: Time Series Forecasting

Trend and seasonality, baselines that are hard to beat, lag features, backtesting, MASE, and forecasting several steps ahead.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Describe a series by its trend, seasonality and noise, and compute naive, seasonal naive and moving-average baselines
  • Turn a series into a supervised problem with past-only lag, rolling and calendar features
  • Validate forecasts with time-ordered splits and backtesting, and report MAE and MASE
  • Compare recursive and direct multi-step forecasting and report accuracy by horizon
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 5: Data, Features & Generalization — Always judge a model on data it hasn't seen: split into train / validation / test, or use k-fold cross-validation. Overfitting = low training error but high test error. Never let test data leak into training.
  • Lesson 6: Linear Regression — Linear regression predicts $\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b$ and chooses the weights that minimise the mean squared error (least squares). $R^2$ measures the share of variance explained.
  • Lesson 13: Decision Trees — A decision tree asks a sequence of 'feature ≤ threshold?' questions chosen to reduce impurity (Gini or entropy). Deep trees overfit and are unstable.

Where this fits: Applies regression (Lesson 6) and gradient boosting (Lesson 13) to ordered data, and replaces the shuffled cross-validation of Lesson 5 with time-ordered backtesting.

1.Why time series are different

How many umbrellas will the shop sell next week? How much electricity will the city need tomorrow evening? How many patients will arrive at A&E on Saturday night? These are forecasting problems: the data is a sequence of measurements over time, and we predict future values from past ones.

Time changes the rules you've learned. Rows aren't independent (today looks like yesterday), the future can differ from the past (trends, holidays, a pandemic), and a random train/test split is badly wrong because it lets the model train on the future (Lesson 5's "Going deeper" showed a shuffled split reporting $R^2 = 0.96$ for a model that couldn't forecast at all). This lesson covers the toolkit: components, baselines, lag features, time-based validation, error metrics for forecasts, and forecasting several days ahead.

The core idea

Turn forecasting into ordinary supervised learning by building features only from the past (lags, rolling averages, calendar fields), always validate by training on the past and testing on the future, and always compare with simple baselines such as "same day last week", which are surprisingly hard to beat.

2.Trend, seasonality and noise

Most series combine three parts:

  • Trend: the long-term direction (a growing shop).
  • Seasonality: patterns that repeat with a fixed period: day of week, month of year, hour of day.
  • Noise: what's left, the unpredictable part.

They can combine additively ($y = \text{trend} + \text{season} + \text{noise}$) or multiplicatively ($y = \text{trend} \times \text{season} \times \text{noise}$), where the seasonal swings grow as the level grows, which is typical of sales. Here is three years of simulated daily sales for a growing shop:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Three years of simulated daily sales for a shop: trend + weekly pattern + yearly season + noise
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
days = pd.date_range("2023-01-01", periods=3 * 365, freq="D")
t = np.arange(len(days))
weekly = np.array([0.9, 0.95, 1.0, 1.0, 1.1, 1.35, 1.25])[days.dayofweek]       # Mon … Sun
yearly = 1 + 0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (days.dayofyear - 80) / 365)
sales = (200 + 0.15 * t) * weekly * yearly * rng.lognormal(0, 0.08, len(t))
s = pd.Series(sales.round(1), index=days, name="sales")
print(s.head(7).to_string())
print("average sales by weekday (Mon … Sun):", s.groupby(s.index.dayofweek).mean().round(0).tolist())
print("average sales by year:", s.groupby(s.index.year).mean().round(0).tolist())

Output:

2023-01-01    203.1
2023-01-02    143.5
2023-01-03    161.4
2023-01-04    163.1
2023-01-05    155.2
2023-01-06    183.8
2023-01-07    243.8
Freq: D
average sales by weekday (Mon … Sun): [254.0, 267.0, 282.0, 281.0, 308.0, 383.0, 349.0]
average sales by year: [245.0, 304.0, 361.0]

The weekday averages show a strong weekly pattern (Saturday sells about 383, against about 254 on Monday), and the yearly averages a rising trend (245, then 304, then 361). A model must capture both. Taking logs turns a multiplicative series into an additive one, which suits linear models (Lesson 6's "Going deeper").

3.Baselines first

Before any model, compute simple forecasts. They set the bar and often turn out to be competitive:

  • Naive: tomorrow equals today.
  • Seasonal naive: tomorrow equals the same day last week (or last year).
  • Moving average: tomorrow equals the average of the last $k$ days.
# Forecast the last 8 weeks with simple baselines, one day ahead each day
test = s[-56:]
naive = s.shift(1)[-56:]                         # tomorrow = today
seasonal = s.shift(7)[-56:]                      # tomorrow = same weekday last week
moving = s.shift(1).rolling(28).mean()[-56:]     # tomorrow = average of the last 4 weeks
mae = lambda f: np.mean(np.abs(test - f))
for name, f in [("naive (yesterday)", naive), ("seasonal naive (last week)", seasonal), ("28-day average", moving)]:
    print(f"{name:27}: MAE {mae(f):6.1f}")

Output:

naive (yesterday)          : MAE   50.0
seasonal naive (last week) : MAE   32.6
28-day average             : MAE   45.3

Each forecast is made one day ahead, using only data up to the previous day, for the last 8 weeks. The seasonal naive forecast wins clearly (MAE 32.6), because it captures the weekly pattern for free. "Yesterday" ignores the weekly cycle (50.0), and the 28-day average smooths it away (45.3). Any model you build must beat 32.6 to be worth its complexity.

4.Try it: four baselines

Switch between the four simple forecasts and compare their errors over the last 4 weeks. Notice how the weekly peaks are missed by the methods that ignore the weekday.

5.Turning a series into features

To use the models you already know, build one row per day with features that only look backwards:

  • Lags: the value 1, 7, 14 and 28 days earlier.
  • Rolling statistics: the mean (or max, or standard deviation) of the previous 7 or 28 days. Shift before rolling, so the window excludes the day being predicted.
  • Calendar: day of week (one-hot), month, holidays, and smooth yearly position as $\sin$ and $\cos$ of the day of year, so that 31 December and 1 January are close.
  • Known future inputs: things known in advance, such as planned promotions or the weather forecast.
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

# Features that only use the past: lags, rolling means and calendar fields
df = pd.DataFrame({"y": s})
for lag in [1, 7, 14, 28]:
    df[f"lag_{lag}"] = s.shift(lag)
df["roll_7"] = s.shift(1).rolling(7).mean()
df["roll_28"] = s.shift(1).rolling(28).mean()
df["dow"] = df.index.dayofweek
df["doy_sin"], df["doy_cos"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df.index.dayofyear / 365), np.cos(2 * np.pi * df.index.dayofyear / 365)
df = df.dropna()
Xf = pd.get_dummies(df.drop(columns="y"), columns=["dow"], dtype=float)
start = s.index[-56]                                                    # the last 56 days are the test period
train, test_idx = Xf.index < start, Xf.index >= start
yt = df.y[train].to_numpy()
scale = np.mean(np.abs(yt[7:] - yt[:-7]))                               # seasonal-naive MAE on training data, for MASE
for name, m in [("ridge on lag features", Ridge(1.0)), ("gradient boosting", HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0))]:
    pred = m.fit(Xf[train], df.y[train]).predict(Xf[test_idx])
    err = np.mean(np.abs(df.y[test_idx] - pred))
    print(f"{name:22}: MAE {err:6.1f}   MASE {err / scale:.2f}")

Output:

ridge on lag features : MAE   26.2   MASE 0.98
gradient boosting     : MAE   28.9   MASE 1.08
Worked example — MASE, the scaled error

MAE is in the data's units, so "MAE 26" means nothing on its own. The mean absolute scaled error divides by the error of the seasonal naive forecast on the training data:

$$\text{MASE} = \frac{\text{MAE of the model}}{\text{MAE of seasonal naive on training data}}$$

Here the seasonal naive MAE on the training data is about 26.75. Ridge's test MAE is 26.2, so MASE $= 26.2/26.75 \approx 0.98$: just under 1, so a little better than the baseline. Gradient boosting's MAE of 28.9 gives MASE $1.08$: worse than the baseline. A MASE below 1 means the model earns its keep; it works for any series and avoids MAPE's problems with values near zero.

Ridge on lag features reaches an MAE of 26.2 on the 8-week test period, beating the seasonal naive's 32.6 on the same days. Gradient boosting does slightly worse (28.9): tree models can't extrapolate the rising trend beyond the values seen in training (Lesson 13's "Going deeper"), a common surprise with growing series. Fixes include modelling the change from last week instead of the level, or detrending first.

6.Validating forecasts: backtesting

One test period can be lucky. Backtesting (rolling-origin evaluation) repeats "train on everything up to a date, forecast the next block" for several dates in a row. Scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit does this:

from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

# Backtesting: repeat "train on the past, test on the next 8 weeks" several times
maes = []
for tr, te in TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, test_size=56).split(Xf):
    pred = Ridge(1.0).fit(Xf.iloc[tr], df.y.iloc[tr]).predict(Xf.iloc[te])
    maes.append(np.mean(np.abs(df.y.iloc[te] - pred)))
print("MAE in each backtest window:", np.round(maes, 1))
print("average:", round(np.mean(maes), 1))

Output:

MAE in each backtest window: [21.9 28.3 28.6 19.8 26.2]
average: 25.0

Across five consecutive 8-week windows, the error ranges from 19.8 to 28.6: real variation from period to period that a single test window would hide. Report the average (25.0) and the spread. Two more rules: leave a gap between training and test if your features need recent data that won't be available in time, and re-run the backtest whenever you change a feature.

7.Forecasting several steps ahead

Businesses usually need more than tomorrow: a 14-day plan, a 12-month budget. Two strategies:

  • Recursive: predict tomorrow, feed that prediction back in as a lag, predict the next day, and so on. One model, but errors can compound.
  • Direct: train a separate model for each horizon ("7 days ahead" uses only features known 7 days earlier). More models, but no compounding.
# Forecasting 14 days ahead recursively: each prediction becomes the next day's lag
history = s[s.index < start].copy()
model = Ridge(1.0).fit(Xf[train], df.y[train])
cols = Xf.columns
for step in range(14):
    day = history.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(days=1)
    row = {f"lag_{l}": history.iloc[-l] for l in [1, 7, 14, 28]}
    row.update(roll_7=history.iloc[-7:].mean(), roll_28=history.iloc[-28:].mean(),
               doy_sin=np.sin(2 * np.pi * day.dayofyear / 365), doy_cos=np.cos(2 * np.pi * day.dayofyear / 365))
    row.update({f"dow_{d}": float(day.dayofweek == d) for d in range(7)})
    history.loc[day] = model.predict(pd.DataFrame([row])[cols])[0]
err = np.abs(history[-14:] - s[history.index[-14:]])
print("absolute error, days 1–7 ahead: ", round(err[:7].mean(), 1))
print("absolute error, days 8–14 ahead:", round(err[7:].mean(), 1))

Output:

absolute error, days 1–7 ahead:  28.1
absolute error, days 8–14 ahead: 24.8

Forecasting recursively from the start of the test period, the error is 28.1 for days 1–7 and 24.8 for days 8–14. On this smooth, strongly seasonal series it doesn't grow, because the 7-day lag mostly comes from real data and the pattern repeats. With shocks or weaker seasonality, recursive errors usually grow with the horizon, so always report accuracy by horizon.

8.The wider toolkit

ApproachGood for
Seasonal naive, moving averagesBaselines; surprisingly strong on stable series
Exponential smoothing (Holt–Winters, ETS)Single series with trend and seasonality; fast and robust
ARIMA / SARIMASingle series with autocorrelation; classical statistics with prediction intervals
Regression or gradient boosting on lag featuresMany related series (thousands of products), extra inputs such as prices and promotions
Deep learning (sequence models, transformers)Very many long series; usually needs lots of data to beat the above

The statsmodels library provides exponential smoothing and ARIMA; this lesson uses only scikit-learn and pandas. In forecasting competitions, simple methods and gradient boosting on well-engineered features have been very hard to beat (the M-competitions).

9.In Python: a compact forecasting pipeline

A reusable function that builds past-only features, trains, and scores against the seasonal naive baseline on a time-ordered test period:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
idx = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=730, freq="D")
y = pd.Series((100 + 0.05 * np.arange(730)) * np.array([0.9, 1, 1, 1, 1.1, 1.3, 1.2])[idx.dayofweek]
              * rng.lognormal(0, 0.1, 730), index=idx)

def make_features(y):
    X = pd.DataFrame({f"lag_{l}": y.shift(l) for l in [1, 7, 14]}, index=y.index)
    X["roll_7"] = y.shift(1).rolling(7).mean()
    return X.join(pd.get_dummies(pd.Series(y.index.dayofweek, index=y.index), prefix="dow", dtype=float))

X = make_features(y).dropna(); target = y[X.index]
cut = X.index[-60]                                        # the last 60 days are the test period
model = Ridge(1.0).fit(X[X.index < cut], target[target.index < cut])
pred = model.predict(X[X.index >= cut])
actual, base = target[target.index >= cut], y.shift(7)[target.index[target.index >= cut]]
print("model MAE:", round(np.mean(np.abs(actual - pred)), 2), "  seasonal naive MAE:", round(np.mean(np.abs(actual - base)), 2))

Output:

model MAE: 14.52   seasonal naive MAE: 20.01

On this second simulated series, the lag-feature model beats the seasonal naive baseline on the 60-day test period. The same structure (past-only features, a time cut-off, a baseline) scales to thousands of series, with an extra "series id" feature or one model per group.

10.Running example: Chennai Homes

The houses file has no dates, so this example simulates a monthly Chennai price index for 3 years, starting from the average price of the 12 homes, with gentle growth and a small yearly cycle. Over the last 6 months, "same as last month" has an MAE of 1.08 lakh, while "same month last year" has 4.77: here the trend dominates the weak seasonality, so the seasonal naive forecast lags a whole year of growth behind. Which baseline is best depends on the series, which is why you compute several.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
months = pd.date_range("2023-01-01", periods=36, freq="MS")
level = df.price_lakh.mean() * (1 + 0.006 * np.arange(36)) * (1 + 0.03 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * months.month / 12))
index = pd.Series(level * rng.normal(1, 0.01, 36), index=months).round(1)   # a simulated monthly price index
test = index.index >= "2025-07-01"
naive, seasonal = index.shift(1)[test], index.shift(12)[test]
print("last 6 months:", index[test].tolist())
print("MAE, last month:", round((index[test] - naive).abs().mean(), 2), "  MAE, same month last year:", round((index[test] - seasonal).abs().mean(), 2))

Output:

last 6 months: [82.9, 83.1, 83.2, 84.6, 85.7, 87.5]
MAE, last month: 1.08   MAE, same month last year: 4.77
Where this is used
  • Demand and sales forecasting for stock and staffing
  • Electricity load, traffic and call-centre volume planning
  • Budgeting, capacity planning and early warnings when a metric drifts from its forecast

Choose it when: Whenever you need a number for a future date and you have a history of that number.

Think twice when: the future is driven by a one-off change the history never saw: then forecasts need scenarios and judgement, not just models.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythA complex model will always beat a simple forecast.

RealitySeasonal naive and exponential smoothing often win on stable series; in this lesson, gradient boosting lost to the baseline.

MythRandom cross-validation is fine if the model is regularised.

RealityShuffling lets the model see the future; validation must respect time order.

MythA low MAE means a good forecast.

RealityMAE depends on the scale of the series; compare with a baseline using MASE.

Responsible AI · Forecasts become decisions

A demand forecast sets staffing rotas, stock in poorer neighbourhoods and hospital beds. A forecast that's systematically low for some stores or regions quietly under-serves them, and a forecast trained on a period of under-supply learns that low demand is normal. Check errors by segment, not just overall, and communicate uncertainty so planners don't treat a point forecast as a promise.

11.Questions beginners often ask

How much history do I need?

At least two full seasonal cycles to learn a seasonal pattern (two years for a yearly pattern), and more if you want to backtest over several periods.

Should I use ARIMA or a machine-learning model?

For one series, exponential smoothing or ARIMA are strong and quick. For many related series, or when you have extra inputs such as prices and promotions, gradient boosting on lag features usually wins. Backtest both against the seasonal naive baseline.

How do I give prediction intervals?

Statistical models give them directly. For ML models, train quantile models (for example loss="quantile" in gradient boosting) or use the spread of backtest errors at each horizon.

Can I use future values of other features?

Only if they'll really be known at prediction time, such as the calendar or planned promotions. A feature like "actual temperature tomorrow" must be replaced by the forecast you'd have had.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Shuffling rows before splitting, so the model trains on the future.
  • Computing a rolling mean that includes the day being predicted.
  • Not comparing with a seasonal naive baseline.
  • Reporting one test window instead of a backtest across several.
  • Using a tree model on a trending level without detrending or modelling changes.
Interview corner

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

Why can't you use ordinary k-fold cross-validation for a forecasting model?

The trap: "You can, if you shuffle."

Shuffled folds train on days after the ones they test, and neighbouring days are similar, so the model effectively sees the future and the score is far too optimistic. Use time-ordered splits: train on the past, test on the next block, and repeat for several cut-off dates (backtesting).

What baseline would you compare a daily sales forecast with?

The trap: Comparing only with a constant mean.

The seasonal naive forecast (same day last week), plus the naive forecast and a moving average. Seasonal naive is often hard to beat. Report MASE, the model's MAE divided by the seasonal naive MAE, so below 1 means the model adds value.

Your gradient boosting forecast is fine on old data but always too low recently, as sales grow. Why?

The trap: Blaming not enough trees.

Trees predict averages of training targets, so they can't extrapolate a rising level beyond what they've seen. Model the change or ratio from a lag (for example y / y_{t−7}), detrend first, or combine with a linear model for the trend.

Recursive or direct multi-step forecasting: what's the trade-off?

The trap: Not knowing the difference.

Recursive uses one one-step model and feeds its predictions back as lags: simple, but errors can compound. Direct trains one model per horizon on features available that far ahead: no compounding, but more models and less use of recent data. Report accuracy by horizon either way.

All 5 hidden questions for this lesson →

12.Key takeaways

  • Time series have trend, seasonality and noise; rows are not independent.
  • Always compute baselines (naive, seasonal naive, moving average); seasonal naive is often hard to beat.
  • Build features only from the past: lags, shifted rolling statistics, calendar fields and known future inputs.
  • Validate with time-ordered splits and backtesting, never shuffled folds.
  • Report MAE and the scale-free MASE (below 1 beats seasonal naive), and accuracy by horizon.
  • Tree models can't extrapolate trends; model changes or detrend first.

13.Check your understanding

1. For daily sales with a strong weekly pattern, the "seasonal naive" forecast for next Saturday is…

It repeats the value from one season (one week) earlier.

2. Why is a shuffled k-fold split wrong for forecasting?

Neighbouring days are similar, so the model "remembers" nearby values it won't have in real use.

3. A model has MASE 1.3. What does that mean?

MASE divides by the seasonal naive error; above 1 means worse than the baseline.

4. Which feature leaks when predicting day $d$?

Shift the series before rolling, so the window ends at day $d - 1$.

5. Sales grow steadily every year. Why might a random forest on the raw sales level forecast poorly?

A tree's prediction is an average of training targets, so it can't follow a trend beyond them. Model the change, or detrend.

14.Going deeper: choosing lags and honest prediction intervals

In plain wordsHow to choose lags by looking at which past values the series correlates with (here 7, 14 and 21 days), and how to build a 90% prediction interval from held-out errors, which on a growing series actually covers only about 86%.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

Two practical skills: reading the autocorrelation of a series to decide which lags to use, and turning held-out forecast errors into prediction intervals, then checking whether they really cover what they claim.

You'll need: this lesson, correlation from Lesson 3, and quantiles from Lesson 2.

Autocorrelation: which lags matter?

The autocorrelation at lag $k$ is the correlation between the series and itself shifted by $k$ steps. Compute it on the changes (or after detrending), because a trend makes every lag look correlated. Peaks show the seasonal period, and so which lags to give a model:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
t = np.arange(730)
y = pd.Series((200 + 0.15 * t) * np.array([0.85, 0.9, 0.95, 1.0, 1.05, 1.25, 1.1])[t % 7] * rng.lognormal(0, 0.08, 730))
change = y.diff(1)                                   # remove the trend first
acf = {lag: round(float(change.autocorr(lag)), 2) for lag in [1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 21]}
print("autocorrelation of daily changes by lag:", acf)

Output:

autocorrelation of daily changes by lag: {1: -0.12, 2: -0.32, 3: -0.07, 6: 0.07, 7: 0.61, 14: 0.59, 21: 0.6}

On this daily series, the changes are strongly correlated at lags 7, 14 and 21 (about 0.6) and barely at lags 1 to 6: the series is dominated by its weekly cycle, so 7-day multiples are the lags to use. The negative value at lag 2 is a typical side effect of differencing. Plotting the autocorrelation for lags up to two seasons (the plot_acf function in statsmodels) is a standard first look at any new series.

Prediction intervals from held-out errors

A point forecast says nothing about how wrong it might be. A simple, model-agnostic way to get an interval: forecast a held-out calibration period, take the 5th and 95th percentiles of the errors, and add them to future forecasts. This is the idea behind split conformal prediction. Then check the coverage on a later test period:

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
X = pd.DataFrame({f"lag_{l}": y.shift(l) for l in [7, 14, 21]}).dropna(); target = y[X.index]
cal, test = X.index[(X.index >= 550) & (X.index < 640)], X.index[X.index >= 640]
model = Ridge(1.0).fit(X[X.index < 550], target[target.index < 550])
resid = target[cal] - model.predict(X.loc[cal])
lo, hi = np.quantile(resid, [0.05, 0.95])            # 90% interval from held-out errors
pred = model.predict(X.loc[test])
inside = ((target[test] >= pred + lo) & (target[test] <= pred + hi)).mean()
print("interval offsets:", round(lo, 1), "to", round(hi, 1), "  coverage on the test period:", round(inside, 3))

Output:

interval offsets: -40.3 to 50.2   coverage on the test period: 0.856

The interval was built to cover 90%, but on the test period it covers 85.6%. The reason is the trend: sales, and so the size of the errors, keep growing, so errors from an earlier period understate later ones. Fixes are to model the log of the series (so errors are relative), to use only recent errors, or to recompute the interval at each backtest step. Always report the coverage you actually achieve, by horizon, not just the nominal level.

Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

How would you give prediction intervals for a gradient boosting forecast?

The trap: "Gradient boosting can't give intervals."

Train quantile models (for example the 5th and 95th percentiles with a quantile loss), or use conformal prediction: compute errors on a held-out calibration period and add their quantiles to the point forecast. Either way, backtest the coverage by horizon, because errors usually grow with the horizon and with the series' level, and refresh the calibration regularly.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. Why compute autocorrelation on the changes rather than the raw series?

Removing the trend lets the seasonal peaks stand out.

2. The autocorrelation of daily changes peaks at 7, 14 and 21. Which lags should a model use?

The peaks show a weekly cycle.

3. A 90% interval built from held-out errors covers 86% of test values. What does that mean?

Coverage below the nominal level means it understates uncertainty.

4. Why might errors from an earlier period understate later errors?

Relative (log) errors or recent errors fix this.

5. What does split conformal prediction need?

Its quantiles of errors give the interval, for any model.

Part 6 · Intermediate topics · ~55 min

Lesson 27: Recommender Systems

Explicit and implicit feedback, bias baselines, neighbour-based collaborative filtering, matrix factorisation, ranking metrics, and cold start.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Represent explicit and implicit feedback as a sparse user–item matrix and build bias baselines
  • Compute item–item collaborative filtering with cosine similarity
  • Train a matrix factorisation model with stochastic gradient descent and explain its latent factors
  • Evaluate recommendations with ranking metrics such as precision@k, and handle cold start with content features
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 7: Gradient Descent — Gradient descent trains almost any model: compute the gradient of the loss, step against it, repeat. The learning rate controls the step size; too large diverges. Mini-batches make it fast on big data.
  • Lesson 11: k-Nearest Neighbours — kNN predicts from the $k$ most similar training examples, so it depends on distances — features must be scaled, and it struggles in very high dimensions.
  • Lesson 17: Dimensionality Reduction & PCA —

Where this fits: Uses the similarity and nearest-neighbour ideas of Lesson 11, the gradient descent of Lesson 7 and the low-rank thinking of PCA (Lesson 17) on the user–item matrix.

1.What recommender systems do

Every streaming service, online shop and social feed decides, for each person, which few items out of millions to show next. That's a recommender system, and it's one of the most commercially important uses of ML: a large share of what people watch and buy online comes from recommendations.

The data is usually a huge, mostly empty table of users × items. Most users have interacted with a tiny fraction of the items, and the task is to fill in the blanks: which unseen items would each user like? This lesson builds the main approaches from scratch: popularity baselines, content-based filtering, collaborative filtering (neighbours) and matrix factorisation, then covers how to evaluate rankings and the practical traps of cold start and feedback loops.

The core idea

People who agreed in the past tend to agree in the future. Collaborative filtering exploits this without knowing anything about the items themselves; matrix factorisation makes it scale by describing every user and item with a few hidden "taste" numbers learned from the ratings.

2.Explicit and implicit feedback

  • Explicit feedback: users tell you what they think (star ratings, thumbs up/down). Clear but scarce.
  • Implicit feedback: what users do (clicks, plays, purchases, watch time). Plentiful but noisy, and with no negatives: an unclicked item may be disliked, or simply never seen.

Most real systems run on implicit feedback. We'll use simulated star ratings so we can measure accuracy precisely: 300 users and 60 films, built from 3 hidden tastes per user and film, with each user having rated about 15% of the films.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# 300 users, 60 films. Each user and film has 3 hidden "tastes"; users rate about 15% of films
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_users, n_items, k = 300, 60, 3
U, V = rng.normal(size=(n_users, k)), rng.normal(size=(n_items, k))
popularity = rng.normal(0, 0.5, n_items)
true = 3.2 + U @ V.T * 0.6 + popularity + rng.normal(0, 0.4, (n_users, n_items))
R = np.clip(np.round(true), 1, 5)
mask = rng.random((n_users, n_items)) < 0.15
ratings = pd.DataFrame([(u, i, R[u, i]) for u, i in zip(*np.nonzero(mask))], columns=["user", "item", "rating"])
print(ratings.head(4).to_string(index=False))
print("ratings:", len(ratings), " share of the matrix filled:", round(mask.mean(), 3))

Output:

 user  item  rating
    0     0     3.0
    0     2     2.0
    0    10     4.0
    0    21     4.0
ratings: 2747  share of the matrix filled: 0.153

2,747 ratings fill just 15.3% of the 18,000 cells. Real systems are far sparser: often well under 1%.

3.Baselines: averages and biases

We hold out one rating per user to test on and measure the root mean squared error (RMSE) of the predicted ratings. The simplest predictors use averages:

# Hold out one rating per user (for evaluation) and train on the rest
test = ratings.groupby("user").sample(1, random_state=0)
train = ratings.drop(test.index)
mu = train.rating.mean()
item_mean = train.groupby("item").rating.mean()
user_bias = (train.rating - mu).groupby(train.user).mean()
rmse = lambda p: np.sqrt(np.mean((test.rating.to_numpy() - p) ** 2))
print("global mean      RMSE:", round(rmse(np.full(len(test), mu)), 3))
print("item average     RMSE:", round(rmse(test.item.map(item_mean).fillna(mu).to_numpy()), 3))
print("item + user bias RMSE:", round(rmse((test.item.map(item_mean).fillna(mu) + test.user.map(user_bias).fillna(0)).to_numpy()), 3))

Output:

global mean      RMSE: 1.077
item average     RMSE: 1.024
item + user bias RMSE: 1.057

Predicting the global average gives RMSE 1.077; each film's own average does better (1.024), because some films are simply better liked. Naively adding a "user bias" (how much each user rates above average) makes things worse here (1.057): with only about 9 ratings per user, that bias is noisy, and it double-counts the film effect (a user who happened to rate good films looks generous). Biases must be learned jointly and with regularization, which is exactly what matrix factorisation below does.

4.Collaborative filtering: neighbours

User-based collaborative filtering predicts your rating of a film from the ratings of users similar to you. Item-based filtering predicts it from your ratings of films similar to that film, where "similar films" are ones the same users rated alike. Similarity is usually cosine or Pearson correlation computed on centred ratings (each user's ratings minus their own average), so a harsh rater and a generous rater with the same tastes look alike:

$$\hat{r}_{ui} = \bar{r}_u + \frac{\sum_{j \in N(i)} \text{sim}(i, j)\,(r_{uj} - \bar{r}_u)}{\sum_{j \in N(i)} |\text{sim}(i, j)|}$$

# Item-item collaborative filtering: films are similar if the same users rate them alike
M = np.full((n_users, n_items), np.nan)
M[train.user, train.item] = train.rating
centred = M - np.nanmean(M, axis=1, keepdims=True)            # remove each user's personal scale
C = np.nan_to_num(centred)
norms = np.linalg.norm(C, axis=0) + 1e-9
S = (C.T @ C) / np.outer(norms, norms)                         # cosine similarity between films
np.fill_diagonal(S, 0)

def predict_item_item(u, i, k=10):
    rated = np.flatnonzero(~np.isnan(M[u]))
    top = rated[np.argsort(S[i, rated])[::-1][:k]]
    w = S[i, top]
    base = np.nanmean(M[u])
    return base + (w @ centred[u, top]) / (np.abs(w).sum() + 1e-9) if len(top) else mu

p_ii = np.array([predict_item_item(u, i) for u, i in zip(test.user, test.item)])
print("item-item CF     RMSE:", round(rmse(p_ii), 3))

Output:

item-item CF     RMSE: 1.012

Item-item collaborative filtering reaches RMSE 1.012: a little better than the baselines. With so few ratings per film (about 46), similarities between films are noisy; neighbour methods shine with much denser data. Item-based CF has been widely used in practice ("customers who bought this also bought…") because item similarities are stable and can be computed in advance.

5.Try it: recommendations from similar users

Rate a few films in the "You" row. The demo computes how similar your ratings are to each other user's, and predicts your rating of the films you haven't rated from the users who resemble you. Try rating the sci-fi films high and the romances low, then the reverse.

6.Matrix factorisation

Instead of comparing users directly, matrix factorisation gives every user a vector $\mathbf{p}_u$ and every item a vector $\mathbf{q}_i$ of $k$ hidden factors, plus a bias each, and predicts

$$\hat{r}_{ui} = \mu + b_u + b_i + \mathbf{p}_u\cdot\mathbf{q}_i$$

The factors are learned by minimising squared error on the known ratings, with L2 regularization (Lesson 10) to stop the many parameters from overfitting:

$$\min \sum_{(u,i)\ \text{known}} \big(r_{ui} - \hat{r}_{ui}\big)^2 + \lambda\big(\lVert\mathbf{p}_u\rVert^2 + \lVert\mathbf{q}_i\rVert^2 + b_u^2 + b_i^2\big)$$

It's the low-rank idea from the SVD (Lesson 2's "Going deeper"), adapted to a matrix with missing entries. The factors often end up meaning something ("action vs romance", "mainstream vs art-house") even though nobody labelled them. Below it's trained with stochastic gradient descent (Lesson 7), one rating at a time:

# Matrix factorisation with SGD: learn a vector for every user and film so that rating ≈ mu + b_u + b_i + p_u · q_i
def factorise(train, k=3, epochs=40, lr=0.02, reg=0.05, seed=0):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    P, Q = g.normal(0, 0.1, (n_users, k)), g.normal(0, 0.1, (n_items, k))
    bu, bi = np.zeros(n_users), np.zeros(n_items)
    data = train[["user", "item", "rating"]].to_numpy()
    for ep in range(epochs):
        for u, i, r in data[g.permutation(len(data))]:
            u, i = int(u), int(i)
            e = r - (mu + bu[u] + bi[i] + P[u] @ Q[i])
            bu[u] += lr * (e - reg * bu[u]); bi[i] += lr * (e - reg * bi[i])
            P[u], Q[i] = P[u] + lr * (e * Q[i] - reg * P[u]), Q[i] + lr * (e * P[u] - reg * Q[i])
    return P, Q, bu, bi

P, Q, bu, bi = factorise(train)
p_mf = mu + bu[test.user] + bi[test.item] + np.sum(P[test.user] * Q[test.item], axis=1)
print("matrix factorisation RMSE:", round(rmse(p_mf), 3))

Output:

matrix factorisation RMSE: 0.715
Worked example — one SGD update

Suppose $\mu = 3.5$, $b_u = 0.2$, $b_i = -0.1$, $\mathbf{p}_u = (0.5, 0.1)$, $\mathbf{q}_i = (0.4, -0.2)$, and the true rating is $r = 4$.

Prediction: $3.5 + 0.2 - 0.1 + (0.5 \times 0.4 + 0.1 \times (-0.2)) = 3.6 + 0.18 = 3.78$. Error: $e = 4 - 3.78 = 0.22$.

Update with learning rate $\eta = 0.1$ and $\lambda = 0$: $b_u \leftarrow 0.2 + 0.1 \times 0.22 = 0.222$; $\mathbf{p}_u \leftarrow \mathbf{p}_u + \eta e\,\mathbf{q}_i = (0.5 + 0.0088,\ 0.1 - 0.0044) = (0.5088, 0.0956)$. The user's vector moves slightly towards the film's, so their predicted rating rises.

Matrix factorisation cuts the RMSE to 0.715, far better than every method above, because the 3 learned factors match the hidden structure of the data. On real data the number of factors is a hyperparameter (often 20–200), tuned with the validation methods of Lesson 23. Libraries use alternating least squares (ALS: fix the items and solve for users exactly, then swap), which parallelises well; for implicit feedback, weighted ALS treats every unclicked item as a weak negative.

7.Evaluating recommendations: rankings, not ratings

Users see a short list, not predicted stars. What matters is whether the top few items are good, so ranking metrics are used:

  • Precision@k: the share of the top $k$ recommendations that are relevant.
  • Recall@k and hit rate@k: the share of relevant items (or of users with at least one) that appear in the top $k$.
  • NDCG and MAP: also reward putting relevant items higher in the list.

Because our data is simulated, we know every user's true rating for every film, so we can check the top 10 unseen films we'd recommend each user:

# Ranking quality: of the 10 unseen films we recommend, how many would the user really like (true rating 4 or 5)?
# (We can check this only because the data is simulated and we know every true rating.)
liked = R >= 4
def precision_at_10(score_fn):
    hits = []
    for u in range(n_users):
        scores = score_fn(u).astype(float).copy()
        scores[mask[u]] = -np.inf                                   # don't recommend films they've rated
        top = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:10]
        hits.append(liked[u, top].mean())
    return np.mean(hits)

pop = train.groupby("item").rating.mean().reindex(range(n_items), fill_value=mu).to_numpy()
rand = np.random.default_rng(1)
print("precision@10, random films:          ", round(precision_at_10(lambda u: rand.random(n_items)), 3))
print("precision@10, highest-rated films:   ", round(precision_at_10(lambda u: pop), 3))
print("precision@10, matrix factorisation:  ", round(precision_at_10(lambda u: bi + Q @ P[u]), 3))

Output:

precision@10, random films:           0.447
precision@10, highest-rated films:    0.671
precision@10, matrix factorisation:   0.912

Random films are liked 44.7% of the time (many films are decent). Recommending the highest-rated films to everyone, a popularity baseline, raises that to 67.1%. Matrix factorisation's personalised top 10 is liked 91.2% of the time. On real data you can't see true ratings for unseen items, so offline evaluation hides recent interactions (split by time, Lesson 5), and the final test is an online A/B test (Lesson 4's "Going deeper") on clicks, watch time or purchases.

8.Cold start, content and feedback loops

  • Cold start. A new user or a new item has no interactions, so collaborative methods can't place it. Fall back on popularity, ask new users a few questions, or use content-based features: an item's genre, text description (TF-IDF or embeddings, Lessons 12 and 19), price; a user's stated preferences. Hybrid systems combine both.
  • Two-stage systems. At scale, a fast retrieval stage picks a few hundred candidates (nearest neighbours of a user embedding, Lesson 11's "Going deeper"), then a ranking model (often gradient boosting or a neural network with many features) orders them.
  • Feedback loops and popularity bias. Users can only click what they're shown, so the system's own choices shape its future training data. Popular items get more exposure and look even more popular. Mix in some exploration (Lesson 28's Thompson sampling) and measure diversity and novelty, not just accuracy.
  • What to optimise. Clicks reward clickbait. Long-term satisfaction, return visits and explicit "not interested" signals are better guides.

9.In Python: content-based recommendations

When there are no interactions yet, item descriptions alone can drive recommendations. Here, Chennai Homes listings are recommended by the similarity of their descriptions (TF-IDF and cosine similarity), plus a small bonus for the same area:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
T = TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(df["description"])
sim = cosine_similarity(T) + 0.2 * (df["area"].to_numpy()[:, None] == df["area"].to_numpy()[None, :])
np.fill_diagonal(sim, -1)                         # never recommend the house itself
viewed = 5                                         # a buyer looked at house id 5
row = df.index[df.id == viewed][0]
top = np.argsort(sim[row])[::-1][:3]
print("viewed:", df.description[row])
print(df.loc[top, ["id", "area", "description"]].to_string(index=False))

Output:

viewed: new spacious villa with garden
 id      area                    description
 12    Suburb new spacious villa near school
  8 Outskirts    new large villa with garden
  6    Suburb     old villa needs renovation

A buyer who viewed house 5 ("new spacious villa with garden") is shown other new, spacious villas and houses with gardens first. This needs no ratings at all, so it works from the very first day, and it's easy to explain ("because you viewed…"). It can't discover surprising tastes, which is what collaborative methods add once interactions build up.

10.Running example: Chennai Homes

A buyer looks at a house; which others should the site show? Standardise size, bedrooms, distance, age and price, and recommend the homes with the highest cosine similarity. For the Central flat with id 2, the top matches are ids 11 and 1 (similarity 0.69 and 0.68), both nearby flats; for id 11 they are 1, 4 and 2. This is content-based recommendation: it works with no interaction history at all, which is how the cold-start problem is usually handled.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
cols = ["size_m2", "bedrooms", "dist_km", "age_yrs", "price_lakh"]
Z = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df[cols])
sim = cosine_similarity(Z)
np.fill_diagonal(sim, -1)
for viewed in [2, 11]:
    row = df.index[df.id == viewed][0]
    top = np.argsort(sim[row])[::-1][:3]
    print("viewed", viewed, "→ similar:", df.id.iloc[top].tolist(), " similarity", np.round(sim[row, top], 2).tolist())

Output:

viewed 2 → similar: [11, 1, 3]  similarity [0.69, 0.68, 0.33]
viewed 11 → similar: [1, 4, 2]  similarity [0.86, 0.74, 0.69]
Where this is used
  • Products, films, music and news recommendations
  • Job, property and course matching
  • Ranking search results and choosing which content to show next

Choose it when: Whenever many users interact with many items and you need to choose a few items for each user.

Think twice when: there are few items or no interaction history: then simple rules, popularity or content similarity are enough.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythLower rating error means better recommendations.

RealityUsers see a ranked top few; a model can have good RMSE but rank poorly. Evaluate rankings.

MythMissing ratings mean the user dislikes the item.

RealityMostly they haven't seen it. Treating every missing value as a zero biases the model.

MythMore recommendations of what someone liked is always better.

RealityNarrow feedback loops reduce diversity and discovery; good systems mix in exploration.

Responsible AI · Feedback loops and filter bubbles

A recommender learns from what it showed, so popular items get more popular and niche ones disappear, and users can be pushed towards ever more extreme content if that maximises clicks. Measure diversity, coverage and exposure for item creators, not just clicks; add exploration; and give users controls to see why something was shown and to change it.

11.Questions beginners often ask

What if I only have clicks or purchases, not ratings?

That's implicit feedback: treat interactions as positive signals and unobserved pairs as weak negatives, use methods built for it (weighted matrix factorisation, ranking losses) and evaluate with ranking metrics.

How many latent factors should I use?

Tune it on validation data: typically 10 to 200. More factors fit more detail but overfit sparse data, so tune regularisation at the same time.

How are recommenders built at very large scale?

Usually in two stages: a fast candidate generator (approximate nearest neighbours on embeddings) picks hundreds of items, then a ranking model with many features orders them.

How do I recommend to a brand-new user?

Use popularity, simple questions at sign-up, context (location, device) or content features, then switch to collaborative filtering as interactions arrive.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Evaluating on a random split that lets the model see a user's future interactions.
  • Treating unobserved user–item pairs as negative ratings.
  • Reporting RMSE only, when users experience a ranked list.
  • Forgetting to exclude items the user already has from their recommendations.
  • Comparing only with random recommendations instead of a popularity baseline.
Interview corner

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

What's the difference between collaborative filtering and content-based recommendation?

The trap: Calling them the same thing.

Collaborative filtering uses only interaction patterns (users who liked this also liked that), so it needs history. Content-based uses item features (text, category, price) to find similar items, so it works for new items. Production systems usually combine both.

Why is RMSE on ratings a poor way to evaluate a recommender?

The trap: Saying RMSE is fine because it's standard.

Users see a short ranked list, so what matters is whether the top few items are relevant: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG or hit rate on held-out interactions, split by time. RMSE weighs all items equally, including ones never shown, and ratings are missing not at random.

Explain matrix factorisation for recommendations.

The trap: Describing it as PCA on a filled-in matrix.

Each user and item gets a vector of k latent factors; the predicted rating is the global mean plus user and item biases plus the dot product of the vectors. It's fitted only on observed entries, with L2 regularisation, by SGD or alternating least squares. The factors capture tastes such as genre without being told.

How would you handle cold start for a new item?

The trap: "Wait until it has ratings."

Use its content features (text, category, price) to place it near similar items or to predict its latent factors, show it to a small exploration share of users, and update quickly as interactions arrive. For new users, use popularity, context and a few onboarding questions.

All 5 hidden questions for this lesson →

12.Key takeaways

  • Recommenders fill in a huge, sparse user × item matrix; most data is implicit feedback with no true negatives.
  • Start with popularity and bias baselines, which are strong and simple.
  • Collaborative filtering uses similar users or items, on centred ratings; it needs no item information.
  • Matrix factorisation learns low-dimensional user and item vectors with regularization; trained by SGD or ALS.
  • Evaluate with ranking metrics (precision@k, recall@k, NDCG), time-based splits and, finally, online A/B tests.
  • Handle cold start with content features, and watch for feedback loops and popularity bias.

13.Check your understanding

1. A user never clicked an item. In implicit feedback, that means…

Missing interactions mix "not interested" with "not shown", which is the central difficulty of implicit data.

2. Why are ratings centred (minus each user's average) before computing similarity?

Centring removes each user's personal rating scale.

3. In matrix factorisation, a predicted rating is…

$\hat{r}_{ui} = \mu + b_u + b_i + \mathbf{p}_u\cdot\mathbf{q}_i$.

4. A brand-new film has no ratings. Which method can still recommend it?

Collaborative methods need interactions; content features solve cold start.

5. Of the 10 films recommended to a user, 7 are relevant. What is precision@10?

Precision@k is relevant items in the top k divided by k. (Recall@k would depend on the total number relevant.)

14.Going deeper: alternating least squares and popularity bias

In plain wordsHow alternating least squares trains matrix factorisation by solving one small ridge regression per user and per item in turn, and how catalogue coverage and average popularity reveal a recommender that only pushes what's already popular.

Intermediate · skip on a first read

Two topics behind production recommenders: alternating least squares, the other standard way to train matrix factorisation, and how to measure whether a recommender only pushes what's already popular.

You'll need: this lesson, ridge regression from Lesson 10, and matrix products from Lesson 17.

Alternating least squares

Matrix factorisation's loss is hard to minimise for $P$ and $Q$ together, but if you fix the item factors $Q$, finding each user's vector is just a small ridge regression with a closed-form answer, $\mathbf{p}_u = (Q_u^\top Q_u + \lambda I)^{-1} Q_u^\top \mathbf{r}_u$, using only the items user $u$ rated. Then fix $P$ and solve for every item the same way. Alternating least squares (ALS) repeats these two steps:

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_users, n_items, k = 200, 40, 3
P_true, Q_true = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_users, k)), rng.normal(0, 1, (n_items, k))
R = P_true @ Q_true.T + rng.normal(0, 0.3, (n_users, n_items))
mask = rng.random((n_users, n_items)) < 0.2            # only 20% of ratings observed
test = (rng.random((n_users, n_items)) < 0.25) & mask
train = mask & ~test
P, Q, lam = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (n_users, k)), rng.normal(0, 0.1, (n_items, k)), 1.0
for sweep in range(1, 9):
    for u in range(n_users):                           # fix Q, solve a small ridge problem per user
        Qi = Q[train[u]]
        P[u] = np.linalg.solve(Qi.T @ Qi + lam * np.eye(k), Qi.T @ R[u, train[u]])
    for i in range(n_items):                           # fix P, solve per item
        Pu = P[train[:, i]]
        Q[i] = np.linalg.solve(Pu.T @ Pu + lam * np.eye(k), Pu.T @ R[train[:, i], i])
    if sweep in (1, 2, 4, 8):
        rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((R - P @ Q.T)[test] ** 2))
        print("sweep", sweep, " test RMSE", round(rmse, 3))

Output:

sweep 1  test RMSE 1.635
sweep 2  test RMSE 1.456
sweep 4  test RMSE 0.964
sweep 8  test RMSE 0.762

With 3 true factors and 20% of the ratings observed, the test RMSE falls from 1.635 after one sweep to 0.762 after eight. Every user's (and every item's) update is independent, so ALS parallelises very well, which is why Spark's recommender uses it. It also adapts neatly to implicit feedback, where every unobserved pair counts as a weak zero: the weighted version of Hu, Koren and Volinsky.

Measuring popularity bias

Accuracy metrics reward recommending popular items, because popular items are most likely to appear in anyone's held-out set. Two simple health checks: catalogue coverage (the share of items ever recommended to anyone) and the average popularity of recommended items:

popularity = train.sum(axis=0)                         # how many users interacted with each item
scores_pop = np.tile(popularity, (n_users, 1)).astype(float)
scores_mf = P @ Q.T
for name, S in [("popular", scores_pop), ("matrix factorisation", scores_mf)]:
    S = np.where(train, -np.inf, S)                    # don't recommend items already seen
    top = np.argsort(-S, axis=1)[:, :5]
    coverage = len(np.unique(top)) / n_items
    avg_pop = popularity[top].mean()
    print(f"{name:21s} catalogue coverage {coverage:.2f}   average popularity of recommended items {avg_pop:.1f}")
print("average popularity across all items:", round(popularity.mean(), 1))

Output:

popular               catalogue coverage 0.30   average popularity of recommended items 38.7
matrix factorisation  catalogue coverage 0.85   average popularity of recommended items 30.4
average popularity across all items: 29.2

Recommending the most popular items reaches only 30% of the catalogue, and their average popularity (38.7 users) is well above the catalogue's 29.2. Matrix factorisation recommends 85% of the items, with popularity (30.4) close to average. Track these alongside precision@k: a change that raises precision slightly but halves coverage can make the product worse for users and for the people who supply the items.

Interview corner · intermediate

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

SGD or ALS for matrix factorisation: how do you choose?

The trap: Saying one is always better.

SGD is simple, handles explicit ratings and extra terms (biases, side features) easily and is cheap per step, but needs a tuned learning rate. ALS has closed-form steps, needs no learning rate, parallelises across users and items, and handles implicit feedback with all unobserved pairs efficiently, which is why it's common on Spark. Both need regularisation tuned on validation data.

Check your understanding: going deeper

1. In ALS, with the item factors fixed, each user's vector is found by…

That's the closed-form step.

2. Why does ALS parallelise well?

All users can be solved at once, then all items.

3. A recommender's catalogue coverage is 0.1. What does that mean?

Coverage is the share of distinct items recommended.

4. Why do accuracy metrics tend to favour popular items?

Recommending them is a safe bet for the metric.

5. What's the ALS update for a user vector?

The ridge regression solution.

Part 6 · Intermediate topics · ~55 min

Lesson 28: Bayesian & Probabilistic ML

Priors and posteriors, Bayesian A/B tests, Bayesian linear regression, Gaussian processes, MCMC, and Thompson sampling.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Update a Beta prior with conversion data and answer decision questions such as P(B > A) and expected loss
  • Explain Bayesian linear regression's posterior and why its prediction intervals widen away from the data
  • Describe Gaussian processes and when their uncertainty is useful
  • Sample a posterior with the Metropolis algorithm and use posteriors to decide with Thompson sampling
Before you start

This lesson builds on:

  • Lesson 4: Probability & Statistics — Probabilities run from 0 to 1. Bayes' theorem turns $P(B\mid A)$ into $P(A\mid B)$. Mean and standard deviation summarise data; the z-score $(x-\mu)/\sigma$ standardises it.
  • Lesson 10: Overfitting, Regularization & Bias–Variance — Error = bias² + variance + noise. Regularization adds a penalty on weight size (L2 ridge shrinks weights; L1 lasso zeros some) to reduce variance; its strength is chosen by cross-validation.
  • Lesson 15: Support Vector Machines —

Where this fits: Builds on Bayes' theorem (Lesson 4), shows that ridge (Lesson 10) is a Bayesian posterior mean, and reuses the kernels of Lesson 15 in Gaussian processes.

1.Why think in probabilities about the model itself?

Most models you've built give one answer: one set of weights, one predicted price. But with 10 data points the weights are very uncertain, and with 10 million they're not, and a single number hides that difference. Bayesian machine learning treats everything unknown, including the model's parameters, as uncertain, describes that uncertainty with probability distributions, and updates them as data arrives.

That gives you things ordinary models don't: honest error bars on predictions, sensible behaviour with little data, a principled way to include prior knowledge, and decisions that weigh risks ("the chance that B is worse, and how much we'd lose"). This lesson builds the core tools from scratch: conjugate updating for A/B tests, Bayesian linear regression, Gaussian processes, MCMC sampling, and Thompson sampling for learning while deciding.

The core idea

Start with a prior (what's plausible before the data), multiply by the likelihood (how well each possibility explains the data), and you get the posterior: an updated belief about every possibility. Predictions and decisions then average over the whole posterior instead of trusting a single best guess.

2.Bayes' theorem for parameters

Lesson 4 used Bayes' theorem for events. For a model's parameters $\theta$ and data $D$ it reads:

$$p(\theta \mid D) = \frac{p(D \mid \theta)\,p(\theta)}{p(D)} \;\propto\; \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior}$$

Lesson 4's "Going deeper" showed three useful facts: maximising the likelihood alone gives the MLE; maximising the posterior gives the MAP estimate, which equals ridge or lasso for normal or Laplace priors; and with a conjugate prior, such as a Beta prior for a probability, the posterior has a simple closed form. This lesson uses the whole posterior, not just its peak.

3.A Bayesian A/B test

Lesson 4's "Going deeper" ran a classical test on a checkout page: A converted 120 of 2,400 visitors and B 156 of 2,400, with $p = 0.026$. The Bayesian version gives each page's conversion rate a Beta(1, 1) prior (every rate equally plausible) and updates it with the data. Then it simply asks the questions a manager cares about, by drawing many samples from the two posteriors:

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# A/B test the Bayesian way: Beta(1, 1) priors, then the observed conversions
a_conv, a_n, b_conv, b_n = 120, 2400, 156, 2400
post_a = stats.beta(1 + a_conv, 1 + a_n - a_conv)
post_b = stats.beta(1 + b_conv, 1 + b_n - b_conv)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
da, db = post_a.rvs(200000, random_state=rng), post_b.rvs(200000, random_state=rng)
print("95% credible interval, A:", np.round(post_a.ppf([0.025, 0.975]), 4))
print("95% credible interval, B:", np.round(post_b.ppf([0.025, 0.975]), 4))
print("probability that B converts better than A:", round(np.mean(db > da), 4))
print("expected lift if we switch to B:", round(np.mean(db - da), 4), "  risk (expected loss if B is actually worse):", round(np.mean(np.maximum(da - db, 0)), 5))

Output:

95% credible interval, A: [0.042  0.0595]
95% credible interval, B: [0.0558 0.0756]
probability that B converts better than A: 0.9869
expected lift if we switch to B: 0.015   risk (expected loss if B is actually worse): 3e-05
Worked example — the posterior by hand

A Beta($a$, $b$) prior plus $s$ successes and $f$ failures gives a Beta($a + s$, $b + f$) posterior. For page B: Beta($1 + 156$, $1 + 2{,}244$) = Beta(157, 2,245).

Its mean is $\frac{157}{157 + 2245} = \frac{157}{2402} \approx 0.0654$: very close to the observed $156/2400 = 0.065$, because 2,400 visitors overwhelm a weak prior.

Its standard deviation is $\sqrt{\frac{ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)}} = \sqrt{\frac{157 \times 2245}{2402^2 \times 2403}} \approx 0.0050$, so the rate is about $6.5\% \pm 1.0\%$ (two standard deviations), matching the credible interval above.

There's a 98.7% probability that B really converts better, the expected gain from switching is 1.5 percentage points, and the expected loss if B is actually worse is tiny (0.003 percentage points). These are direct answers about the thing you care about, unlike a p-value (Lesson 4's "Going deeper"). The price is that you must choose a prior; with plenty of data, reasonable priors give almost the same answer.

4.Try it: updating a belief

The grey curve is the prior belief about a conversion rate, centred on 10%; the green curve is the posterior after the visitors you add. Make the prior stronger and see how much more data it takes to move it. Add 100 visitors at a time and watch the curve narrow around 8%.

5.Bayesian linear regression

Give the weights of a linear regression a normal prior, $\mathbf{w} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2 I)$, and assume normal noise with variance $\sigma^2$. The posterior is again normal, with

$$\Sigma_{\text{post}} = \Big(\tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}X^\top X + \tfrac{1}{\tau^2}I\Big)^{-1}, \qquad \mathbf{m}_{\text{post}} = \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\,\Sigma_{\text{post}}X^\top\mathbf{y}$$

The posterior mean is exactly ridge regression with $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$ (Lesson 10). What's new is the covariance $\Sigma_{\text{post}}$: it says how uncertain each weight is, and it gives each prediction its own error bar, $\boldsymbol\phi^\top\Sigma_{\text{post}}\boldsymbol\phi + \sigma^2$, combining uncertainty about the line with the noise.

# Bayesian linear regression: a normal prior on the weights gives a full posterior, not just one line
x = np.array([0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 3.0, 3.5])
y = np.array([1.1, 1.9, 3.2, 5.8, 7.1])
X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])
sigma2, tau2 = 0.25, 10.0                                   # noise variance and prior variance of each weight
S_post = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X / sigma2 + np.eye(2) / tau2)  # posterior covariance
m_post = S_post @ X.T @ y / sigma2                          # posterior mean (= ridge with lambda = sigma2/tau2)
print("posterior mean (intercept, slope):", m_post.round(3))
print("posterior std  (intercept, slope):", np.sqrt(np.diag(S_post)).round(3))
for x_new in [2.0, 6.0]:
    phi = np.array([1, x_new])
    mean, var = phi @ m_post, phi @ S_post @ phi + sigma2
    print(f"x {x_new}: predicted y {mean:.2f}, 95% prediction interval [{mean - 1.96 * np.sqrt(var):.2f}, {mean + 1.96 * np.sqrt(var):.2f}]")

Output:

posterior mean (intercept, slope): [0.086 1.965]
posterior std  (intercept, slope): [0.425 0.192]
x 2.0: predicted y 4.02, 95% prediction interval [2.94, 5.09]
x 6.0: predicted y 11.88, 95% prediction interval [10.00, 13.75]

With five points, the slope is about $1.97 \pm 0.19$. The prediction interval at $x = 2$, inside the data, is about 2.1 units wide; at $x = 6$, beyond the data, it's about 3.8 units wide. The model knows it is extrapolating, which ordinary least squares can't tell you.

6.Gaussian processes

A Gaussian process (GP) goes further: instead of a distribution over a few weights, it puts a prior directly over functions, controlled by a kernel that says how similar nearby outputs are (the RBF kernel from Lesson 15). After seeing data, it predicts a mean and a standard deviation at every point. Lesson 23's "Going deeper" used one to drive Bayesian optimisation.

from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessRegressor
from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import RBF, WhiteKernel

# A Gaussian process: uncertainty grows away from the data
xs = np.array([1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8.0])[:, None]
ys = np.sin(xs[:, 0]) + np.random.default_rng(2).normal(0, 0.1, 6)
gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(RBF(1.0) + WhiteKernel(0.01), random_state=0).fit(xs, ys)
for q in [2.0, 4.5, 11.0]:
    m, s = gp.predict([[q]], return_std=True)
    print(f"x {q:4}: mean {m[0]:+.2f}, std {s[0]:.2f}")

Output:

x  2.0: mean +0.86, std 0.00
x  4.5: mean -1.19, std 0.45
x 11.0: mean -0.01, std 0.99

At $x = 2$, where there's data, the GP is confident (standard deviation about 0). At $x = 4.5$, in the gap between the two groups of points, its uncertainty rises to 0.45. At $x = 11$, far beyond all data, it falls back towards the prior: mean near 0 and standard deviation about 1. GPs are excellent for small, smooth problems (calibration curves, sensor data, experiment design) and give honest uncertainty, but exact GPs cost $O(n^3)$, so they're limited to a few thousand points without approximations.

7.When there's no formula: MCMC

Most posteriors have no neat closed form. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws samples from them anyway. The simplest version, the Metropolis algorithm: propose a small random move; if the posterior is higher there, accept it; if lower, accept it with probability equal to the ratio. The chain then visits each region in proportion to its posterior probability, and only ratios are needed, so the awkward normalising constant $p(D)$ cancels.

Here we estimate the centre of seven measurements, one of which (8.5) looks like a mistake. A Cauchy likelihood, which has heavy tails, makes the model robust to it:

# MCMC from scratch: sample a posterior that has no neat formula with the Metropolis algorithm
data = np.array([2.1, 2.9, 3.4, 2.2, 8.5, 3.0, 2.7])        # one suspicious value (8.5)
def log_post(mu):                                          # Cauchy likelihood (robust to outliers) and normal prior
    return np.sum(stats.cauchy.logpdf(data, loc=mu, scale=0.5)) + stats.norm.logpdf(mu, 0, 10)
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
mu, chain, accepted = 0.0, [], 0
for step in range(20000):
    prop = mu + rng.normal(0, 0.5)                         # propose a small random move
    if np.log(rng.random()) < log_post(prop) - log_post(mu):
        mu, accepted = prop, accepted + 1                  # accept with probability min(1, ratio)
    chain.append(mu)
chain = np.array(chain[2000:])                             # drop the warm-up
print("acceptance rate:", round(accepted / 20000, 2))
print("posterior mean of the centre:", round(chain.mean(), 2), "  95% interval:", np.round(np.percentile(chain, [2.5, 97.5]), 2))
print("ordinary mean of the data, for comparison:", round(data.mean(), 2))

Output:

acceptance rate: 0.52
posterior mean of the centre: 2.76   95% interval: [2.2  3.28]
ordinary mean of the data, for comparison: 3.54

About half of the proposals were accepted, a healthy rate. The posterior mean of the centre is 2.76 with a 95% interval of 2.2 to 3.28, while the ordinary mean (3.54) is dragged up by the outlier. Modern tools (Stan, PyMC, NumPyro) use far more efficient samplers such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and NUTS, but the idea is the same: write down the prior and likelihood, and let the sampler produce the posterior.

8.Deciding under uncertainty: Thompson sampling

A classical A/B test splits traffic evenly until it ends, so half the visitors keep seeing the worse page. A multi-armed bandit learns and earns at the same time. Thompson sampling is the Bayesian way: for each visitor, draw one plausible conversion rate for each design from its current posterior, show the design whose draw is highest, and update that design's posterior with the result. Uncertain designs sometimes win the draw (exploration); clearly good ones win most of the time (exploitation).

# Thompson sampling: a bandit that learns which of 3 page designs converts best while it runs
true_rates = np.array([0.04, 0.05, 0.065])
wins, losses = np.ones(3), np.ones(3)                      # Beta(1, 1) prior for each design
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
shown = np.zeros(3, int)
for visitor in range(10000):
    choice = np.argmax(rng.beta(wins, losses))             # sample a plausible rate for each, show the best
    shown[choice] += 1
    if rng.random() < true_rates[choice]: wins[choice] += 1
    else: losses[choice] += 1
print("visitors shown each design:", shown.tolist())
print("conversions:", int(wins.sum() - 3), "  versus a fixed even split (expected):", round(10000 * true_rates.mean()))

Output:

visitors shown each design: [354, 458, 9188]
conversions: 652   versus a fixed even split (expected): 517

With true rates of 4%, 5% and 6.5%, Thompson sampling quickly shifted traffic: 9,188 of the 10,000 visitors saw the best design. It earned 652 conversions, against about 517 for an even three-way split. Bandits are used for headlines, recommendations (Lesson 27's feedback loops) and ad selection. The trade-off is that the weaker designs get too little traffic for a precise comparison, so use a classical or Bayesian A/B test when you need an exact measurement, and a bandit when you need results now.

9.In Python: Bayesian ridge with uncertainty

Scikit-learn's BayesianRidge learns the noise and prior variances from the data and returns a standard deviation with every prediction:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import BayesianRidge

df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
X, y = df[["size_m2", "dist_km", "age_yrs"]], df["price_lakh"]
model = BayesianRidge().fit(X, y)
new = pd.DataFrame({"size_m2": [100, 200], "dist_km": [8, 30], "age_yrs": [5, 1]})
mean, std = model.predict(new, return_std=True)
for (_, h), m, s in zip(new.iterrows(), mean, std):
    print(f"{h.size_m2:.0f} m², {h.dist_km:.0f} km, {h.age_yrs:.0f} yrs: {m:.0f} lakh ± {1.96 * s:.0f} (95%)")

Output:

100 m², 8 km, 5 yrs: 79 lakh ± 12 (95%)
200 m², 30 km, 1 yrs: 111 lakh ± 20 (95%)

For a typical home (100 m², 8 km, 5 years), the model gives a prediction with a modest interval; for an unusual one (200 m², 30 km away), outside the range of the 12 training homes, the interval is much wider. Communicating that kind of uncertainty is often worth more than a slightly more accurate point prediction.

10.Running example: Chennai Homes

How sure can we be about which areas sell fast, with only 12 homes? Give each area's "sold fast" rate a Beta(1, 1) prior and update it with the area's homes. Central sold 3 of 4 fast (posterior mean 0.67) and the Suburb 3 of 5 (0.57), but their 90% credible intervals, about 0.34 to 0.92 and 0.27 to 0.85, overlap heavily. The Outskirts sold none of 3, yet the posterior still allows rates up to about 0.53. With this little data, the intervals are the honest answer.

Same 12 houses as Lesson 1. With so little data, treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, not as reliable estimates.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")   # download it from Lesson 1
from scipy import stats
for area, g in df.groupby("area"):
    a, b = 1 + g.sold_fast.sum(), 1 + (1 - g.sold_fast).sum()     # Beta(1, 1) prior
    lo, hi = stats.beta(a, b).ppf([0.05, 0.95])
    print(f"{area:9s} sold fast {g.sold_fast.sum()} of {len(g)}  posterior mean {a / (a + b):.2f}  90% interval [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]")

Output:

Central   sold fast 3 of 4  posterior mean 0.67  90% interval [0.34, 0.92]
Outskirts sold fast 0 of 3  posterior mean 0.20  90% interval [0.01, 0.53]
Suburb    sold fast 3 of 5  posterior mean 0.57  90% interval [0.27, 0.85]
Where this is used
  • A/B tests that report the probability one version is better
  • Small-data science and engineering models that need honest error bars
  • Bandits for headlines and offers, and Bayesian optimisation of expensive experiments

Choose it when: Whenever uncertainty matters to the decision, data is limited, or you have real prior knowledge to include.

Think twice when: you have huge data and only need point predictions: then the posterior is narrow and ordinary models are simpler and faster.

Misconceptions to unlearn

MythBayesian methods need lots of computation.

RealityConjugate models such as the Beta A/B test are one line of arithmetic; MCMC is only needed when there's no formula.

MythThe prior lets you get any answer you want.

RealityWith enough data, reasonable priors converge; a prior that changes the conclusion is a sign the data is weak, which is worth knowing.

MythA credible interval and a confidence interval are the same thing.

RealityOnly a credible interval is a direct probability statement about the parameter.

Responsible AI · Priors and uncertainty in high-stakes decisions

A prior encodes assumptions, and in decisions about people (credit, health, policing) a prior built from biased history carries that bias into every new case. State priors openly and test how much they move conclusions. Equally, uncertainty is a responsibility: when an interval is wide, say so, and route the decision to a person rather than presenting a guess as a fact.

11.Questions beginners often ask

Isn't choosing a prior subjective?

Somewhat, but it's explicit and can be checked: try a few reasonable priors and see whether the conclusion changes. With plenty of data the likelihood dominates and they agree.

What's the difference between a credible interval and a confidence interval?

A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% probability given the data and prior. A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that covers the true value in 95% of repeated samples; it isn't a probability statement about this interval.

Which tools do people use for Bayesian modelling?

PyMC, Stan and NumPyro for general models with MCMC or variational inference; scikit-learn's BayesianRidge and GaussianProcessRegressor for the common simple cases.

Can neural networks be Bayesian?

Approximately: ensembles of networks, Monte Carlo dropout and variational methods give useful uncertainty estimates, though exact Bayesian deep learning is too expensive.

Common mistakes to avoid
  • Using a strong prior without checking how much it changes the result.
  • Reporting only the posterior mean and throwing away the uncertainty.
  • Running MCMC without checking the acceptance rate or whether the chain has settled.
  • Using a bandit when you need an unbiased, precise comparison of every option.
  • Using an exact Gaussian process on hundreds of thousands of points.
Interview corner

Hidden questions — answer in your head first, then open.

What's the difference between a credible interval and a confidence interval?

The trap: Saying they're the same.

A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% probability given the data and the prior. A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that covers the true value in 95% of repeated samples; this particular interval either contains it or doesn't.

How would you run a Bayesian A/B test on conversion rates?

The trap: Only computing a p-value.

Give each version's rate a Beta prior, update it to Beta(a + conversions, b + non-conversions), and draw samples from both posteriors to estimate P(B > A), the expected lift and the expected loss of choosing B. Decide when the expected loss falls below a threshold, and check that reasonable priors give the same decision.

Why is ridge regression a Bayesian method in disguise?

The trap: Saying it isn't related.

With Gaussian noise of variance σ² and a Gaussian prior N(0, τ²) on the weights, the posterior mean (and MAP) of the weights is the ridge solution with λ = σ²/τ². A Laplace prior gives lasso at the MAP. The full Bayesian treatment also gives the posterior covariance, and so uncertainty for each prediction.

What's Thompson sampling, and when would you use it instead of an A/B test?

The trap: Calling it random allocation.

For each decision, sample a plausible value of each option's reward from its posterior and choose the best sample; update the chosen option's posterior with the result. It shifts traffic to better options while still exploring uncertain ones. Use it when you want to earn while learning (headlines, offers); use an A/B test when you need an unbiased, precise estimate of each option.
